parts.problemMd:
An organic compound **X** reacts with aqueous sodium carbonate to produce effervescence. The infrared spectrum of **X** is shown.

![Graph of transmittance versus wavenumbers in cm⁻¹. Peaks and troughs indicate spectral data, with transmittance ranging from 0 to 1.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/1-structure-bonding-and-introduction-to-organic-chemistry/1-8-introductory-organic-chemistry/assets/001-graph-of-transmittance-versus-wavenumbers-in-cm-.png)

Which is compound **X**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Three pieces of evidence identify X:
- Effervescence with Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>

  - This means that CO<sub>2</sub> is released
  - Therefore, X is a carboxylic acid as alcohols, aldehydes and ketones do not react
- Sharp absorption at 1710 cm<sup>-1</sup>

  - This is a characteristic peak for a C=O group, found in aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids or esters
- Very broad absorption 3300–2500 cm<sup>-1</sup>

  - This is a characteristic peak of a carboxylic acid O–H as it is much broader and lower than the alcohol O–H at 3750–3200 cm<sup>–¹</sup>

- All three pieces of evidence point to the carboxylic acid, propanoic acid / CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH.

**A** is incorrect as propanal is an aldehyde. It has a sharp C=O at ~1720 cm<sup>–¹</sup> but **no** broad O–H absorption below 3200 cm<sup>–¹</sup>. It also does not react with Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>.

**C** is incorrect as propan-1-ol is an alcohol. It has a broad O–H at 3750–3200 cm<sup>–¹</sup> (alcohol range, not carboxylic acid range) and no C=O peak. It also does not react with Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>.

**D** is incorrect as propanone is a ketone. It has a sharp C=O at ~1715 cm<sup>–¹</sup> but no O–H, and it does not react with Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>.

> **[exam-tip]**
> To identify a carboxylic acid on paper 2, combine three diagnostic signals:
> 
> - Reaction with Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> or NaHCO<sub>3</sub>
> 
> - Effervescence shows that CO<sub>2</sub> is released, which is unique to carboxylic acids.
> - IR: very broad O–H at 3300–2500 cm<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> - This is much broader and extends lower than the alcohol O–H at 3750–3200 cm<sup>–¹</sup>.
> - Mixing these two up is a common IR mistake flagged in examiner reports.
> - IR: sharp C=O at ~1710 cm<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> - This is also present in aldehydes, ketones and esters, so it's not diagnostic on its own.
> 
> When writing the functional group name in structured questions, always write "carboxylic acid" in full. Mark schemes explicitly reject just "acid", you need the full term.
> 
> When quoting an IR peak, always give both the bond **AND **the wavenumber range. Examiner reports flagged candidates who gave only one of the two as a recurring mark-loss. Full-mark phrasing looks like: "O–H in a carboxylic acid at 3300–2500 cm<sup>-1</sup>".

parts.problemMd:

**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- The propagation step involves a bromine free radical attacking cyclopentane:

  - C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> + Br• → C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>9</sub>• + HBr
- In the termination step, two free radicals react:

  - C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>9</sub>• + Br• → C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>9</sub>Br
- This gives the overall reaction:

  - C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>9</sub>Br + HBr

**C** is incorrect as many more propagation than termination reactions occur

**D** is incorrect as additional substitution products are likely to form

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the amount of water of crystallisation in hydrated magnesium sulfate, MgSO4 **·x**H2O. The value of **x** in the formula was determined in an experiment. **Procedure** | Step **1** | A crucible was weighed, a spatula measure of hydrated magnesium sulfate was added and the crucible was reweighed. | |---|---| | Step** 2** | The crucible containing the hydrated magnesium sulfate was heated using the apparatus shown.

Give your answer to the nearest whole number. [Ar values: H = 1.0 O = 16.0 Mg = 24.3 S = 32.1] **(4)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) The completed table is:

| **Measurement** | **Mass / g** |
|---|---|
| Mass of empty crucible | 21.21 |
| Mass of crucible and hydrated magnesium sulfate before heating | 26.71 |
| Mass of crucible and magnesium sulfate after heating for two minutes | 24.12 |
| Mass of magnesium sulfate after heating for two minutes | **Final answer:** **2.91** |
| Mass of water lost | **Final answer:** **2.59** |

- Both masses required; **[1 mark]**

ii) The value of **x** in MgSO<sub>4</sub> ·**x**H<sub>2</sub>O is:

- *M*<sub>r</sub> of MgSO<sub>4</sub>: (24.3 + 32.1 + (4 × 16)) = 120.4; **[1 mark]**
- Moles of MgSO<sub>4</sub>: (2.91 ÷ 120.4) = 0.024169 / 2.4169 × 10<sup>-2</sup> (mol); **[1 mark]**
- Moles of H<sub>2</sub>O: (2.59 ÷ 18) = 0.14389 / 1.4389 × 10<sup>-1 (</sup>mol); **[1 mark]**
- Ratio of moles of water to moles of magnesium sulfate to the nearest whole number: (0.1438889 ÷ 0.0241694) = 5.9533:1 x = 6; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *To calculate the mass of the magnesium sulfate after heating: *

  - *mass of crucible and magnesium sulfate after heating for two minutes - mass of empty crucible*
- *To calculate the mass of water lost:*

  - *mass of crucible and magnesium sulfate after heating for two minutes - Mass of crucible and hydrated magnesium sulfate before heating*
- *The value of x is found the same way you complete an empirical formula calculation *

  - *Find the mass of both the magnesium sulfate and water *
  - *Find the moles of both the magnesium sulfate and water *

parts.problemMd:
An organic compound, **X**, contains only the elements carbon and hydrogen.

When 0.560 g of **X** is completely combusted in excess oxygen, 1.760 g of carbon dioxide and 0.720 g of water are produced.

Calculate the empirical formula of **X**. You must show all your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the empirical formula of **X**:

- All carbon in CO<sub>2</sub> originates from X (carbon is conserved during combustion), so the mass of C in the sample equals the mass of C in 1.760 g of CO<sub>2</sub>:

m(C) = (12/44) × 1.760 = **0.480 g**

- All hydrogen in H<sub>2</sub>O originates from X, by the same reasoning:

m(H) = (2/18) × 0.720 = **0.080 g**

- Mass balance check: m(C) + m(H) = 0.480 + 0.080 = 0.560 g, which equals the mass of X — confirming X contains no oxygen and is a pure hydrocarbon. **[1 mark]**

- The empirical formula represents the simplest mole ratio of atoms, so convert each mass into moles by dividing by the relative atomic mass:

| Element | Mass (g) | ÷ A<sub>r</sub> | Moles |
|---|---|---|---|
| C | 0.480 | ÷ 12 | 0.0400 |
| H | 0.080 | ÷ 1 | 0.0800 |

**[1 mark]**

- Divide each by the smallest mole value (0.0400) to scale the ratio to whole numbers:

C : H = 0.0400/0.0400 : 0.0800/0.0400 = 1 : 2

- The empirical formula of **X** is:

**CH~2~** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for **m(C) = 0.480 g AND m(H) = 0.080 g** (both required)
> 
> Method mark only: correct substitutions (12/44) × 1.760 AND (2/18) × 0.720 if a numerical slip leads to incorrect masses
> 
> 1 mark for **moles of C = 0.0400 AND moles of H = 0.0800** (both required; ecf from incorrect masses)
> 
> 1 mark for **empirical formula CH~2~** (ecf from mole values, provided the simplest whole-number ratio is taken)
> 
> Reject any answer containing oxygen — the mass balance shows X is a pure hydrocarbon
> 
> Reject use of atomic numbers (C = 6, H = 1) instead of relative atomic masses
> 
> No working scores 0 (per Edexcel convention)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The mass balance (m(C) + m(H) = m(X)) is the step that tells you X contains no oxygen. If the sum had been less than 0.560 g, the difference would be the mass of oxygen, found by **subtraction**, never directly from the CO<sub>2</sub> or H<sub>2</sub>O (the oxygen in those products comes from the excess O<sub>2</sub> supplied, not from X).
> 
> Set out your moles conversion as a table and divide every value by the smallest. Using atomic numbers instead of A<sub>r</sub> values is the most common error in empirical formula questions.

parts.problemMd:
The relative molecular mass, *M*<sub>r</sub>, of **X** is 56.

Deduce the molecular formula of **X**.
parts.solutionMd:
To deduce the molecular formula of **X**:

- The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, so first find the empirical formula mass of CH<sub>2</sub>:

12 + 2(1) = 14

- Find n by dividing the molecular mass by the empirical formula mass:

n = M<sub>r</sub>(molecule) ÷ M<sub>r</sub>(empirical formula) = 56 ÷ 14 = 4 **[1 mark]**

- Multiply every subscript in the empirical formula by n = 4:

**C**<sub>**4**</sub>**H**<sub>**8**</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for **n = 56 ÷ 14 = 4**
> 
> Accept calculation only, even if empirical formula mass is not separately stated
> 
> 1 mark for **molecular formula C**<sub>**4**</sub>**H**<sub>**8**</sub>
> 
> ecf from incorrect empirical formula in part (a), provided the method is correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always SHOW the step that links empirical and molecular formulas:
> 
> n = M<sub>r</sub> ÷ (empirical formula mass)
> 
> Writing the molecular formula with no working risks losing the method mark even if the final answer is correct. Once you have n, multiply EVERY subscript in the empirical formula by it.

parts.problemMd:
When **X** is added to bromine water, the orange colour decolourises.

i) Name the functional group in **X** responsible for this reaction.

[1]

ii) Given that **X** has the C=C double bond at the end of the carbon chain, draw the displayed formula of **X**.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
**i)**

- The functional group responsible is the **carbon–carbon double bond (C=C / alkene group)**. **[1 mark]**

**ii)**

- The straight-chain alkene with molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> and the C=C at the end of the carbon chain is **but-1-ene**, CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>:

![Structural formula of but-1-ene, showing four carbon atoms with single and double bonds, and hydrogen atoms attached.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/1-structure-bonding-and-introduction-to-organic-chemistry/1-1-formulae-and-equations/assets/001-structural-formula-of-but-1-ene-showing-four-car.png)

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) 1 mark for **C=C / carbon–carbon double bond / alkene group / alkene functional group**
> 
> Accept "double bond" only if context makes clear it refers to the C=C
> 
> Reject "covalent bond" alone
> 
> Reject "hydroxyl" or any non-alkene group
> 
> ii) 1 mark for correct displayed formula of **but-1-ene** (CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>)
> 
> All 8 hydrogens must be shown with bonds (displayed formula required)
> 
> The C=C must be shown as a double bond between C1 and C2 (terminal position)
> 
> Reject but-2-ene (C=C in middle of chain — does not match "at the end of the chain")
> 
> Reject 2-methylpropene (branched, not straight-chain)
> 
> Reject skeletal or condensed formulae

> **[exam-tip]**
> The standard observation when an alkene reacts with bromine water is **orange (or red-brown) → colourless** — never write "clear" (a clear solution can still be coloured). For displayed formulae every bond and every hydrogen must be drawn explicitly; a skeletal formula scores zero. The C=C at the end of a chain produces a terminal alkene (but-1-ene); a C=C in the middle gives but-2-ene, which would additionally need E/Z labelling.

![Structural formula of isobutane, displaying four carbon atoms bonded in a branched chain, with hydrogen atoms filling the remaining valences.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/1-structure-bonding-and-introduction-to-organic-chemistry/1-1-formulae-and-equations/assets/002-structural-formula-of-isobutane-displaying-four-.png)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark each (max 2) for any TWO correctly drawn displayed formulae of:
> 
> - **but-2-ene** — CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub> (positional isomer, internal C=C)
> - **2-methylpropene** — (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH<sub>2</sub> (chain isomer, branched alkene)

parts.problemMd:
This question is about iron and some of its compounds.

Complete the table to show the numbers of subatomic particles in <sup>56</sup>Fe<sup>2+</sup>.

| **Number of protons** | **Number of neutrons** | **Number of electrons** |
|---|---|---|
|   |   |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The numbers of subatomic particles in <sup>56</sup>Fe<sup>2+</sup> are:

- Protons = 26 
**AND**
Neutrons = 30 
**AND **
Electrons = 24; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *Iron has an atomic number of 26*
- *This means that it normally has 26 protons and 26 electrons*

  - *Since this is a 2+ ion, it has lost 2 electrons *

parts.problemMd:
A sample of iron contains the following isotopes.

|---|---|

| <sup>56</sup>Fe | 91.68 |
| <sup>57</sup>Fe | 2.17 |
| <sup>58</sup>Fe | 0.31 |

Calculate the relative atomic mass of this sample of iron. Give your answer to** three** significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
The relative atomic mass of this sample of iron to** three** significant figures is:

- 55.9; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
The ionic equation, including state symbols, for the reaction of magnesium with aqueous iron(II) sulfate in a displacement reaction is:

Mg (s) + Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) → Fe (s) + Mg<sup>2+</sup> (aq)

- All state symbols correct; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
25.00 g of a compound contains 6.98 g of iron and 6.03 g of sulfur.

The remaining mass is oxygen.

Calculate the **empirical** formula of this compound.

[A<sub>r</sub> values: O = 16.0 S = 32.1 Fe = 55.8]
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the **empirical** formula of this compound:

- Mass of oxygen = 11.99 (g)
**AND**
Evidence of workings to calculate moles for Fe, S and O; **[1 mark]**
- Moles of Fe = 0.12509
**AND**
Moles of S = 0.18785
**AND**
Moles of O = 0.74938; **[1 mark]**
- Simplest whole number ratio = 2Fe : 3S : 12O
**AND**
Empirical formula = Fe<sub>2</sub>S<sub>3</sub>O<sub>12</sub> **OR **Fe<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *To calculate the empirical formula of the compound, you need to know the mass of oxygen 25.00 - 6.98 - 6.03 = 11.99 g*
- *You can then complete a standard empirical formula calculation:* | > *Elements * | > *Fe* | > *S* | > *O* |
|---|---|---|---|
| > *Mass* | > *6.98* | > *6.03* | > *11.99* |
| > *A*<sub>*r*</sub>* * | > *55.8* | > *32.1* | > *16.0* |
| > *Moles = *$\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{A_{r}}$ | > $\frac{6.98}{55.8}$* = 0.12509* | > $\frac{6.03}{32.1}$* = 0.18785* | > $\frac{11.99}{16.0}$* = 0.74398* |
| > *Ratio* | > $\frac{0.12509}{0.12509}$* = 1* | > $\frac{0.18785}{0.12509}$* = 1.5* | > $\frac{0.74938}{0.12509}$* = 6* |
| > *Whole number ratio * | > *2* | > *3* | > *12* |
- *This gives a final empirical formula of Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*S*<sub>*3*</sub>*O*<sub>*12*</sub>* *

parts.problemMd:
When 6.95 g of FeSO<sub>4</sub>•**x**H<sub>2</sub>O is heated, 2.00 g of iron(III) oxide, 0.80 g of sulfur dioxide and 1.00 g of sulfur trioxide are produced. 
The only other product is water.

Deduce the overall equation for the reaction using these data. State symbols are not required.

You **must **show your working.

[*A*<sub>r</sub> values: H = 1.0   O = 16.0    S = 32.1    Fe = 55.8]
parts.solutionMd:
To deduce the overall equation for the reaction:

- Moles of Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> = 0.012531 **OR **1.2531 x 10<sup>-2</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- Moles of SO<sub>2</sub> = 0.0124805 **OR **1.24805 x 10<sup>−2</sup> 
**AND**
Moles of SO<sub>3</sub> = 0.012484 **OR** 1.2484 x 10<sup>−2</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- Mass of H<sub>2</sub>O = 3.15 (g)
**AND**
Moles of H<sub>2</sub>O = 0.175; **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, **x** = 7; **[1 mark]**
- 2FeSO<sub>4</sub>•7H<sub>2</sub>O → Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + SO<sub>2</sub> + SO<sub>3</sub> + 14H<sub>2</sub>O; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *The first line of the question gives you an initial unbalanced chemical equation  FeSO*<sub>*4*</sub>*•**x**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O → Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*3*</sub>* + SO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + SO*<sub>*3*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *You have the information to calculate the moles of Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*3*</sub>*, SO*<sub>*2*</sub>*, SO*<sub>*3*</sub>* and H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O *
*Fe*<sub>2</sub>*O*<sub>3</sub>* = *$\frac{2.00}{159.6}$* = 0.012531 *
*SO*<sub>2</sub>* = *$\frac{0.80}{64.1}$* = 0.0124805 *
*SO*<sub>3</sub>* = *$\frac{1.00}{80.1}$* = 0.012484 *
*H*<sub>2</sub>*O = *$\frac{3.15}{18}$* = 0.175*
- *This gives a ratio of 1SO*<sub>*2*</sub>* : 1SO*<sub>*3*</sub>* : 14H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O for the products*

  - *But the iron-based reactant has one iron atom, while the iron product is Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*3*</sub>* with two iron atoms*
  - *This means that 2FeSO*<sub>*4*</sub>*•**x**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O make 14 water molecules*
  - *Therefore, **x** must be 7, i.e. FeSO*<sub>*4*</sub>*•**7**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *This information can now be used to build the complete equation **2**FeSO*<sub>*4*</sub>*•**7**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O → Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*3*</sub>* + SO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + SO*<sub>*3*</sub>* + **14**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*

A sample of octadecane can be obtained from a mixture of alkanes by:

The equation for the complete combustion of butane is shown.

2C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>(g) + 13O<sub>2</sub>(g) → 8CO<sub>2</sub>(g) + 10H<sub>2</sub>O(l)

35.0 cm<sup>3</sup> butane is completely burned in 300 cm<sup>3</sup> oxygen.

Calculate the final total volume of gas in cm<sup>3</sup>.

All volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure.

**(3)**

ii) Explain the main hazard when using butane as a fuel in a portable heater in an enclosed space.

**(2)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) The final total volume of gas in cm<sup>3</sup> is:

- Volume of CO<sub>2</sub> produced: 4 x 35 = 140 (cm<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**
- Volume of oxygen used: 6.5 x 35 = 227.5 / 228 (cm<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**
- Total volume of gas remaining: 300 - 227.5 + 140 (cm<sup>3</sup>) =212.5 / 213 (cm<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**

Alternative method:

- Moles of CO<sub>2</sub> produced: 35 / 24000 = 1.4583 x 10<sup>-3</sup> / 1.458 x 10<sup>-3</sup> / 1.46 x 10<sup>-3</sup> 1.4583 x 10<sup>-3</sup> x 4 = 5.8333 x 10<sup>-3</sup> / 5.83 x 10<sup>-3</sup> **OR **5.84 x 10<sup>-3</sup> if rounded previously; **[1 mark]**
- Moles of oxygen remaining: 300 / 24000 = 1.25 x 10<sup>-2</sup> (1.46 x 10<sup>-3</sup> ) x 6.5 = 9.49 x 10<sup>-3</sup> moles (1.25 x 10<sup>-2 </sup>) – (9.49 x 10<sup>-3</sup>) = 3.01 x 10<sup>-3</sup> (mol); **[1 mark]**
- Total volume remaining: [(5.83 x 10<sup>-3 </sup>) + (3.01 x 10<sup>-3</sup> )] x 24000 = 212.16 / 212 (cm<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**

ii) The main hazard when using butane as a fuel in a portable heater in an enclosed space is:

- **Carbon monoxide **may be produced (incomplete combustion may occur); **[1 mark]**
- Which is toxic / combines(irreversibly) with haemoglobin; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *Careful**: The answer needs to be given in cm*<sup>*3*</sup>*, so when calculating the volume, use 24 000 as the molar volume*
- *As this is complete combustion, there is an excess of oxygen so all of the butane will be used up*
- *The final volume of gas will contain the CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* produced and any oxygen remaining*
- *As molar gas volumes are the same under the same conditions you can use the volumes and molar ratios to work out the volumes of gases used up or produced*

  - *Carbon dioxide has 4 times the volume of butane = 4 x 35 = 140 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
  - *The volume of oxygen used up is 13/2 times greater than the volume of butane = 35 x 13/2 = 227.5 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
  - *Initially there was 300 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of oxygen so the oxygen remaining = 300 - 227.5 = 72.5 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
  
    - *So the total volume is 140 + 72.5 = 212.5 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
- *The alternative method uses moles:*

  - *The number of moles of CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* produced will be 4 times the number of moles of butane that combusted as it is a 2:8 or 1:4 molar ratio*
  - *The molar ratio of butane : oxygen is 2 : 13, so the number of moles of oxygen used = number of moles of butane x *$\frac{13}{2}$
  - *The number of moles of oxygen remaining = the number of moles of oxygen in 300 cm*<sup>*3 *</sup>*- moles of oxygen used up*
- *For part (ii), you must state that it is carbon monoxide that is the main hazard: whilst particulates are produced, they are not the main hazard, so you would not be awarded the mark*

  - *The second mark is only awarded if there is a clear link to the gas being produced*
  - *Any references to the flammability of butane, global warming or greenhouse gases would be ignored*
  - *If no other mark has been awarded you would gain 1 mark for stating that carbon dioxide causes suffocation*

parts.solutionMd:
The equation for the incomplete combustion of **one mole **of propene to form carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, carbon and water as the only products is:

C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6 </sub>(g) + 3O<sub>2 </sub>(g) → CO<sub>2 </sub>(g) + CO (g) + C (s) + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

- State symbols; **[1 mark]**

  - *C*<sub>*3*</sub>*H*<sub>*6 *</sub>* + O*<sub>*2 *</sub>* → CO*<sub>*2 *</sub>* + CO + C + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O *
- *When balancing combustion reactions, balance the carbon atoms first:*

  - *The carbon atoms are already balanced*
- *Next, balance the hydrogen atoms:*

  - *C*<sub>*3*</sub>*H*<sub>*6 *</sub>* + O*<sub>*2 *</sub>* → CO*<sub>*2 *</sub>* + CO + C + **3**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O *
- *Finally, balance the oxygen atoms:*

  - *C*<sub>*3*</sub>*H*<sub>*6 *</sub>* + **3**O*<sub>*2 *</sub>* → CO*<sub>*2 *</sub>* + CO + C + 3H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O *

  - *C*<sub>*3*</sub>*H*<sub>*6 *</sub>*(g) + 3O*<sub>*2 *</sub>*(g) → CO*<sub>*2 *</sub>*(g) + CO (g) + C (s) + 3H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O (l)*

An alkene has a molar mass of 112 g mol<sup>−1</sup>.

parts.solutionMd:
The molecular formula of the alkene with a molar mass of 112 g mol<sup>−1</sup> is:

- C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>16</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *The general formula of an alkene is C*<sub>*n*</sub>*H*<sub>*2n*</sub>* *
- *There are twice as many hydrogen atoms as there are carbon atoms, giving the empirical formula of an alkene as CH*<sub>*2*</sub>
- *The molecular formula can be found by dividing the relative formula mass of the molecular formula by the relative formula mass of the empirical formula*
- *The** M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of the empirical formula = 12.0 + (2 x 1.0) = 14.0 g mol*<sup>*-1*</sup>

  - *You can use this piece of information to determine the molecular formula *$\frac{112}{14}$*= 8*
  - *So, there are 8 CH*<sub>*2*</sub>* units in the alkene with a molar mass of 112 g mol*<sup>*−1*</sup>* *
  - *This means that it contains 8 carbon atoms and 16 hydrogen atoms, i.e. C*<sub>*8*</sub>*H*<sub>*16*</sub>* *

parts.solutionMd:

**OR **
*n* = $\frac{\left(1 . 24 \times 10^{5}\right) \times \left(6 \times 10^{- 4}\right)}{8 . 31 \times 298}$; **[1 mark]**

**AND **
There are 3 double bonds; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

  - *This means that you have to convert the volume to m*<sup>*3*</sup>*  *$\frac{600}{1\times10^{6}}$* = 6 x 10*<sup>*-4*</sup>* m*<sup>*3*</sup>* *

parts.problemMd:
Squalane can be produced from squalene, an alkene present in shark liver oil, by reaction with hydrogen gas in the presence of a suitable catalyst.

i) Give the name of a suitable catalyst for the hydrogenation of squalene.

**(1)**

ii) Squalane used in cosmetic products must contain no more than 0.2 ppm by mass of catalyst.

Calculate the maximum permitted mass of catalyst in a product containing 50 g of squalane.

**(1)**

iii) A reactor at 200 °C contains 8500 mol of liquid squalene, and hydrogen gas at a pressure of 4.0 × 10<sup>5 </sup>Pa.

Under these conditions, the complete hydrogenation of squalene requires 500 m<sup>3</sup> of hydrogen gas.

Calculate the number of C=C bonds in one molecule of squalene. You **must** show your working. [*pV = nRT*          R = 8.31 J mol<sup>-1 </sup>K<sup>-1</sup>]

**(4)**

iv) Write the equation, using molecular formulae, for the complete hydrogenation of squalene to squalane. State symbols are **not** required.

**(1)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) The name of a suitable catalyst for the hydrogenation of squalene is:

- Nickel; **[1 mark]**

ii) The maximum permitted mass of catalyst in a product containing 50 g of squalane is:

- 0.00001 / (1 ×) 10<sup>-5</sup> (g); **[1 mark]**

iii) The number of C=C bonds in one molecule of squalene is:

- Conversion of temperature to K: *T* = 200 + 273 = 473 (K); **[1 mark]**
- Rearrangement of ideal gas equation:
*n* = $\frac{pV}{RT}$
**OR**
*n* = $\frac{4.0\times10^{5}\times500}{8.31\times473}$; **[1 mark]**
- Moles of hydrogen = 50882.429; **[1 mark]**
- Mole ratio *n*(H<sub>2</sub>): *n*(squalene):
50882 : 8500
6 : 1
**AND**
6 C=C bonds per molecule; **[1 mark]**

iv) The equation for the complete hydrogenation of squalene to squalane is:

- C<sub>30</sub>H<sub>50</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>30</sub>H<sub>62</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 7 marks]**

- *Other suitable catalysts for hydrogenation are palladium or platinum*
- *To calculate the maximum permitted mass of catalyst in a product containing 50 g squalene, use the following equation:*

  - *concentration in ppm = *$\frac{\mathrm{mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{catalyst}\times10^{6}}{\mathrm{mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{squalene}}$
- *Rearrange to give the mass of catalyst:*

  - $\mathrm{mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{catalyst}=\frac{\mathrm{concentration} \mathrm{in} \mathrm{ppm}\times\mathrm{mass} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{squalene}}{10^{6}}=\frac{0.2\times50}{10^{6}}=1\times10^{-5}g$
- *You would be given the mark if you had expressed this as 10μg or 0.01 mg*
- *To find the number of C=C bonds, remember that 1 hydrogen molecule is added across every C=C double bond so the ratio of the number of moles of hydrogen to squalene will tell you how many C=C double bonds each molecule of squalene has*
- *Careful**: Make sure you check and convert the units as necessary when using the ideal gas equation*
- *If you used 24 dm*<sup>*3*</sup>* as the molar gas volume instead of using the ideal gas equation, you would have scored 2 marks if you found 2 C=C bonds per molecule*
- *In part (iv), if you had not stated  the number of C=C bonds, you could gain 1 mark if the equation given was in the form:*

  - *C*<sub>*n*</sub>*H*<sub>*2n-2y+2*</sub>* + yH*<sub>*2*</sub>* → C*<sub>*n*</sub>*H*<sub>*2n+2*</sub>
  - *Where 24 ≤ n ≤ 30 and 1 ≤ y ≤ 14*

parts.problemMd:
Globally, 2.8 million dm<sup>3</sup> of squalene is used each year.

Traditionally squalene was obtained exclusively from shark liver oil, which is a mixture of liquids. The liver of a shark yields 300 g of squalene.

i) Suggest the name of a suitable technique to obtain squalene from shark liver oil.

**(1)**

ii) Calculate the minimum number of sharks that would be needed to produce 2.8 million dm<sup>3</sup> of squalene. [Density of squalene = 0.86 g cm<sup>-3</sup>]

**(2)**

iii) Many large corporations now use squalane obtained entirely from plants. Squalane can be obtained sustainably from corn starch with a yield of 23% by mass.

The production of 1 tonne of corn starch requires 0.093 hectares of land. Calculate the area of land, **in km**<sup>**2**</sup>, required to produce 2500 tonnes of squalane from corn starch.

[1 tonne = 1000 kg   1 hectare = 0.01 km<sup>2</sup>]

**(3)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) The name of a suitable technique to obtain squalene from shark liver oil is:

- (Fractional) distillation; **[1 mark]**

ii) The minimum number of sharks that would be needed to produce 2.8 million dm<sup>3</sup> of squalene is:

Method 1

- Mass of squalene in 2.8 million dm<sup>3</sup> = 2.8 x 10<sup>9</sup> x 0.86 = 2.408 x 10<sup>9</sup> (g); **[1 mark]**
- Number of sharks required: $\frac{2.408\times10^{9}}{300}$ = 8.0 x 10<sup>6</sup>; **[1 mark]**

Method 2

- Volume of squalene per shark = $\frac{300}{0.86}$ = 348.8372 (cm<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**
- Number of sharks required = $\frac{2.8\times10^{9}}{348.8372}$ = 8.0 x 10<sup>6</sup>; **[1 mark]**

iii) The area of land, **in km**<sup>**2**</sup>, required to produce 2500 tonnes of squalane from corn starch is:

Method 1

- Mass of corn starch required = $\frac{2500}{23}$ x 100 = 10869.57 (tonnes); **[1 mark]**
- Required land area in hectares = 10869.57 x 0.093 = 1010.87 (hectares); **[1 mark]**
- Land area in km<sup>2</sup> = 1010.87 x 0.01 = 10.1087 = 10 (km<sup>2</sup>); **[1 mark]**

Method 2

- Conversion of land area from hectares to km<sup>2</sup> = 0.093 x 0.01 = 0.00093 / 9.3 x 10<sup>−4</sup> (km<sup>2</sup>); **[1 mark]**
- Required land area in km<sup>2</sup> to produce 2500 tonnes of corn starch = 0.00093 x 2500 = 2.325 km<sup>2</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- Required land area in km<sup>2</sup> to produce 2500 tonnes of squalene = $\frac{2.325}{23}$ x 100 = 10.1087 = 10 (km<sup>2</sup>); **[1 mark]**

Method 3

- Required land area in hectares to produce 2500 tonnes of corn starch = 2500 x 0.093 = 232.5 (hectares); **[1 mark]**
- Required land area in hectares to produce 2500 tonnes of squalene = $\frac{232.5}{23}$ x 100 = 1010.87 (hectares); **[1 mark]**
- Land area in km<sup>2</sup> = 1010.87 x 0.01 = 10.1087 = 10 (km<sup>2</sup>); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *Don't be put off by the unusual nature of this question - you need to be able to apply your knowledge of density, percentage yield and converting between units to answer this*
- *There are different ways in which you can go about each calculation, if you didn't get the answer correct, look through each of the methods and see which one makes the most sense to you*
- *Remember**: density = *$\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{\mathrm{volume}}$
- *You can use this to find the mass of squalene in 2.8 million dm*<sup>*3*</sup>* or the volume of squalene per shark*
- *Careful**: Convert the mass of squalene to cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* as the density is given in cm*<sup>*3*</sup>

  - *2.8 million dm*<sup>*3*</sup>* = 2.8 x 10*<sup>*6*</sup>* dm*<sup>*3*</sup>* = 2.8 x 10*<sup>*9*</sup>* cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
- *In part (iii), make sure you take into account the 23% yield, whichever method you choose*

> **[exam-tip]**
> Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different carbon skeletons (or different positions of functional groups). E/Z isomers have the same structural formula but different arrangements around a C=C double bond. E/Z isomerism requires two conditions: (1) restricted rotation around the C=C, and (2) each carbon of the C=C must have two different groups attached, both must be stated for full marks (1 mark each). Missing either condition means no E/Z isomerism.

parts.problemMd:
When 2-methylbutane reacts with chlorine in the presence of ultraviolet (UV) light, the major product is 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, formed by free radical substitution at the tertiary carbon.

Write equations to show the mechanism for this free radical substitution. Curly arrows are not required.

Your answer must include:

- the initiation step
- both propagation steps
- one termination step that regenerates the starting chlorine molecule.

[4]

State **one** reason why this reaction has limited use for synthesising pure 2-chloro-2-methylbutane in a laboratory.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
The mechanism is:

- Initiation:

`\text{Cl}_{2} \overset{\text{UV}}{\rightarrow} 2 \text{Cl}^{\cdot}` **[1 mark]**

- Propagation step 1 (Cl• abstracts the tertiary H at C2):

`(\text{CH}_{3} )_{2} \text{CHCH}_{2} \text{CH}_{3} + \text{Cl}^{\cdot} \rightarrow (\text{CH}_{3} )_{2} \overset{\cdot}{\text{C}} \text{CH}_{2} \text{CH}_{3} + \text{HCl}` **[1 mark]**

- Propagation step 2 (alkyl radical reacts with Cl<sub>2</sub>):

`(\text{CH}_{3} )_{2} \overset{\cdot}{\text{C}} \text{CH}_{2} \text{CH}_{3} + \text{Cl}_{2} \rightarrow (\text{CH}_{3} )_{2} \text{C}(\text{Cl})\text{CH}_{2} \text{CH}_{3} + \text{Cl}^{\cdot}` **[1 mark]**

- Termination (regenerating Cl<sub>2</sub>):

`\text{Cl}^{\cdot} + \text{Cl}^{\cdot} \rightarrow \text{Cl}_{2}` **[1 mark]**

**One** reason why this reaction has limited use for synthesising pure 2-chloro-2-methylbutane in a laboratory is:

- Further substitution occurs — the product 2-chloro-2-methylbutane still contains C–H bonds that can be attacked by Cl• radicals, giving di-, tri- and poly-chlorinated by-products. A **mixture of products** is therefore obtained, making this reaction unsuitable for preparing pure 2-chloro-2-methylbutane. **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for initiation: Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2Cl• with **UV** shown above the arrow
> 
> Both Cl• radicals must carry the dot
> 
> Accept "hν" or "UV light" notation
> 
> 1 mark for propagation step 1: alkane + Cl• → tertiary alkyl radical + HCl
> 
> - Radical dot mandatory on both Cl• and the alkyl radical
> - HCl must appear as a product (not H• alone)
> - Accept the alkyl radical drawn in any reasonable notation (structural, displayed, or skeletal with • on C2)
> 
> 1 mark for propagation step 2: alkyl radical + Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2-chloro-2-methylbutane + Cl•
> 
> Must react alkyl• with Cl<sub>2</sub> (molecule), NOT Cl• (that would be termination)
> 
> Cl• regenerated
> 
> 1 mark for ONE correct termination step: Cl• + Cl• → Cl<sub>2</sub>
> 
> Only the one asked for (regenerating Cl<sub>2</sub>) is required
> 
> 1 mark for limitation: further substitution / mixture of (di-/tri-)chlorinated products formed
> 
> Accept "mixture of isomers" (positional isomers at different carbons are also formed)
> 
> Reject "slow" or "reversible" — these are incorrect limitations

> **[exam-tip]**
> Key radical mechanism checks:
> 
> 1. Radical dot on every radical species;
> 2. Propagation step 2 reacts with Cl<sub>2</sub> (molecule), not Cl• (which would be termination);
> 3. HCl is produced in propagation 1, not 2;
> 4. Curly arrows are not required for radical equations — just write the species with dots clearly indicated. For the limitation question, the correct answer is "further substitution" giving a mixture — not "slow" or "reversible".

parts.problemMd:
Propene reacts with hydrogen bromide, HBr, via an electrophilic addition mechanism.

Give the mechanism for this reaction. Include curly arrows, and relevant lone pairs and dipoles.

Assume the major product is formed.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
The full mechanism is:

![Chemical reaction diagram showing alkene reacting with H-Br, forming a carbocation intermediate, then a final alkane with a bromine atom attached.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/1-structure-bonding-and-introduction-to-organic-chemistry/1-10-alkenes/assets/007-chemical-reaction-diagram-showing-alkene-reactin.png)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 4 marks total, 1 mark for each of the following elements:
> 
> 1 mark for δ+ on H and δ- on Br of HBr correctly labelled
> 
> Both partial charges must be shown; missing either loses the mark
> 
> 1 mark for curly arrow from the C=C bond to the δ+ H atom of HBr (NOT from a C atom or from the middle of the carbon)
> 
> Arrow must originate from the bond, not from an atom symbol
> 
> 1 mark for carbocation intermediate drawn with ⁺ charge on the correct (central/secondary) carbon, AND a second curly arrow from the H–Br bond to the Br atom (forming Br⁻)
> 
> ⁺ must be explicitly shown on the correct C
> 
> The positive carbon should have only 3 bonds (trigonal planar)
> 
> Do not accept a partial charge (δ+) on the carbocation — must be a full + charge
> 
> 1 mark for the final step: curly arrow from a lone pair on Br⁻ to the carbocation carbon, giving 2-bromopropane (CH<sub>3</sub>CHBrCH<sub>3</sub>) as the final product
> 
> Arrow must originate from a lone pair on Br⁻ (explicitly drawn or implied)
> 
> Product must be clearly 2-bromopropane, not 1-bromopropane

> **[exam-tip]**
> The four marks in the mechanism come from:
> 
> 1. δ+/δ- labels on the electrophile
> 2. Curly arrow from the C=C bond (not atom)
> 3. Carbocation with a full + charge (not δ+)
> 4. Curly arrow from a Br⁻ lone pair
> 
> All four elements are independently examined, missing any one costs a mark. The Edexcel command for this style of question is concise: "Include curly arrows, and relevant lone pairs and dipoles", you are expected to know that the carbocation intermediate and the final product must also be drawn.

parts.problemMd:
The major product of the reaction between propene and HBr is 2-bromopropane (not 1-bromopropane).

Explain why 2-bromopropane is the major organic product.
parts.solutionMd:
2-bromopropane is the major product because:

- If H adds to C1 of propene, the carbocation intermediate is secondary (CH<sub>3</sub>–⁺CH–CH<sub>3</sub>); if H adds to C2, the carbocation would be primary (⁺CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub>). **[1 mark]**
- The secondary carbocation is more stable than the primary because alkyl groups donate electron density to the positively charged carbon, stabilising the charge. The more stable secondary carbocation forms preferentially, and so 2-bromopropane is the major product. **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for identifying the secondary carbocation as the intermediate leading to 2-bromopropane (vs primary carbocation leading to 1-bromopropane)
> 
> Accept structures or written reasoning showing both possible carbocations
> 
> 1 mark for secondary carbocation more stable than primary AND alkyl groups donate electron density / stabilise the positive charge
> 
> Both elements required: stability comparison AND the reason
> 
> Stating "secondary is more stable" without the reason scores only 1 mark for identifying the carbocation type
> 
> Ignore any reference to Markovnikov's rule (Markovnikov's rule is not on the specification)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The specification expects you to explain the major product purely in terms of **carbocation stability**, Edexcel mark schemes explicitly state "ignore any reference to Markovnikov's rule" because Markovnikov's rule is not on the specification.
> 
> The reasoning chain is: identify the two possible carbocations (secondary vs primary) → secondary is more stable because alkyl groups donate electron density → secondary forms preferentially → 2-bromopropane is the major product.

parts.problemMd:
Propene can be polymerised to form poly(propene).

i) Draw the structure of poly(propene) showing **two** repeat units.

[1]

ii) State **one** environmental problem caused by the disposal of poly(propene), and **one** method used to reduce this problem.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The structure of poly(propene) showing two repeat units is:

![Structural formula of 2,3-dimethylbutane, showing carbon and hydrogen atoms with CH3 groups attached to the second and third carbon atoms.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/1-structure-bonding-and-introduction-to-organic-chemistry/1-10-alkenes/assets/008-structural-formula-of-2-3-dimethylbutane-showing.png)

**[1 mark]**

ii) Environmental problem AND method to reduce it:

- Problem: Poly(propene) is non-biodegradable — it cannot be broken down by natural processes (enzymes, bacteria), so it persists in landfill sites for hundreds of years, causing long-term waste accumulation and pollution (including microplastic pollution of oceans). **[1 mark]**

- Method: Recycle used poly(propene) by collecting, sorting, cleaning, melting and re-moulding it into new plastic items. (Alternatively: incinerate for energy recovery — combustion releases energy that can generate electricity.) **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) 1 mark for correct structure showing two repeat units:
> 
> - 4-carbon backbone (2 × 2-carbon repeat units)
> - CH<sub>3</sub> as a side chain on every alternate carbon (NOT in the main chain)
> - All hydrogens shown explicitly
> 
> Brackets and the subscript n are NOT required (per Edexcel MS convention, ignore brackets/n requirement)
> 
> Accept condensed notation if clear (e.g. –CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–CH<sub>2</sub>–)
> 
> ii) 1 mark for ONE valid environmental problem:
> 
> Non-biodegradable / persists in landfill / microplastic pollution
> 
> Produces toxic gases (e.g. CO, dioxins) if incinerated without controls
> 
> Takes up landfill space
> 
> 1 mark for one valid reduction method that matches the problem cited:
> 
> For landfill/non-biodegradability: recycle / reuse / incinerate for energy
> 
> For toxic combustion gases: use controlled incineration with scrubbers
> 
> Reject generic statements (e.g. "don't throw it away") without a named method.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Common errors on poly(propene) repeat units:
> 
> 1. Drawing a 3-carbon backbone with CH<sub>3</sub> in the main chain, the repeat unit is always 2 carbons for vinyl polymers;
> 2. Showing only one repeat unit when two are asked for. Edexcel mark schemes for repeat unit questions ignore brackets and the subscript n, so focus on getting the structure correct rather than the bracket notation.
> 
> For the environmental question, the reduction method must directly address the problem cited, a generic "recycle" doesn't score if the problem is about toxic fumes from incineration.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about silicon and carbon.

Silicon is a semiconductor.

i) Data obtained using the mass spectrum of silicon are shown.

| **Isotope mass number** | **Relative abundance** |
|---|---|
| 28 | 92.17 |
| 29 | 4.71 |
| 30 | 3.12 |

Calculate the relative atomic mass of silicon to **two** decimal places.

**(2)**

ii) Suggest a reason why there is a small peak in the mass spectrum of silicon at *m / z *= 14

**(1)**

iii) Complete the table to show the number of protons and neutrons in each isotope of silicon.

| **Isotope** | **Number of protons** | **Number of neutrons** |
|---|---|---|
| <sup>28</sup>Si |   |   |
| <sup>29</sup>Si |   |   |
| <sup>30</sup>Si |   |   |

**(1)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) The relative atomic mass of silicon to **two** decimal places is:

- *A*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{\left(28 \times 92 . 17\right) + \left(29 \times 4 . 71\right) + \left(30 \times 3 . 12\right)}{100}$ = 28.1095; **[1 mark]**
- To two decimal places: = 28.11; **[1 mark]**

ii) A reason why there is a small peak in the mass spectrum of silicon at *m / z *= 14 is:

- Some silicon atoms (of mass 28) lose two electrons / have a charge of 2+; **[1 mark]**

iii) The completed table is:

| **Isotope** | **Number of protons** | **Number of neutrons** |
|---|---|---|
| <sup>28</sup>Si | **Final answer:** **14** | **Final answer:** **14** |
| <sup>29</sup>Si | **Final answer:** **14** | **Final answer:** **15** |
| <sup>30</sup>Si | **Final answer:** **14** | **Final answer:** **16** |

- All values correct; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Ensure you give calculated values to the required number of decimal places - this is an easy mark to lose!*
- *A correct value for **A*<sub>*r*</sub>* scores 2 marks without working*
- *The only acceptable units for **A*<sub>*r*</sub>* are g mol*<sup>*-1*</sup>* or a.m.u. *
- *If you obtain a value between 28 and 30 but the expression used is incorrect, you would score 1 mark*
- *Remember**: The peaks on a mass spectrum occur at **m** / **z** values, which is the mass to charge ratio*
- *In most cases, the charge is +1, so the **m** / **z** value is just the mass of the ion*
- *In this case, the **m** / z value for the Si*<sup>*2+*</sup>* ion is 28 / 2 = 14*

**(1)**

parts.problemMd:
Silicon dioxide, SiO<sub>2</sub> , is the main constituent of sand and has a giant lattice structure similar to that of diamond.

![q13b-paper-1-oct-2021-edexcel-ial-chemistry](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/1-structure-bonding-and-introduction-to-organic-chemistry/1-2-amount-of-substance/assets/004-q13b-paper-1-oct-2021-edexcel-ial-chemistry.png)

Crystalline silicon dioxide is used on the surface of semiconductor devices to provide a heat-resistant, electrically insulating layer.

Explain how the structure and bonding of silicon dioxide make it useful for this application.
parts.solutionMd:
The structure and bonding of silicon dioxide make it useful for a heat-resistant, electrically insulating layers because:

- **All **atoms are joined together by covalent bonds / giant covalent (structure);** [1 mark]**
- These are strong / take a lot of energy to break (so melting temperature is very high); **[1 mark]**
- No electrons are free (to move) / mobile / delocalised / (so charge cannot be carried); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *There are two properties that make silicon dioxide useful in this application:*

  - *High melting temperature so it can withstand heat*
  - *Non-conductor of electricity so it can act as an electrical insulator*
- *Whenever referring to the properties of substances, you must explain how the bonds / forces within the structure give rise to these properties*
- *You are told that silicon dioxide has a similar structure to diamond, so the same explanations from the properties of diamond can be applied to silicon dioxide*

  - *There are no intermolecular forces, just strong covalent bonds between all of the atoms which require a large amount of energy to overcome, giving it a high melting temperature*
  
    - *You would not be given credit if you refer to a high boiling temperature as this is not relevant in this application*
  - *All of the outer electrons of silicon and oxygen are involved in bonding so there are no free electrons to carry charge*

parts.problemMd:
Calcium silicate is formed in the removal of silicon dioxide impurities in the extraction of iron from its ores. A sample of calcium silicate composed of calcium, silicon and oxygen was found to contain 12.0 g of calcium, 8.43 g of silicon and 14.47 g of oxygen.

Determine the empirical formula of calcium silicate. You **must** show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
The empirical formula of calcium silicate is:

- Calculation of number of moles: $\mathrm{Ca}:\frac{12}{40.1}\mathrm{Si}:\frac{8.43}{28.1}O:\frac{14.47}{16}$ 
**OR**
Ca : Si : O = 0.299 : 0.30 : 0.904; **[1 mark]**
- Calculation of whole number mole ratio: 1 : 1 : 3; **[1 mark]**
- Empirical formula: CaSiO<sub>3</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *To find the whole number ratio, divide the number of moles of each element by the smallest number of moles*
- *It is a common mistake for students to forget to give the empirical formula once they have calculated the whole number ratio - a frustrating mark to lose when the hard work has been done!*

parts.problemMd:
Carbon dioxide is a gas at room temperature. A fizzy drink is canned at 5.0°C and 1.3 × 10<sup>5 </sup>Pa and contains approximately 3 g of carbon dioxide.

Calculate the volume, in cm<sup>3</sup>, occupied by 3.00 g of carbon dioxide gas at 5.0°C and 1.3 × 10<sup>5 </sup>Pa.

[*pV = nRT*     R = 8.31 Jmol<sup>−1</sup>K<sup>−1</sup>]
parts.solutionMd:
The volume, in cm<sup>3</sup>, occupied by 3.00 g of carbon dioxide gas at 5.0 °C and 1.3 × 10<sup>5 </sup>Pa is:

- Calculation of moles carbon dioxide: 3 ÷ 44 = 0.06818;** [1 mark]**
- Conversion of temperature to K: 273 + 5 = 278; **[1 mark]**
- Rearrangement of expression: *V *= $\frac{nRT}{p}=\frac{0.06818\times8.31\times278}{1.3\times10^{5}}$ (= 1.2116 x 10<sup>-3</sup> m<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**
- Evaluation of answer in cm<sup>3</sup>: = 1211.6 / 1212 / 1210 /1200 (cm<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *The most common mistakes made with these types of calculations are not converting / incorrectly converting to the correct units and not rearranging the expression correctly*
- *To convert from m*<sup>*3*</sup>* to cm*<sup>*3*</sup>*, multiply by 10*<sup>*6*</sup>
- *If you are not confident in rearranging, it can be best to substitute values into the equation **pV** = **nRT **first:*

  - *1.3 x 10*<sup>*5*</sup>* x **V** = 0.06818 x 8.31 x 278*
- *Then simplify:*

  - *1.3 x 10*<sup>*5*</sup>* x **V** = 157.508*
- *Then rearrange:*

  - *V** = *$\frac{157.508}{1.3\times10^{5}}$* = 1.2116 x 10*<sup>*-3 *</sup>*m*<sup>*3*</sup>

parts.problemMd:
A 0.210 g sample of a volatile organic liquid **C** is injected into a gas syringe and heated in an oven. At 100 kPa and 358 K, the syringe contains 72.5 cm<sup>3 </sup>of gas.

Calculate the molar mass of **C**. 
[*pV = nRT        R* = 8.31 J mol<sup>−1</sup> K<sup>−1</sup> ]
parts.solutionMd:
The molar mass of **C **is:

- Conversion of volume to m<sup>3</sup> 72.5 × 10<sup>-6</sup> = 7.25 × 10<sup>-5</sup> / 0.0000725 (m<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**
- Rearrangement of Ideal Gas Equation *n =* $\frac{pV}{RT}$; **[1 mark]**
- Conversion of pressure and evaluation to give number of moles $\frac{100000\times7.25x10^{-5}}{8.31\times358}$= 2.4370 × 10<sup>− 3</sup> / 0.002437(mol); **[1 mark]**
- Calculation of molar mass $\frac{0.210}{2.4370\times10^{-3}}=$86.172 = 86 (g mol<sup>-1</sup>); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *You must know the ideal gas equation, **pV **= **nRT **and be able to rearrange it*
- *Don't forget that units for volume and pressure should be m*<sup>*3*</sup>* and Pa respectively *

  - *To convert from cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* to m*<sup>*3*</sup>* divide 72.5 by 1 000 000*
  - *To convert from kPa to Pa, multiply 100 by 1000*
- *Once the number of moles have been calculated, use *$\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{\mathrm{number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{moles}}$* to find the molar mass of **C*

parts.problemMd: The organic liquid **C** is a hydrocarbon. Give a possible name or formula for **C**, using your answer in (a).
parts.solutionMd:
A possible name or formula for **C**, using your answer in (a) is:

- Hexane or any alkane with the molecular formula of C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *Being told the compound is a hydrocarbon narrows it down to an alkane or an alkene*
- *Have a play around with the numbers until you find a combination that equals 86*

  - *(6 x 12) + (14 x 1) = 86 g mol*<sup>*-1*</sup>

parts.problemMd:
Arsine is a reducing agent and reacts with cerium(IV) sulfate solution, forming arsenic.

The data from an experiment are shown.

Volume of arsine gas = 350 cm<sup>3</sup> at 115000 Pa and 20 °C

Volume of cerium(IV) sulfate solution = 488 cm<sup>3 </sup>

Concentration of cerium(IV) sulfate solution = 0.102 mol dm<sup>−3</sup>

i) Complete the half‐equation.

**(1)**

AsH<sub>3</sub> → As

ii) Calculate the final oxidation state of the cerium ion formed in the reaction.

**(6)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) The completed half equation is:

- AsH<sub>3</sub> → As + 3H<sup>+</sup> + 3e(<sup>−</sup>); **[1 mark] **

ii) To calculate the final oxidation state of the cerium ion formed in the reaction:

- Moles of Ce<sup>4+</sup> $\frac{488}{1000}\times0.102$ = 0.049776 (mol);** [1 mark] **
- Calculation of *T* in *K *and *V* in m<sup>3</sup> *T* = 293 K 
**AND **
*V* =** **350 × 10<sup>−6</sup> m<sup>3</sup>;** [1 mark] **
- Rearrangement of* pV = nRT* *n* = $\frac{PV}{RT}$; **[1 mark] **
- Calculation of *n *for arsine *n* = $\frac{115000\times350\times10^{-6}}{8.31\times293}$ = 0.016531; **[1 mark] **
- Deduction of whole number ratio of AsH<sub>3</sub> : Ce<sup>4+</sup> $\frac{0.049776}{0.016531}$ = 1 : 3;** [1 mark] **
- The oxidation state of cerium in the product = Ce<sup>3+</sup> / (+)3; **[1 mark] **

**Final answer:** **[Total: 7 marks] **

- *The first step is to calculate the number of moles of Ce*<sup>*4+*</sup>* by using moles = volume (dm*<sup>*3*</sup>*) x concentration *

  - *If you use volume in cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* then you must divide by 1000*
- *Conversion of units for the **PV** = **nRT** equation is essential*

  - *To convert the temperature from °C to K, you add 273*
  - *To convert the volume from cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* to m*<sup>*3*</sup>*, you divide by 10*<sup>*6*</sup>
  - *Pressure is given to you in Pa, so there is no need to change this*
- *You will score a mark for rearranging the equation to find **n*
- *The ratio between the number of moles of arsine and Ce*<sup>*4+*</sup>* will give the oxidation state of Ce*<sup>*3+*</sup>* in the product *
- *This is because we need to multiply the half equation for the reduction of Ce4+ by 3 to form a full equation *

  - *Ce*<sup>*4+*</sup>* + e*<sup>*-*</sup>* → Ce*<sup>*3+*</sup>* (x3)*
  - *AsH*<sub>*3*</sub>* → As + 3H*<sup>*+*</sup>* + 3e*<sup>*−*</sup>
  - *AsH*<sub>*3 *</sub>*+ 3Ce*<sup>*4+*</sup>* → As + 3Ce*<sup>*3+*</sup>* *

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the element sulfur.

Complete the diagram to show the electronic configuration for a sulfur atom in the ground state. Include labels for each subshell.

![q18a-paper-1-jan-2021-edexcel-ial-chemistry](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/1-structure-bonding-and-introduction-to-organic-chemistry/1-3-atomic-structure/assets/003-q18a-paper-1-jan-2021-edexcel-ial-chemistry.png)
parts.solutionMd:
The diagram to show the electronic configuration for a sulfur atom in the ground state is:

![sulfur-electrons-in-boxes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/1-structure-bonding-and-introduction-to-organic-chemistry/1-3-atomic-structure/assets/004-sulfur-electrons-in-boxes.png)

- Correctly labelled subshells; **[1 mark]**
- Correctly filled boxes / orbitals; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *A sulfur atom has 16 electrons so will have the electronic configuration 1s*<sup>*2*</sup>*2s*<sup>*2*</sup>*2p*<sup>*6*</sup>*3s*<sup>*2*</sup>*3p*<sup>*4*</sup>
- *The 1s subshell is the lowest in energy which corresponds to the lowest box, followed by 2s, 2p, 3s and 3p *
- *All orbitals in 1s, 2s,2p and 3s are filled with 2 electrons, these electrons must be represented by 2 arrows pointing in the opposite direction to represent the opposite spin of the electrons*
- *When filling the 3p subshell, each orbital fills with 1 electron first, all with their spins in the same direction, so all arrows pointing in the same direction, the fourth electron will pair with one of these electrons but will have an opposite spin*

  - *So, one 3p orbital contains 2 electrons with opposite spin and two orbitals contain one electron only*
- *It does not matter which 3p orbital you pair and you can show the unpaired 3p electron as spin down*
- *You can represent the electrons using half arrows but not using vertical lines, as this does not show the direction of spin*
- *You would not gain the second mark if you showed the paired electrons with parallel spins*

parts.problemMd: Write an equation for the **first** ionisation energy of sulfur. Include state symbols.
parts.solutionMd:
The **first** ionisation energy of sulfur is:

S (g) → S<sup>+</sup> (g) + e(<sup>–</sup>)    
**OR**    
S (g) - e(<sup>–</sup>) → S<sup>+</sup> (g)

- Species and balancing; **[1 mark]**
- Correct state symbols; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *The first ionisation energy of an element is the amount of energy required to remove one mole of electrons from one mole of gaseous atoms of an element to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions*

  - *On the LHS of the equation, you need to show one mole of gaseous atoms*
  - *On the RHS, you need to show one mole of gaseous 1+ ions and one mole of electrons*
- *You must show state symbols when giving the equation for ionisation energies, even if not prompted to do so in the question*

parts.problemMd: Explain why the first ionisation energy of sulfur is less than the first ionisation energies of** both** phosphorus and chlorine.
parts.solutionMd:
The first ionisation energy of sulfur is less than the first ionisation energies of** both** phosphorus and chlorine because:

- The outermost electrons are in the same subshell / (quantum) shell; **[1 mark]**
- Cl contains the greatest number of protons / more protons than S; **[1 mark]**
- There is (spin-spin) repulsion between (paired) electrons in (3)**p** orbital / subshell in S; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *You need to be able to explain the overall trend across Periods 2 and 3 and the dips in the trend between the 2nd and 3rd elements and the 5th and 6th element*
- *There are a number of ways of wording this explanation that are creditworthy*
- *Choose an explanation that you understand the most and learn it*
- *For the first mark, you would gain a mark for:*

  - *The outermost electrons have similar / the same (electron) shielding*
  - *There are the same number of shells*
  - *A correct reference to full or partial electronic configurations for two or three elements*
  - *You would **not **gain the mark for any incorrect electronic configurations*
- *For the second mark:*

  - *Cl has the greatest **nuclear **charge*
  - *Cl has the smallest **atomic **radius / smaller atomic radius than S*
- *For the third mark:*

  - *A correct reference to a stable half-full p subshell: e.g. there is a stable half-full p subshell in P **OR **removing an electron from S gives a stable half-full p subshell*

parts.problemMd:
A sample of sulfur contains four isotopes.

| **Isotope** | <sup>32</sup>S | <sup>33</sup>S | <sup>34</sup>S | <sup>36</sup>S |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Percentage abundance** | 94.88 | 0.83 | 4.27 | 0.02 |

i) State what is meant by the term **isotopes**, in terms of subatomic particles.

**(2)**

ii) Calculate the relative atomic mass of sulfur in this sample. 
Give your answer to **two **decimal places.

**(2)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) The term **isotopes**, in terms of subatomic particles, means:

- (Atoms with the) same number of protons; **[1 mark]**
- (And) different number of neutrons; **[1 mark]**

ii) The relative atomic mass of sulfur in this sample is:

- *A*<sub>r</sub> = $\frac{\left(32 \times 94 . 88\right) + \left(33 \times 0 . 83\right) + \left(34 \times 4 . 27\right) + \left(36 \times 0 . 02\right)}{100}$; **[1 mark]**
- *A*<sub>r</sub> = 32.09; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *The question tells you to define isotopes in terms of subatomic particles, so any reference to mass number or atomic number is not accepted*
- *Make sure you use the term atom, not species, particles or molecules - any of these will be penalised once *
- *When calculating the relative atomic mass, make sure that you take into account all of the isotopes*
- *It is very easy to make mistakes when entering numbers into your calculator - think about what value you would expect*

  - *The mass of the isotopes ranges from 32 to 36, so your answer has to be between 32 and 36*
  - <sup>*32*</sup>*S is the most abundant, so you should expect that the number will be much closer to 32*
- *If you do not show any working, you will score 1 mark for a correct answer*

parts.problemMd:
The mass spectrum of a sample of sulfur with <sup>32</sup>S as the only isotope is shown.

![q18e-paper-1-jan-2021-edexcel-ial-chemistry](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/1-structure-bonding-and-introduction-to-organic-chemistry/1-3-atomic-structure/assets/005-q18e-paper-1-jan-2021-edexcel-ial-chemistry.png)

i) Calculate the number of sulfur atoms in the molecular ion.
You **must **show your working.

**(1)**

ii) Suggest the **formula **of the **most stable ion **shown by this spectrum.

**(2)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) The number of sulfur atoms in the molecular ion is:

- $\frac{256}{32}$ = 8 (atoms); **[1 mark]**

ii) The **formula **of the **most stable ion **shown by this spectrum is:

- A species containing 2 sulfur atoms, e.g. S<sub>2</sub> / S-S / SS / S,S; **[1 mark]**
- An ion with a 1+ charge; S<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> / [S-S]<sup>+</sup> / SS<sup>+</sup> / S,S<sup>+</sup>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *The molecular ion peak is the peak with the highest **m** / **z ** value = 256*

  - *This value is equal to the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of a sulfur molecule*
- *One atom of sulfur has a mass of 32, therefore a molecule must have 256 ÷ 32 = 8 atoms*
- *The most stable ion has the highest peak, so its **m **/ **z **value is 64*
- *The most stable ion will have a 1+ charge, therefore its mass is 64 so will contain 64 ÷ 32 = 2 sulfur atoms: S*<sub>*2*</sub><sup>*+*</sup>
- *S*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*2+*</sup>* also has an **m** / **z** value of 64: (4 x 32) ÷ 2 = 64*

  - *However, the 2+ ion is not as stable as the 1+ ion, but you would score 1 mark for this ion*

parts.problemMd:
A sample of copper contains the isotopes <sup>63</sup>Cu and <sup>65</sup>Cu.

i) Complete the table to show the numbers of subatomic particles in the atoms of these two isotopes of copper.

**(2)**

| **Isotope** | **Protons** | **Neutrons** | **Electrons** |
|---|---|---|---|
| <sup>63</sup>Cu |   |   |   |
| <sup>65</sup>Cu |   |   |   |

ii) Explain the term isotopes, using the information in the table.

**(2)**

iii) State why the two isotopes of copper have the same chemical reactions.

**(1)**

iv) The relative atomic mass of copper in this sample is 63.4. Calculate the percentage abundances of the isotopes <sup>63</sup>Cu and <sup>65</sup>Cu in this sample. 
You** must** show your working.

**(2)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) The completed table is:

| **Isotope** | **Protons** | **Neutrons** | **Electrons** |
|---|---|---|---|
| <sup>63</sup>Cu | **29** | **34** | **29** |
| <sup>65</sup>Cu | **29** | **36** | **29** |

- Each correct row: **[1 mark]**
- Four or five correct; **1 mark]**

ii) The term isotope means:

- (Atoms / elements that have) same number of protons / same proton number / quoted same number of protons even if wrong; **[1 mark]**
- (But) different numbers of neutrons / neutron number; **[1 mark]**

iii) Two isotopes of copper have the same chemical reactions because:

- (Isotopes have) the same electronic configuration
**OR**
Same number of electrons
**OR**
Same electron arrangement; **[1 mark]**

iv) The percentage abundances of the isotopes <sup>63</sup>Cu and <sup>65</sup>Cu in this sample are:

- Expression relating isotopic masses *A*<sub>r</sub> and X  $63 . 4 = \frac{\left(\left(1 - X\right) \times 65\right) + \left(X \times 63\right)}{1}$; **[1 mark]**
- Abundance of (Cu) 63 = 0.8 or 80%  
**AND** 
Abundance of (Cu) 65 = 0.2 or 20%; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 7 marks]**

- *You can use a Periodic Table to find the atomic number for copper which is 29*

  - *The atomic number is the number of protons so there are 29 protons in each isotope*
  - *In an atom, the number of protons and electrons are equal so there are 29 electrons in each isotope*
  - *Take the atomic number away from the mass number for each isotope to deduce the number of neutrons *
- *Remember: **Chemical properties are determined by the number of electrons in the outer shell so if there are the same number of electrons, the isotopes will react in the same way*
- *Part iv) requires manipulation of the equation used to calculate RAM:*

  - $\frac{\left(abundance of isotope x mass\right) + \left(abundance of isotope x mass\right)}{100}$
- *There are many ways this calculation can be done so a correct answer with no workings scores 2 marks*
- *An alternative method is:*

  - $63.4=\frac{(100-X)\times65)+(X\times63)}{100}$
  - *6340 = 6500 – 65X + 63X*
  - *6340 = 6500 – 2X*
  - *−160 = −2X*
  - *X **OR **63 = 80%*

parts.problemMd:
Copper(II) sulfate, CuSO<sub>4</sub>, can be made by reacting solid copper(II) carbonate with dilute sulfuric acid.

i) Write an equation for the reaction that occurs. State symbols are not required.

**(1)**

ii) An experiment was carried out to produce pure, dry crystals of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO<sub>4</sub> •5H<sub>2</sub>O. 
Copper(II) carbonate was mixed with 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 1.00 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> sulfuric acid until no more reacted. The mass of CuSO<sub>4</sub> •5H<sub>2</sub>O obtained was 10.87g.

Calculate the percentage yield for this reaction, giving your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures.
[Molar mass of CuSO<sub>4</sub> •5H<sub>2</sub>O = 249.6 g mol<sup>−1</sup> ]

**(4)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) An equation for the reaction that occurs is:

- CuCO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → CuSO<sub>4 </sub>+ CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O 
**OR** CuCO<sub>3</sub> + 2H<sup>+</sup> → Cu<sup>2+</sup> + CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O; **[1 mark]**

ii) The percentage yield for this reaction, giving your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures is:

- Moles of sulfuric acid 50 × 1.00 ÷ 1000 = 0.05 (mol); **[1 mark]**
- Maximum mass of copper(II) sulfate 0.05 (mol) × 249.6 = 12.48 (g); **[1 mark]**
- Percentage yield calculation: 100 × 10.87 ÷ 12.48 = 87.099; **[1 mark]**
- Answer to 2 or 3 SF 87(%) / 87.1(%); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *Remember: **The general equation for the reaction between a metal carbonate and acid is:*

  - *Metal carbonate + acid     →    salt + water + carbon dioxide*
- *The equations required to answer part ii) are:*

  - *Number of moles = concentration x volume*
  
    - *Don't forget to convert the volume into dm*<sup>*3*</sup>
  - *Mass = molar mass x number of moles*
  
    - *The ratio of moles of sulfuric acid to copper sulfate is 1:1 so the number of moles of each substance is equal *
  - *Percentage yield = *$\frac{\mathrm{actual} \mathrm{yield}}{\mathrm{theoretical} \mathrm{yield}}\times100$
  - *If you don't give your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures, you will not score the last mark *
  
    - *Two or three significant figures are considered appropriate *
- *An alternative method for ii) is:*

  - *Moles of sulfuric acid: 50 × 1.00 ÷ 1000 = 0.05 (mol)*
  - *Moles of copper sulfate:  10.87 (g) /: 249.6 (g) = 0.04355 (mol)*
  - *Percentage yield calculation: 100 × 0.04355 ÷ 0.05*
  - *Answer to 2 or 3 SF: 87(%) / 87.1(%)*
- *Marking point 4 can still be achieved even if the answer is incorrect as long as the calculation involves mass or moles*

parts.problemMd:
Aluminium is an abundant metal with many uses.

The first four ionisation energies of aluminium are shown.

| **Ionisation number** | **Energy / kJ mol**<sup>**−1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| 1 | 578 |
| 2 | 1820 |
| 3 | 2750 |
| 4 | 11600 |

Explain how this information shows that aluminium is in Group 3 of the Periodic Table.
parts.solutionMd:
The information shows that aluminium is in Group 3 of the Periodic Table because:

- There is a “jump” / much bigger increase between the third and fourth ionisation energies; **[1 mark]**
- (First) 3 electrons in outer shell 
**OR** 
The fourth electron is removed from a different (quantum) **shell **(which is closer to the nucleus); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *When there is a big increase between successive ionisation energies, it marks the beginning of a new shell, closer to the nucleus as more energy was required to remove an outer electron*
- *This means that the outer electron must be more strongly attracted to the nucleus which occurs when the electron is closer to the nucleus*

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the ionisation energies of the elements in Period 2 of the Periodic Table.

The first ionisation energies of the Period 2 elements are shown.

![q23a-paper-1-jan-2022-edexcel-ial-chemistry](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/1-structure-bonding-and-introduction-to-organic-chemistry/1-5-the-periodic-table/assets/003-q23a-paper-1-jan-2022-edexcel-ial-chemistry.png)

i) Give an equation that represents the first ionisation energy of lithium.

ii) Explain why there is a general increase in the first ionisation energy across the period.

parts.solutionMd:
i) An equation that represents the first ionisation energy of lithium is:

- Li(g) → Li<sup>+</sup>(g) + e(<sup>−</sup>); **[1 mark]**

ii) There is a general increase in the first ionisation energy across the period because:

- (On moving across the period) there is an increase in the number of protons / atomic number / nuclear charge; **[1 mark]**
- (The electrons are in the same shell so there is a) greater attraction between the nucleus and electron(s); **[1 mark]**

iii) The first ionisation energy of oxygen is lower than that of nitrogen because:

Answer in terms of oxygen

- The electron is being removed from a (2)p orbital that is paired / full; **[1 mark]**

Answer in terms of nitrogen:

**OR**
The electron is being removed from a half-filled (2)p orbital ; **[1 mark]**
