parts.problemMd:
All the successive ionisation energies of nitrogen are shown in the table.

| **Ionisation number** | **1** | **2** | **3** | **4** | **5** | **6** | **7** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Ionisation energy** **/ kJ mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> | 1402 | 2856 | 4578 | 7475 | 9445 | 53267 | 64360 |

Explain the trend in the successive ionisation energies of nitrogen.
parts.solutionMd:
Explain the trend in the successive ionisation energies of nitrogen:

- (General increase because there is the same positive charge) but fewer electrons / less repulsion between electrons / electrons getting closer to the nucleus / ion becoming increasingly more positive / increase in effective nuclear charge; **[1 mark]**
- There is a big jump between 5th - 6th ionisation energies as the 6th electron is removed from a new shell / quantum shell / energy level (closer to the nucleus); **[1 mark]**
- There is a jump between 3rd - 4th ionisation energies as the 4th electron is removed from a new sub shell / 2s (closer to the nucleus); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *It is helpful to write out the electronic configuration for the element as it is easier to visualise where the electrons are being lost from*
- *The electronic configuration of nitrogen is: 1s*<sup>*2*</sup>*2s*<sup>*2*</sup>*2p*<sup>*3*</sup>

  - *The first three electrons are removed from the 2p orbital*
  
    - *Each time an electron is removed the nuclear charge increases so more energy is needed to remove the next electron down *
  - *The fourth electron is removed from a subshell closer to the nucleus - 2s so there will be a much greater amount of energy needed to remove the electron from here compared to 2p*
  - *This is the same for the sixth ionisation energy whereby the electron is being removed from the 1s subshell as opposed to 2s*

parts.problemMd:
This question is about atomic structure, mass spectrometry and ionisation energies.

i) State what is meant by the term **first ionisation energy**.

[2]

ii) Write an equation, including state symbols, to represent the first ionisation energy of sodium.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
**i)** The first ionisation energy is:

- The energy required to remove one mole of electrons **[1 mark]**
- from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions **[1 mark]**

**ii)** Equation for the first ionisation energy of sodium:

Na (g) → Na⁺ (g) + e⁻ **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) 1 mark for "energy required / needed to remove one mole of electrons" — must reference "one mole of electrons" or equivalent ("a mole of electrons"); reject "an electron" alone
> 
> 1 mark for "from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous 1+ ions" — state symbol (g) or word "gaseous" required for both atoms AND ions
> 
> Reject definitions that omit either the "one mole" specification or the gaseous state
> 
> ii) 1 mark for Na (g) → Na⁺ (g) + e⁻
> 
> State symbols (g) on both species mandatory
> 
> Accept e⁻ or e on RHS
> 
> Reject: missing state symbols; Na₂(g) (refers to a molecule, not an atom); removing more than one electron in a single step; products without (g)

> **[exam-tip]**
> When you define first ionisation energy, two scoring components must appear: "one mole of electrons" and "one mole of gaseous atoms → one mole of gaseous 1+ ions". State symbols **(g)** on both sides of the equation are mandatory — omitting them is the most common cause of lost marks in this style of question. Remember: only **one** electron is removed per ionisation step (the second IE is a separate process), and the starting species is always a single gaseous atom — never write Na₂(g), which refers to a molecule.

parts.problemMd:
The mass spectrum of a sample of magnesium shows three peaks with the following relative abundances.

| Isotope | ²⁴Mg | ²⁵Mg | ²⁶Mg |
|---|---|---|---|
| Relative abundance / % | 79.0 | 10.0 | 11.0 |

Calculate the relative atomic mass, *A*<sub>r</sub>, of magnesium in this sample. Give your answer to two decimal places.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the relative atomic mass of magnesium in this sample, use the weighted mean of the three isotopic masses (each isotopic mass weighted by its % abundance):

*A*<sub>r</sub> = Σ(isotopic mass × % abundance) ÷ 100

*A*<sub>r</sub> = [(24 × 79.0) + (25 × 10.0) + (26 × 11.0)] ÷ 100 **[1 mark]**

*A*<sub>r</sub> = (1896 + 250 + 286) ÷ 100 = 2432 ÷ 100

*A*<sub>r</sub> = **24.32** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct method / substitution: weighted-mean expression with all three isotopic masses and abundances substituted correctly
> 
> 1 mark for *A*<sub>r</sub> = 24.32 (to 2 decimal places, as specified)
> 
> Correct answer with no working scores 2 (per Edexcel convention for *A*<sub>r</sub> calculations)
> 
> 24.3 scores method mark only; 24.32 required for the accuracy mark
> 
> ecf from a transcription error in the abundance table if method is otherwise correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always read the question carefully for the d.p. or s.f. specification and round your final answer accordingly, but never round intermediate values.
> 
> Dividing by 100 is correct because the abundances sum to 100%; if they summed to a different total, you would divide by that number instead.
> 
> For *A*<sub>r</sub> calculations, a correct final answer alone scores full marks even without working, but always show the substitution step as a safety net in case of arithmetic slips.

parts.problemMd:
i) Give the electronic configuration of an aluminium atom, using the s, p, d notation.

[1]

ii) Explain why the first ionisation energy of aluminium is **lower** than that of magnesium.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
**i)** Electronic configuration of aluminium (atomic number 13):

1s²2s²2p<sup>6</sup>3s²3p¹** ****[1 mark]**

**ii)** Explanation:

- Magnesium's outermost electron is in the **3s** sub-shell; aluminium's outermost electron is in the **3p** sub-shell **[1 mark]**
- The 3p sub-shell is at a **higher energy** than the 3s sub-shell (and is more shielded by the filled 3s electrons), so less energy is required to remove aluminium's outermost electron, its first ionisation energy is therefore lower than that of magnesium **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) 1 mark for 1s²2s²2p<sup>6</sup>3s²3p¹
> 
> Correct superscripts; correct order; no missing sub-shells
> 
> Accept "1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p1" if superscripts are clearly intended
> 
> ii) 1 mark for identifying **3s for Mg AND 3p for Al** (both sub-shells must be named explicitly; "different sub-shell" alone scores zero)
> 
> 1 mark for **3p is at higher energy AND/OR more shielded than 3s**
> 
> Accept: "3p electron is further from nucleus / more shielded by 3s / at a higher sub-shell energy"
> 
> Reject: vague statements like "different orbital" without naming 3s and 3p explicitly

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always name both sub-shells (3s for Mg, 3p for Al), writing "different sub-shell" alone does not score.
> 
> The Group 2 → Group 3 anomaly hinges on the p sub-shell being at a higher energy and more shielded by the filled s sub-shell beneath it; this effect outweighs the small increase in nuclear charge from Mg to Al, which is why aluminium's first IE is lower despite having one more proton.

parts.problemMd: Explain the **general increase** in first ionisation energy across Period 3 from sodium to argon.
parts.solutionMd:
The general increase in first ionisation energy across Period 3 from sodium to argon is because:

- **Nuclear charge increases** across the period (Na has 11 protons; Ar has 18) **[1 mark]**
- Electrons are being added to the **same quantum shell** (n = 3), so shielding by inner-shell electrons stays approximately the same, the outer electron experiences a greater attraction to the nucleus, so more energy is required to remove it **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for **nuclear charge increases / number of protons increases** across the period
> 
> Reject "atomic number increases" alone (does not explicitly link to attractive force)
> 
> 1 mark for **same quantum shell / similar shielding** linked to **greater attraction → higher IE**
> 
> Accept "electrons added to the same shell", "shielding stays (approximately) the same"
> 
> Reject "no shielding" or "shielding increases"
> 
> Both points required — simply stating "IE increases" is not enough

> **[exam-tip]**
> Edexcel mark schemes for "explain the trend across Period 3" award marks for: (1) what changes (nuclear charge increases), and (2) what stays the same plus its consequence (same shell / similar shielding → greater attraction → higher IE). Do **not** state "atomic radius decreases" as a cause, the decreasing radius is a consequence of the same underlying effect, not a separate reason.

parts.problemMd:
The first four successive ionisation energies of an unknown element **Z** are shown in the table.

| Ionisation energy | 1st | 2nd | 3rd | 4th |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Value / kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> | 577 | 1820 | 2740 | 11 580 |

Deduce which group of the Periodic Table **Z** belongs to. Justify your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The group of the Periodic Table **Z** belongs to is:

- The largest jump in successive ionisation energies occurs between the 3rd and 4th IE (from 2740 to 11 580 kJ mol⁻¹, roughly a 4-fold increase) **[1 mark]**

- This indicates that the 4th electron is being removed from a new (inner) quantum shell, so Z has three electrons in its outermost shell, Z is therefore in Group 3 **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for identifying the largest jump between the 3rd and 4th IE
> 
> Accept any quantitative reference (e.g. "from 2740 to 11 580", "~4× increase")
> 
> 1 mark for concluding **Group 3**
> 
> Accept "3 outer electrons" if combined with the jump-rule reasoning
> 
> Reject Group 4 (mistakenly counting the large value as part of the outer shell)
> 
> Reject Group 1 (confusing "largest jump position" with element number)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The "jump rule" for successive IEs: if the largest jump is between the nth and (n+1)th IE, the element is in Group n. This is because the (n+1)th electron is being removed from a deeper (inner) shell, which takes much more energy. Always look for the biggest SINGLE jump, not the overall trend.

parts.problemMd:
i) Write an equation, including state symbols, to represent the **second ionisation energy** of magnesium.

[1]

ii) Suggest why the relative abundance of ²⁴Mg is much greater than that of <sup>25</sup>Mg or <sup>26</sup>Mg.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) Equation for the second ionisation energy of magnesium:

Mg⁺ (g) → Mg²⁺ (g) + e⁻ **[1 mark]**

ii)

- <sup>24</sup>Mg has a more stable nuclear configuration than ²⁵Mg or ²⁶Mg — its even number of protons and neutrons (12 of each) gives it a balanced neutron-to-proton ratio and greater nuclear stability, so it is the most abundant isotope. **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) 1 mark for **Mg⁺ (g) → Mg²⁺ (g) + e⁻**
> 
> State symbols (g) on both species mandatory
> 
> Accept e⁻ or e on RHS
> 
> Reject: missing state symbols; starting from Mg(g) (that would represent the 1st IE); products without (g); writing 2e⁻ on the RHS (only one electron is removed per ionisation step)
> 
> ii) 1 mark for any **one** valid reason linked to nuclear stability, e.g.:
> 
> - <sup>24</sup>Mg has a more stable nucleus / a more balanced neutron-to-proton ratio
> - <sup>24</sup>Mg has an even number of both protons and neutrons (12 each), giving greater nuclear stability
> 
> Accept any reasonable reference to nuclear stability / proton–neutron balance
> 
> Reject vague answers like "²⁴Mg is just more common" without giving a reason

> **[exam-tip]**
> The second ionisation energy starts from the **gaseous 1+ ion** (Mg⁺(g)), not the gaseous atom, a common error is to write Mg(g) instead of Mg⁺(g), which gives the 1st IE equation. State symbols (g) on both sides remain mandatory, and only **one** electron is removed per ionisation step. For isotope abundance, the underlying reason is nuclear stability: isotopes with even numbers of both protons and neutrons (like <sup>24</sup>Mg with 12p + 12n) tend to be more abundant due to nuclear shell effects.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about bonding and structure in a range of chlorides.

Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for magnesium chloride, MgCl<sub>2</sub>. Show outer shell electrons only.
parts.solutionMd:
The dot-and-cross diagram for MgCl<sub>2</sub> is:

![Diagram of magnesium chloride ionic bonding showing two chloride ions and a central magnesium ion with outer electron shells depicted.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/1-structure-bonding-and-introduction-to-organic-chemistry/1-6-ionic-and-metallic-bonding-and-structure/assets/002-diagram-of-magnesium-chloride-ionic-bonding-show.png)

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> 1 mark for **both Cl⁻ ions shown with 8 outer electrons** (7 of one symbol + 1 of the other, clearly distinguishing the donated electron) each in square brackets with 1− charge
> 
> Accept any combination of dots and crosses, provided the donated electron is clearly distinguished from the 7 original Cl electrons
> 
> Accept arrangement in any spatial position
>

> **[exam-tip]**

The electrons are indistinguishable in reality, but the diagram convention makes the transfer visible. Don't forget to bracket each ion with its charge, un-bracketed "Mg" and "Cl" labels score zero.

parts.problemMd:
Phosphorus pentachloride, PCl<sub>5</sub>, has the shape shown.

![Chemical structure of phosphorus pentachloride (PCl5) showing central phosphorus atom bonded to five chlorine atoms in a trigonal bipyramidal shape.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/1-structure-bonding-and-introduction-to-organic-chemistry/1-6-ionic-and-metallic-bonding-and-structure/assets/003-chemical-structure-of-phosphorus-pentachloride-p.png)

Explain the shape of a PCl<sub>5</sub> molecule and state its bond angles.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
To explain the shape of PCl<sub>5</sub> and its bond angles:

- The central P atom has **5 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs** of electrons **[1 mark]**
- These 5 electron pairs arrange themselves at **maximum separation / minimum repulsion** (VSEPR theory) **[1 mark]**
- The shape is therefore **trigonal bipyramidal** **[1 mark]**
- The bond angles are **120°** (between the three Cl atoms in the central plane) and **90°** (between those Cl atoms and the two Cl atoms above/below the plane) **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for identifying **5 bonding pairs AND 0 lone pairs** on the central P atom
> 
> Accept "5 bonding pairs, no lone pairs" or "5 electron pairs" if context makes clear these are bonding
> 
> 1 mark for **maximum separation / minimum repulsion** of electron pairs
> 
> Accept "repel equally", "as far apart as possible", "minimum electron-pair repulsion"
> 
> Accept reference to VSEPR theory
> 
> 1 mark for **trigonal bipyramidal**
> 
> Must include "bi" (or "bi-pyramidal" / "bipyramid")
> 
> Reject "trigonal pyramidal" (this is a different shape — NH<sub>3</sub> geometry)
> 
> 1 mark for **both bond angles 90° AND 120°** (both required for the mark)
> 
> Reject if only one angle is given

> **[exam-tip]**
> The most common error on PCl<sub>5</sub> is writing "trigonal **pyramidal**" (dropping the "bi") these are completely different shapes. PCl<sub>5</sub> has two distinct bond angles: **120°** between the three Cl atoms in the central plane, and **90°** between those and the two Cl atoms above/below. State both for full marks. The full chain of reasoning is: count electron pairs → apply VSEPR (max separation) → name the shape → state the angles.

parts.problemMd:
i) Explain why magnesium chloride, MgCl<sub>2</sub>, has more covalent character than barium chloride, BaCl<sub>2</sub>.

[2]

ii) Aluminium chloride can exist as the dimer Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub> in the gas phase. The dimer contains two dative (coordinate) covalent bonds.

State what is meant by a dative covalent bond, and draw the structure of Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub>, clearly showing all bonds (including the dative covalent bonds).

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
**i)** MgCl<sub>2</sub> has more covalent character than BaCl<sub>2</sub> because:

- Mg²⁺ is a smaller ion than Ba²⁺ (smaller ionic radius), so Mg²⁺ has a higher charge density / polarising power than Ba²⁺ **[1 mark]**
- The greater polarising power of Mg²⁺ distorts the electron cloud of the Cl⁻ anion more than Ba²⁺ does, resulting in more shared electron density between the ions, this is covalent character **[1 mark]**

**ii)** A dative covalent bond is:

- A covalent bond in which both shared electrons are donated by the same atom (one atom provides the entire electron pair). **[1 mark]**

The structure of Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub>:

![Structure of aluminium chloride dimer Al₂Cl₆ showing two Al atoms each bonded to 4 Cl atoms, with two bridging Cl atoms forming dative bonds to the Al atoms; arrows indicate dative bond direction (Cl → Al).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/1-structure-bonding-and-introduction-to-organic-chemistry/1-6-ionic-and-metallic-bonding-and-structure/assets/004-structure-of-aluminium-chloride-dimer-al-cl-show.png)

- Each Al is bonded to 4 Cl atoms; two Cl atoms bridge the two Al atoms via dative bonds (each bridging Cl donates a lone pair to the electron-deficient Al on the other side). **[1 mark]**
- The two dative bonds are clearly indicated by arrows pointing from bridging Cl to Al. **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) 1 mark for Mg²⁺ is smaller / has a smaller ionic radius than Ba²⁺ → higher charge density / polarising power
> 
> Accept either phrasing of cation comparison
> 
> 1 mark for greater polarisation / distortion of Cl⁻ electron cloud → more shared electron density → more covalent character
> 
> Must include both the distortion step AND the covalent-character consequence
> 
> ii) 1 mark for dative covalent bond definition: both shared electrons come from the same atom / one atom donates the entire electron pair
> 
> Accept "coordinate covalent bond" as an alternative name
> 
> 1 mark for correct overall structure of Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub>: 2 Al atoms each bonded to 4 Cl atoms, with 2 bridging Cl atoms (4 terminal Cl + 2 bridging Cl)
> 
> 1 mark for the two dative bonds clearly indicated by arrows pointing from bridging Cl to Al (or explicitly labelled as dative)
> 
> Accept any clear notation showing the dative direction (Cl → Al)
> 
> Reject Al → Cl arrows (wrong direction, Al is electron-deficient)

> **[exam-tip]**
> For polarisation comparisons: identify which ion differs (cation or anion), then apply the correct rule. If the cation changes, polarising power matters (small + highly charged → more polarising). If the anion changes, polarisability matters (large + more negative → more polarisable).
> 
> For Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub>: AlCl<sub>3</sub> has only 6 outer electrons on Al, so Al is electron-deficient and accepts a lone pair from a chlorine on a neighbouring AlCl<sub>3</sub> to form a dative covalent bond.
> 
> The dative arrow always points from the donor (Cl) TO the acceptor (Al). The Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub> structure is a specified content point and features regularly in Edexcel exams.

parts.problemMd:
Magnesium chloride conducts electricity in some physical states but not others.

Explain why MgCl<sub>2</sub> does not conduct electricity when solid, but does conduct electricity when molten or in aqueous solution.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
To explain the conductivity of MgCl<sub>2</sub> in different states:

- In **solid** MgCl<sub>2</sub>, the Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are held in fixed positions in an ionic lattice, they cannot move, so there are no mobile charge carriers and the solid does not conduct. **[1 mark]**
- In **molten** MgCl<sub>2</sub>, heating breaks down the ionic lattice; the Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions become free to move and so can carry charge through the liquid. **[1 mark]**
- In **aqueous** MgCl<sub>2</sub>, the ionic lattice dissociates in water, giving mobile hydrated Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions that are free to move through the solution and carry charge. **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for solid does not conduct linked to ions held in fixed positions / cannot move / no mobile charge carriers
> 
> 1 mark for molten conducts linked to ions free to move (lattice broken by heating)
> 
> 1 mark for aqueous conducts linked to ions dissociate / become hydrated / free to move in solution
> 
> Accept "ions carry charge" as equivalent to "conducting"
> 
> Reject "electrons move", that is the metallic conduction mechanism, not ionic
> 
> All three states must be addressed for full marks

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ionic conduction depends entirely on whether the **ions** can move. Electron conduction (as in metals) is a different mechanism, stating that MgCl<sub>2</sub> "conducts because electrons move" scores zero.
> 
> Always link: state of matter → arrangement of ions → can they move → can they conduct. Solid: ions fixed; molten: lattice broken, ions free; aqueous: lattice dissociated, ions hydrated and free.

In the solid state, beryllium chloride forms a polymeric structure.

parts.problemMd:

Predict the two bond angles, justifying your answers by referring to electron-pair repulsion theory.
parts.solutionMd:
Predicting the two bond angles, and a justification:

- The bond angle in BeCl<sub>2 </sub>(g) / linear is 180°; **[1 mark]**
- The bond angle in BeCl<sub>2 </sub>(s) / polymeric is 109.5°; **[1 mark]**
- Electron pairs / bonds repel each other to minimise repulsion; **[1 mark]**
- 4 electron pairs / bonds in solid 
**OR** 
2 bonding pairs / 2 bonds (no lone pairs) in gas; **[1 mark]**

- *You should know the bond angle for BeCl*<sub>*2*</sub>* (g)*

parts.problemMd:
Anhydrous calcium chloride is a crystalline, ionic solid which melts at 772°C.

Draw a dot-and-cross diagram for calcium chloride.

Show the outer electrons only.

parts.problemMd: Explain why gaseous beryllium chloride and solid calcium chloride have different types of bonding.
parts.solutionMd:
Gaseous beryllium chloride and solid calcium chloride have different types of bonding because:

- Beryllium is smaller / has fewer electron shells / has a higher charge density (than calcium)
**OR**
Beryllium is more electronegative (than calcium); **[1 mark]**
- Beryllium ion / Be<sup>2+</sup> is more polarising (than calcium ion / Ca<sup>2+</sup>)
**OR**
Calcium loses (outer) electrons more easily (than beryllium)
**OR**
The difference in electronegativity between calcium and chlorine is greater (than between beryllium and chlorine); **[1 mark]**
- The beryllium-chlorine bond has a higher degree of covalency (than the calcium-chlorine bond); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Whilst it is ions that cause polarisation, you would not be penalised for saying that beryllium is more polarising than calcium as opposed to beryllium ions / calcium ions*
- *For the final mark, you could state that the bonding in beryllium is (more) covalent or the bonding in calcium chloride is (more) ionic*
- *The final mark is only awarded if one of the other two marks is scored*
- *As a rule of thumb, if the difference in electronegativity between two atoms is greater than 2 on the Pauling scale, an ionic bond will form and less than two will lead to a covalent bond forming*

Antimony(V) chloride (SbCl<sub>5</sub>) is a liquid made up of SbCl<sub>5</sub> molecules.

**(2)**

ii) Draw a dot-and-cross diagram to show the bonding in a molecule of SbCl<sub>5.</sub> 
Use dots (•) to represent the Sb electrons, and crosses (**x**) to represent the Cl electrons. 
Show outer electrons only.

**(2)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) PCl<sub>5</sub> has a higher melting temperature than SbCl<sub>5</sub> because:

- Strong(er) (electrostatic) attraction between ions (in PCl<sub>5</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- (Than) weak intermolecular forces (in SbCl<sub>5</sub>); **[1 mark]**

ii) A dot-and-cross diagram to show the bonding in a molecule of SbCl<sub>5</sub>:

![sbcl5-dot-and-cross](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/1-structure-bonding-and-introduction-to-organic-chemistry/1-7-covalent-bonding-and-structure/assets/006-sbcl5-dot-and-cross.png)

- Central Sb with five bond pairs and no lone pairs; **[1 mark]**
- Five Cl atoms each with one bond pair and three lone pairs; **[1 mark]**

- *Phosphorous(V) chloride is an ionic compound whereas antimony(V) chloride is a simple molecule*

- *You can explain the electrostatic attraction in a number of ways that are creditworthy:*

  - *PCl*<sub>*5*</sub>* has strong ionic bonds or a strong ionic lattice*
  - *There is a strong attraction between positive and negative charges / cations and anions / PCl*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*+*</sup>* and PCl*<sub>*6*</sub><sup>*–*</sup>
- *You can refer to the intermolecular forces as London, van der Waals, dispersion, temporary-induced  dipole or instantaneous-induced dipole forces*
- *Stating that ionic bonding is stronger than intermolecular forces will score 2 marks*
- *Antimony, Sb, is in Group 5 so will have 5 electrons in its outer shell*

parts.problemMd:
Arsenic also forms a pentachloride with the formula AsCl<sub>5</sub>.

Give **one** possible reason why nitrogen is the only Group 5 element that does **not** form a pentachloride.
parts.solutionMd:
**One** possible reason why nitrogen is the only Group 5 element that does **not** form a pentachloride is:

Any **one** from:

- (Nitrogen has) no 2d orbitals; **[1 mark]**
- (Nitrogen) cannot expand its octet / cannot have more than 8 electrons in its outer shell; **[1 mark]**
- (Nitrogen is) too small (to bond to 5 atoms); **[1 mark]**
- Repulsion between electron pairs would be too great; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *Expansion of the octet can occur if the outer shell has enough orbitals to accommodate more electrons*
- *This can happen in elements that have access to d orbitals*
- *Nitrogen has the electronic configuration of 1s*<sup>*2*</sup>*2s*<sup>*2*</sup>*2p*<sup>*3*</sup>* so can only accommodate 3 more electrons to fill the n = 2 shell; there is no 2d subshell available so no more electrons can be accomodated*
- *The elements below nitrogen in Group 5 have access to a d orbital which will accommodate extra electrons so can form pentachloride compounds*

Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are metals.

ii) Melting temperature depends on the strength of metallic bonding.

Explain why the metallic bonding in magnesium is much stronger than that in sodium.

parts.solutionMd:
i) Metallic bonding is:

- The attraction between positive ions / cations and delocalised electrons; **[1 mark]**

- Mg<sup>2+</sup> is smaller (than Na<sup>+</sup>); **[1 mark]**
- Mg<sup>2+</sup> has a higher charge (than Na<sup>+</sup>); **[1 mark]**
- Greater attraction between the delocalised electrons and the Mg<sup>2+ </sup>ions / Mg<sup>2+</sup> nuclei; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
Heptane, C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub> , is an alkane found in crude oil.

Heptane can undergo incomplete combustion.

i) Give a reason why incomplete combustion sometimes occurs.

**(1)**

i) Write the equation for the incomplete combustion of heptane, forming carbon monoxide and water as the **only** products. State symbols are not required.

**(1)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) Incomplete combustion sometimes occurs because:

- There is a limited supply / lack of oxygen / air; **[1 mark]**

i) The equation for the incomplete combustion of heptane, forming carbon monoxide and water as the **only** products is:

- 2C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub> + 15O<sub>2</sub> → 14CO + 16H<sub>2</sub>O 
**OR **
C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub> + 7½O<sub>2</sub> → 7CO + 8H<sub>2</sub>O; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Remember:** Complete combustion has a plentiful supply of oxygen / air while incomplete combustion has a limited supply *

  - *For incomplete combustion, you will normally be told the products as carbon monoxide / carbon can be formed alongside water*
- *To write the equation:*

  - *You are told that it is a combustion reaction, so oxygen is one of the reactants*
  - *The question tells you that the products are carbon monoxide and water C*<sub>*7*</sub>*H*<sub>*16*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → CO + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *The seven carbons in heptane will make 7 carbon dioxides The sixteen hydrogens in heptane will make 8 waters C*<sub>*7*</sub>*H*<sub>*16*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **7**CO + **8**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *This means that fifteen atoms of oxygen are needed, which come from 7½ oxygen molecules C*<sub>*7*</sub>*H*<sub>*16*</sub>* + **7½**O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **7**CO + **8**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*

parts.problemMd:
Heptane, C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub> , reacts with chlorine in the presence of ultraviolet radiation.

i) State the type and mechanism of this reaction.

**(2)**

ii) Give the mechanism for the reaction to produce C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>15</sub>Cl, C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>30</sub> and HCl as the **only **products.

Include the name of each of the steps in your mechanism. 
Curly half-arrows are **not **required.

**(7)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) The type and mechanism of this reaction are:

- Type: (Free) radical; **[1 mark]**
- Mechanism: Substitution; **[1 mark]**

ii) The mechanism for the reaction to produce C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>15</sub>Cl, C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>30</sub> and HCl as the **only **products is:

- Initiation (step); **[1 mark]**
- Example initiation equation Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2Cl• **OR **1⁄2Cl<sub>2</sub> → Cl•; **[1 mark]**
- Propagation / propagating (step); **[1 mark]**
- Propagation step 1: C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub> + Cl• → C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>15</sub>• + HCl; **[1 mark]**
- Propagation step 2: C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>15</sub>• + Cl<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>15</sub>Cl + Cl•; **[1 mark]**
- Termination / terminating (step); **[1 mark]**
- 2C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>15</sub>• → C<sub>14</sub>H<sub>30</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 7 marks]**

- *"The presence of ultraviolet radiation" is a good indicator for a free radical substitution reaction*
- *Initiation step:*

  - *Since the reaction is with chlorine, the initiation step will be the homolytic fission of the chlorine molecule to form two chlorine radicals, Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 2Cl•*
- *Propagation steps:*

  - *Write the overall reaction equation twice (in pencil) 1) C*<sub>*7*</sub>*H*<sub>*16*</sub>* + Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* → C*<sub>*7*</sub>*H*<sub>*15*</sub>*Cl + HCl 2) C*<sub>*7*</sub>*H*<sub>*16*</sub>* + Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* → C*<sub>*7*</sub>*H*<sub>*15*</sub>*Cl + HCl*
  - *Remove a chlorine atom from both sides of equation 1 and replace it with a radical symbol Do not form hydrogen radicals 1) C*<sub>*7*</sub>*H*<sub>*16*</sub>* + Cl• → C*<sub>*7*</sub>*H*<sub>*15*</sub>*• + HCl*
  - *Remove a hydrogen atom from both sides of equation 2 and replace it with a radical symbol 2) C*<sub>*7*</sub>*H*<sub>*15*</sub>*• + Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* → C*<sub>*7*</sub>*H*<sub>*15*</sub>*Cl + Cl•*
  - *You can double-check that your equations are correct - when the two equations are combined, you should get the overall equation again*
- *Termination step:*

  - *There are three possible termination steps (but not all of them will score any marks)*
  - *2Cl• → Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* *
  
    - *This equation will rarely score any marks for a termination step as it is essentially undoing the initiation step *

parts.problemMd:
Using excess oxygen, 25 cm<sup>3</sup> of a gaseous hydrocarbon C<sub>x</sub>H<sub>y</sub> was burned completely.

After cooling to room temperature the total gas volume was measured and found to be 75 cm<sup>3</sup> less than the total gas volume before the mixture was ignited.

When the product gases were shaken with potassium hydroxide solution, the total gas volume decreased by a further 100 cm<sup>3</sup>.

All gas volumes were measured at room temperature and pressure.

A general equation for the combustion of a hydrocarbon is

$C_{x} H_{y}  +  \left(x + \frac{y}{4}\right)  O_{2}  \rightarrow  xCO_{2} +  \left(\frac{y}{2}\right)  H_{2} O$

Determine the molecular formula of C<sub>x</sub>H<sub>y</sub>. You **must** show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
To determine the molecular formula of C<sub>x</sub>H<sub>y</sub>:

- Identification of correct algebraic equation for x 
**AND **
Solves equation to obtain x From equation 1 mol of C<sub>x</sub>H<sub>y</sub> gives x mol of CO<sub>2</sub> so 25 mol will give 25x mol CO<sub>2</sub> and 25 cm<sup>3</sup> will give 25x cm<sup>3 </sup>CO<sub>2</sub> 25x = 100 and x = 4; **[1 mark] **
- Identification of correct algebraic equation for x and y Change in volume is (25 + 25(x + $\frac{y}{4}$) − 25x = 75; **[1 mark] **
- Solves equation to obtain y and gives the formula of the hydrocarbon $\frac{25y}{4}$ = 50 therefore y = 8 and C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>;** [1 mark] **

**Final answer:** **[Total: 3 marks] **

- *In order to work out the formula of the cyclic hydrocarbon, you need to work out x and y*
- *CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* reacts with KOH to give potassium carbonate K*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>* and water in a neutralisation reaction*

  - *CO*<sub>*2 *</sub>*+ 2KOH → K*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3 *</sub>*+ H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *Therefore, the volume of CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* is 100 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
  - *As the volume of the hydrocarbon gas is 25 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* we know x to be *$\frac{100}{25}$* or 4*
- *To work out y*

  - *You know the total volume of CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* is 100 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* and the hydrocarbon has a volume of 25 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* so we can use this in our equation *
  - *You also need to include the fact that the overall volume decreased by 75 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
  - *As you know x you can include this in 4 + (*$\frac{y}{4}$*)*
  - *Finally, we must include in the volume of oxygen the 25 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of the hydrocarbon*
  
    - *Imagine the 25 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* represents 1 mole of the hydrocarbon *
    - *(25 + 25(4 + (*$\frac{y}{4}$*) − (25 x 4) = 75) so y = 8*

parts.problemMd:
The reaction profile for an endothermic reaction is shown.

![Energy profile diagram showing an endothermic reaction: reactants to products, peak activation energy of +150 kJ mol⁻¹ and enthalpy change of +80 kJ mol⁻¹](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/2-energetics-group-chemistry-halogenoalkanes-and-alcohols/2-1-energetics/assets/001-energy-profile-diagram-showing-an-endothermic-re.png)

What is the activation energy of the **reverse** reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- For an endothermic reaction, the products sit Δ*H* **above** the reactants on the enthalpy profile, so:

  - Forward *E*<sub>a</sub> = reactants → transition state peak
  - Reverse *E*<sub>a</sub> = products → transition state peak
- Since products are higher than reactants, the reverse *E*<sub>a</sub> is **smaller** than the forward *E*<sub>a</sub> by exactly Δ*H*

reverse *E*<sub>a</sub> = forward *E*<sub>a</sub> − Δ*H* = 150 − 80 = +70 kJ mol<sup>–¹</sup>

**A** is incorrect as activation energies are always **positive**. A negative *E*<sub>a</sub> is physically meaningless. This answer comes from doing Δ*H* − forward *E*<sub>a</sub> the wrong way round.

**C** is incorrect as +80 kJ mol<sup>–¹</sup> is just Δ*H*, this isn't the activation energy. Δ*H* and *E*<sub>a</sub> are two different quantities.

**D** is incorrect as +230 kJ mol<sup>–¹</sup> comes from adding Δ*H* instead of subtracting, this would be correct for an exothermic reaction (where Δ*H* is negative), but here Δ*H* is positive so subtraction is needed

> **[exam-tip]**
> For any reaction, the forward and reverse activation energies are linked by Δ*H* through a single formula:
> 
> reverse *E*<sub>a</sub> = forward *E*<sub>a</sub> − Δ*H*
> 
> This one formula works for both endothermic and exothermic reactions, as long as you use the signed value of Δ*H*:
> 
> - **Endothermic** (Δ*H* positive): subtracting a positive Δ*H* gives a smaller result → reverse *E*<sub>a</sub> < forward *E*<sub>a</sub>
> - **Exothermic** (Δ*H* negative): subtracting a negative Δ*H* is the same as adding → reverse *E*<sub>a</sub> > forward *E*<sub>a</sub>
> 
> Edexcel past papers usually test this visually using an enthalpy profile with lettered arrows (e.g. W, X, Y, Z), and ask you to identify the algebraic relationship between the arrows. The mark schemes express it as forward ***E***<sub>a</sub> - reverse ***E***<sub>**a**</sub> = Δ***H***, which is the same formula rearranged.
> 
> Two common slips to watch out for:
> 
> - Confusing Δ*H* with *E*<sub>a</sub>, they are different quantities. Δ*H* is the overall enthalpy change (positive for endothermic, negative for exothermic); *E*<sub>a</sub> is the energy barrier a collision must overcome (**always positive**).
> - Getting a negative answer for *E*<sub>a</sub>, this is physically impossible. If your working gives you a negative activation energy, you've made a sign error (usually adding instead of subtracting Δ*H*).
> 
> Check your answer by picturing the enthalpy profile:
> 
> - For endothermic reactions:
> 
>   - The products sit higher than reactants
>   - So, the reverse *E*<sub>a</sub> must be smaller than forward *E*<sub>a</sub>.
> - For exothermic reactions
> 
>   - The products sit lower than the reactants
>   - So, the reverse *E*<sub>a</sub> must be larger than forward *E*<sub>a</sub>.

parts.problemMd:
The enthalpy changes of combustion, Δ<sub>c</sub>*H*, are given below.

| Substance | Δ<sub>c</sub>*H* / kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> |
|---|---|
| C (s) | –394 |
| H<sub>2</sub> (g) | –286 |
| CH<sub>3</sub>OH (l) | –726 |

What is the enthalpy change of formation, Δ<sub>f</sub>*H*, of methanol, CH<sub>3</sub>OH (l)?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The formation reaction:

C (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub> (g) + ½O<sub>2</sub> (g) → CH<sub>3</sub>OH (l)

- Using the Hess cycle formula for combustion data:

Δ*H*<sub>f</sub> = Σ Δ*H*<sub>c</sub>(reactants) − Σ Δ*H*<sub>c</sub>(products)

Δ*H*<sub>f</sub> = [Δ*H*<sub>c</sub>(C) + 2Δ*H*<sub>c</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>)] − Δ*H*<sub>c</sub>(CH<sub>3</sub>OH)

Δ*H*<sub>f</sub> = [−394 + 2(−286)] − (−726)

Δ*H*<sub>f</sub> = −966 + 726 = −240 kJ mol<sup>−¹</sup>

**B** is incorrect as +240 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> comes from subtracting reactants from products instead of products from reactants (the formula reversed) — right magnitude, wrong sign

**C** is incorrect as −966 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> is the sum of the combustion enthalpies of the reactants only [Δ*H*<sub>c</sub>(C) + 2Δ*H*<sub>c</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>) = −394 + 2(−286) = −966]; the methanol combustion enthalpy must still be subtracted

**D** is incorrect as −1406 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> is obtained by (i) using 1× H<sub>2</sub> instead of 2×, AND (ii) summing all three combustion enthalpies instead of subtracting Δ*H*<sub>c</sub>(CH<sub>3</sub>OH): −394 + (−286) + (−726) = −1406

> **[exam-tip]**
> The two Hess-cycle formulas go in opposite directions, memorise both and check which data type you've been given:
> 
> - **Combustion** data: Δ*H* = Σ Δ*H*<sub>c</sub>(reactants) − Σ Δ*H*<sub>c</sub>(products)
> - **Formation** data: Δ*H* = Σ Δ*H*<sub>f</sub>(products) − Σ Δ*H*<sub>f</sub>(reactants)
> 
> Three common slips to avoid in Hess calculations:
> 
> - **Applying the formation formula to a combustion cycle** (or vice versa), gives the right magnitude but the wrong sign
> - **Forgetting the stoichiometric coefficient**; e.g. 2 mol H<sub>2</sub> in this question must be multiplied by Δ*H*<sub>c</sub>(H<sub>2</sub>)
> - **Missing the sign check**; combustion values MUST be negative; a positive answer for Δ*H*<sub>c</sub> is always wrong
> 
> Examiner reports flagged a Hess calculation as one of the most challenging questions on the paper, with candidates routinely reversing signs or missing coefficients.

parts.problemMd: Which reagent produces a silver mirror when warmed with propanal but **not** when warmed with propanone?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Tollens’ reagent (ammoniacal silver nitrate) oxidises aldehydes to carboxylic acids, reducing Ag⁺ ions to metallic silver, which deposits as a silver mirror on the inside of the test tube
- Propanal (aldehyde) → silver mirror observed
- Propanone (ketone) cannot be easily oxidised under these conditions → no reaction

**A** is incorrect as 2,4-DNPH produces a **yellow or orange precipitate** with **both** aldehydes and ketones (it tests for the C=O group, not specifically for aldehydes), so it does not give a silver mirror

**B** is incorrect as acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> distinguishes aldehydes from ketones by an **orange → green** colour change, not a silver mirror

**C** is incorrect as Fehling’s solution distinguishes aldehydes from ketones by forming a **brick-red precipitate** of Cu<sub>2</sub>O, not a silver mirror

> **[exam-tip]**
> Silver mirror observation is **exclusive** to Tollens’ reagent. The three common tests for distinguishing aldehydes from ketones each give distinct observations:
> 
> - **Tollens’** → silver mirror
> - **Fehling’s / Benedict’s** → brick-red (Cu<sub>2</sub>O) precipitate
> - **Acidified K~2~Cr~2~O~7~** → orange to green colour change
> 
> All three require **warming** or **heating under reflux**; a Paper 4 examiner-report flag is candidates omitting the heat condition.

parts.problemMd:
A colourless liquid, **Z**, is known to be either ethanol (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) or methoxymethane (CH<sub>3</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub>).

The mass spectrum and infrared spectrum of **Z** are shown.

![Mass spectrum graph showing relative intensity versus m/z (mass-to-charge) ratio. Peaks at m/z 30, 40, 45, highest at 30.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/2-energetics-group-chemistry-halogenoalkanes-and-alcohols/2-10-organic-chemistry-techniques-and-spectra/assets/001-mass-spectrum-graph-showing-relative-intensity-v.png)

![IR spectrum of ethanol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/2-energetics-group-chemistry-halogenoalkanes-and-alcohols/2-10-organic-chemistry-techniques-and-spectra/assets/002-ir-spectrum-of-ethanol.png)

What is the relative molecular mass, *M*<sub>r</sub>, of compound **Z**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The **molecular ion peak** (M<sup>+</sup>) in a mass spectrum corresponds to the mass of the whole intact molecule (less one electron, which has negligible mass)
- M<sup>+</sup> is always the peak at the **highest m/z**

  - Ignoring small isotope peaks at M+1, M+2
- M<sup>+</sup> = 46

  - So, *M*<sub>r</sub>(Z) = 46
- Both ethanol (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) and methoxymethane (CH<sub>3</sub>OCH<sub>3</sub>) have *M*<sub>r</sub> = 46, they are **structural isomers**, so the mass spectrum alone cannot distinguish them

**A** is incorrect as 30 is *M*<sub>r</sub> of methanal (HCHO)

**B** is incorrect as 44 is *M*<sub>r</sub> of CO<sub>2</sub>, propane, or ethanal (CH<sub>3</sub>CHO), not Z

**D** is incorrect as 60 is *M*<sub>r</sub> of propan-1-ol or ethanoic acid

> **[exam-tip]**
> The molecular ion peak (M<sup>+</sup>) is always the highest-m/z peak, NOT the tallest peak. The tallest peak is the base peak, which represents the most stable fragment; these are usually different peaks.
> 
> Ethanol (an alcohol, with C–O–H bonds) and methoxymethane (an ether, with C–O–C bonds) are structural isomers, identical *M*<sub>r</sub> but different functional groups, so IR is needed to tell them apart (see parts b and c).
> 
> When writing fragment ions, always include the positive charge: CH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>, not CH<sub>3</sub> or CH<sub>3</sub>•. The mass spectrometer only detects positive ions, so every fragment ion must carry a + charge in your answer.

parts.problemMd: The broad IR absorption in the range 3230–3550 cm<sup>–1</sup> is characteristic of which bond?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- A broad absorption in the range 3230–3550 cm<sup>–¹</sup> is characteristic of the O–H bond of an alcohol
- Key IR absorption bands to memorise for paper 2:

  - O–H (alcohol): broad, 3230–3550 cm<sup>–¹</sup>
  - O–H (carboxylic acid): very broad, 2500–3300 cm<sup>–¹</sup> (extends below 3200; the distinguishing feature)
  - N–H (amine): sharp, 3300–3500 cm<sup>–¹</sup>
  - C=O: sharp, 1680–1750 cm<sup>–¹</sup>
  - C–H: 2850–3100 cm<sup>–¹</sup>
  - C=C: 1620–1680 cm<sup>–¹</sup>

**A** is incorrect as C=C absorbs near 1650 cm<sup>–¹</sup> (well below the stated range)

**B** is incorrect as C=O absorbs at 1680–1750 cm<sup>–¹</sup> (sharp), not 3230–3550 cm<sup>–¹</sup>

**C** is incorrect as C–H absorbs near 3000 cm<sup>–¹</sup> (medium width, lower in the range)

> **[exam-tip]**
> The IR absorption table is in the paper 2 data booklet. Use it, don't guess. Two key shape distinctions:
> 
> 1. O–H is broad
> 2. C=O is sharp
> 
> Watch for the alcohol-vs-carboxylic-acid O–H trap. These two peaks sit in different positions and have different breadths:
> 
> - Alcohol O–H: 3230–3550 cm<sup>–¹</sup> (broad)
> - Carboxylic acid O–H: 3300–2500 cm<sup>–¹</sup> (much broader, extending lower)
> 
> If a peak reaches down into 2500–2800 cm<sup>–¹</sup>, that's a carboxylic acid, not an alcohol.
> 
> For full marks in structured questions, you need to state **both** the specific bond (e.g. "O–H in an alcohol") **AND **the wavenumber range when justifying the presence of a functional group. Giving one without the other loses the mark.

- Ethanol (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) has an O–H bond

  - This gives a broad absorption at 3200–3550 cm<sup>–¹</sup>
- Methoxymethane (CH<sub>3</sub>–O–CH<sub>3</sub>) is an ether with a C–O–C linkage but no O–H

  - It would show no absorption in the 3200–3550 cm<sup>–¹</sup> region

**D** is incorrect as methoxymethane is an ether (CH<sub>3</sub>–O–CH<sub>3</sub>) with no O–H bond. The broad 3200–3550 cm<sup>–¹</sup> absorption actually rules methoxymethane OUT, not in

> **[exam-tip]**
> When identifying a compound from combined mass spectra and infrared data, always cite the specific spectral evidence. Give the bond **AND **the wavenumber range.
> 
> For example, full-mark phrasing looks like: "the broad peak at 3200–3550 cm<sup>-1</sup> indicates an O–H bond in an alcohol".  The generic phrasing "because IR shows alcohol" loses marks in structured questions.
> 
> When two compounds are structural isomers (same *M*<sub>r</sub>, different connectivity), *M*<sub>r</sub> alone can't tell them apart.
> 
> The IR evidence is load-bearing. Before interpreting the IR, think about which functional groups each candidate compound actually contains:
> 
> - Alcohols → O–H (broad, 3200–3550 cm<sup>–¹</sup>)
> - Ethers → C–O–C (weak, 1000–1300 cm<sup>–¹</sup>)
> - Aldehydes / ketones / carboxylic acids → C=O (sharp, 1680–1750 cm<sup>–¹</sup>)

**C** is incorrect as covalent bonds are not broken when a substance boils, only intermolecular forces are; both isomers contain the same C–C and C–H bonds

> **[exam-tip]**
> For comparisons of structural isomers, electron count is identical, so London dispersion forces depend on **shape and surface contact**:
> 
> - Long, straight molecules pack closely → stronger LDF → higher boiling point
> - Branched, spherical molecules pack poorly → weaker LDF → lower boiling point
> 
> A common slip is reaching for "more electrons" before checking the molecular formulas, always count electrons first to decide whether LDF strength comparisons are in play at all.

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: Pentane has greater surface contact between its molecules

parts.problemMd: What is the oxidation number of chromium in Na<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- The sum of the oxidation numbers for a substance with no charge should be 0
- In Na<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>:

  - Sodium is a Group 1 metal so its oxidation number is always +1
  - Oxygen always has an oxidation number of -2 (unless in a peroxide)
  
    - (-2 x 7) + (+1 x 2)= - 12
    - There are two chromium atoms so each one must have an oxidation number of +6 to achieve 0 overall

**A** is incorrect as this does not consider the numbers of oxygen and sodium atoms in the compound

**B** is incorrect as  this is the number of chromium atoms in the compound

**C** is incorrect as  this does not consider the oxidation numbers of sodium and oxygen

parts.problemMd:
In an oxide of nitrogen, the oxidation number of nitrogen is +4.

Which is the formula of the oxide?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- The oxidation number of oxygen is +2
- The sum of the oxidation number for N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4 </sub>should equal 0

  - There are four oxygen atoms so 4 x -2 = -8
  - There are two nitrogen atoms so -8 ÷ 2 = -4
  - To bring the overall oxidation state to 0, the oxidation number of N must be +4

**A** is incorrect as the oxidation number of nitrogen is +1

**B** is incorrect as  the oxidation number of nitrogen averages +3

**D** is incorrect as  the oxidation number of nitrogen is +5

parts.problemMd: What is the oxidation number of phosphorus in the phosphate ion, P$O_{4}^{3-}$?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is**** C**** because:**

- For an ion, the sum of the oxidation numbers should equal the charge on the ion

  - For this question, the charge on the ion is -3
- Oxygen always has an oxidation number of -2 (unless it is a peroxide)

  - There are 4 oxygen atoms which give a total of -8
- There is only one phosphorus atom

  - So, to bring the overall charge up to -3, phosphorus must have an oxidation number of +5

**A**, **B** and **D** are incorrect as  these are the wrong value

parts.problemMd: What is the oxidation number of manganese in the ion MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Each O has an oxidation number of –2 (standard rule for oxyanions)
- Total O contribution: 4 x (-2) = -8
- Overall charge on MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>–</sup> is –1

Mn + (–8) = –1, giving Mn = **+7**

**A** is incorrect as it assumes oxygen is -1 or ignores overall charge

**B** is incorrect as it ignores the overall -1 charge of the ion (calculates as if 
MnO<sub>4</sub> is neutral)

**C** is incorrect as it assumes oxygen is -2 but misses the -1 ion charge, making Mn = 8

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always write oxidation numbers in the sign-first format (+7, not 7+). The ionic-charge form loses the mark. A useful shortcut is that if the compound's name contains a Roman numeral (e.g. manganate(VII), chromate(VI)), that number is the oxidation state of the element.
> 
> Some common slips to avoid when assigning oxidation numbers:
> 
> - Applying O = –2 in compounds containing fluorine
> - F forces O to be positive
> - Assigning H = +1 in metal hydrides like NaH, LiH or LiAlH<sub>4</sub>
> - H is actually –1 in these

parts.problemMd: Which reaction is an example of disproportionation?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Disproportionation is where the same element, in the same starting** **species, is simultaneously oxidised AND reduced in the same reaction
- In C: chlorine starts at oxidation number 0 in Cl<sub>2</sub> and ends up in two different oxidation states:

  - –1 in NaCl (reduced; Cl gained an electron)
  - +1 in NaClO (oxidised; Cl lost an electron)
- Chlorine from a single starting species (Cl<sub>2</sub>) has been both oxidised and reduced.

**A** is incorrect as this is thermal decomposition. No oxidation number changes at all (not a redox reaction)

**B** is incorrect as this is halogen displacement. Cl<sub>2</sub> is reduced (0 → –1) but the Br<sup>–</sup> is oxidised (–1 → 0). So, two different species change, not one

**D** is incorrect as Na is oxidised and H<sup>+</sup> in H<sub>2</sub>O is reduced. Again two different species change

> **[exam-tip]**
> The disproportionation test has three parts, all must be met:
> 
> - the same element
> - in the same reactant species
> - is simultaneously oxidised AND reduced
> 
> Cl<sub>2</sub> + NaOH is the common example you should learn:
> 
> **Cl**<sub>2</sub>** (0) → Cl**<sup>-</sup>** (–1, reduced) + ClO**<sup>-</sup>** (+1, oxidised)**
> 
> Some points to consider include:
> 
> - Marks are awarded for explicit oxidation-number values, not electron descriptions.
> - Writing "Cl gains / loses electrons" on its own is not enough, always give the numbers.
> - Watch out for false positives
> 
>   - IO<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup> + I<sup>–</sup> → I<sub>2</sub> is not** **disproportionation
>   - It's comproportionation, where two different species of the same element combine.
>   - If the element comes from two different reactants, it fails the test.

parts.problemMd:
Hydrogen peroxide, H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, breaks down into water and oxygen.

In terms of oxidation and reduction, how do hydrogen and oxygen change in this reaction?

|   | ** ** | **Hydrogen** | **Oxygen** |
|---|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **A** | oxidised | reduced |
| ☐ | **B** | oxidised and reduced | unchanged |
| ☐ | **C** | reduced | oxidised |
| ☐ | **D** | unchanged | oxidised and reduced |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- 2H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2 </sub>→ 2H<sub>2</sub>O + O<sub>2</sub>
- For oxygen:

  - The oxidation number of oxygen in a peroxide is -1
  - The oxidation number of oxygen in its elemental state is 0
  - The oxidation number of oxygen in water is -2
  - There has been both an increase and decrease in oxidation number so it has been both reduced and oxidised
- For hydrogen:

  - The oxidation number of hydrogen in a peroxide is +1
  - The oxidation number of hydrogen in water is +1
  - The oxidation number is unchanged so hydrogen is neither reduced or oxidised

**A** is incorrect as  hydrogen is unchanged and oxygen is both oxidised and reduced

**B** is incorrect as hydrogen is unchanged and oxygen is both oxidised and reduced

**C** is incorrect as hydrogen is unchanged and oxygen is both oxidised and reduced

**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- **x** IO<sub>3</sub><sup>-</sup> + **y** S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>6</sub><sup>2-</sup> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O → **z **SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> + 8H<sup>+</sup>+ I<sub>2</sub>

- The change in oxidation number of S must therefore be +10
- The oxidation number of S in S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>6</sub><sup>2- </sup>is +5 and in SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> is +6

parts.problemMd:
Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid.

Mg (s) + 2HCl (aq) → MgCl<sub>2 </sub>(aq) + H<sub>2 </sub>(g)

Which statement about this reaction is correct?

- Hydrogen ions, therefore, act as an oxidising agent

parts.problemMd:
A diprotic acid, H<sub>2</sub>A, was titrated with sodium hydroxide solution.

A 25.0 cm<sup>3 </sup>portion of 0.100 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> sodium hydroxide solution required 12.80 cm<sup>3</sup> of the solution of the diprotic acid for complete neutralisation. What is the concentration of H<sub>2</sub>A in mol dm<sup>−3</sup>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- The number of moles of NaOH = 0.025 x 0.1 = 0.0025 mol
- The ratio of H<sub>2</sub>A to NaOH is 1:2 so the moles of H<sub>2</sub>A is $\frac{0.0025}{2}$= 0.00125 mol
- The concentration of H<sub>2</sub>A is $\frac{0.0125}{0.0128}$= 9.77 × 10<sup>−2</sup> dm<sup>3</sup>
- Don't forget to convert the volumes from cm<sup>3</sup> to dm<sup>3 </sup>

**A **is incorrect as  the two volumes have been reversed

parts.problemMd: In which compound is the oxidation number of nitrogen +5?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because:**

- The oxidation number of nitrogen in Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> is +5
- One method to find the oxidation number is to construct a table with the information that you do know:

|   | Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> |
|---|---|
| 1 x Ca | +2 |
| 2 x N | 2 x N |
| 6 x O | 6 x -2 = -12 |
| **Total** | **0** |

- The oxidation number of Ca is +2 as it is in Group 2
- Oxygen has an oxidation number of -2 and there are 6 oxygen atoms
- The total oxidation number of all of the atoms must add up to the overall oxidation number of the compound, which is 0 as it is neutral
- This means the oxidation number of 2 x N must equal +10, therefore, each nitrogen atom must be +5, using a table can make the sum more obvious:

|   | Ca(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> |
|---|---|
| 1 x Ca | +2 |
| 2 x N | 2 x N = **+10** |
| 6 x O | 6 x -2 = -12 |
| **Total** | **0** |

**B** is incorrect as  the oxidation number of nitrogen is -3

**C** is incorrect as  the oxidation number of nitrogen is +3

**D** is incorrect as  the oxidation number of nitrogen is +3

parts.problemMd: Which reaction is **not** a redox reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B ****because:**

- A redox reaction occurs when reduction and oxidation happen simultaneously

  - Reduction involves the gain of electrons and is shown by the oxidation number of a species decreasing
  - Oxidation involves the loss of electrons and is shown by the oxidation number of a species increasing
- Within the equation:

  - 2HCl (aq) + Ba(OH)<sub>2</sub> (aq) → BaCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) the oxidation state of each species within the reactants and products remains the same
  
    - H = +1
    - Cl = -1
    - Ba = +2
    - O = -2

**A** is incorrect as the chlorine is both reduced and oxidised (disproportionation)

**C** is incorrect as  Zn is oxidised and Cu is reduced

**D** is incorrect as  chlorine is both reduced and oxidised (disproportionation)

- An oxidising agent is a substance that oxidises another atom or ion by causing it to lose electrons
- An oxidising agent itself gets reduced, i.e. it gains electrons and its oxidation number decreases

  - Cu<sup>2+</sup> (oxidation number +2) gains 2e<sup>-</sup> to form Cu (oxidation number 0)
  - Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>-</sup> → Cu

parts.problemMd:
Two half‐equations for a reaction are shown.

Cu → Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup>

NO<sub>3</sub><sup>− </sup>+ 4H<sup>+</sup> + 3e<sup>−</sup> → NO + 2H<sub>2</sub>O

What is the overall ionic equation for this reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- To form an ionic equation, the two half equations need to be combined, but the number of electrons must be the same so that they cancel out
- First, multiply both equations to give the same number of electrons
- In this case, multiply the first half equation by 3 and the second half equation by 2, giving both equations 6 e<sup>-</sup>:

  - 3Cu → 3Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 6e<sup>−</sup>
  - 2NO<sub>3</sub><sup>- </sup>+ 8H<sup>+</sup>+ 6e<sup>−</sup>→ 2NO + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
- Now add all of the reactants and products, the electrons will cancel, giving:

  - 3Cu + 2NO<sub>3</sub><sup>- </sup>+ 8H<sup>+ </sup>→ 3Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2NO + 4H<sub>2</sub>O

**A**, **B **& **D** are incorrect as the charges have not been balanced

parts.problemMd:
A titre of 13.25 cm<sup>3</sup> was obtained using a 50 cm<sup>3 </sup>burette.

What is the percentage uncertainty in the titre?

[Each reading of the burette has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm<sup>3</sup>]
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- To calculate the percentage uncertainty, use the equation:
- Percentage uncertainty = $\frac{\mathrm{total} \mathrm{uncertainty}}{\mathrm{measured} \mathrm{value}}\times100$
- When using a burette, two readings are taken to obtain the titre (an initial reading and a final reading), each has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm<sup>3 </sup>so the total uncertainty = 2 x 0.05
- So, percentage uncertainty = $\frac{2 \times 0.05}{13.25} \times 100 = 0.75 \%$

**A** is incorrect as only one of the readings has been taken into account

**C** is incorrect as both the uncertainty and the number of readings have been doubled

parts.problemMd:

Some pellets were dissolved to make 350 cm<sup>3 </sup>of 0.25 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> solution.

- Therefore the mass of NaOH required: 0.0875 x 40 = 3.5 g
- So the number of pellets needed = $\frac{3.5}{0.700}$ = 5

**A** is incorrect as this is the rounded number of grams of NaOH needed

**C** is incorrect as this is the mass of a pellet divided by the moles of NaOH

**D** is incorrect as because this is the moles of NaOH multiplied by 1000 and divided by 0.7

parts.problemMd:
The Haber process is used industrially to manufacture ammonia:

N<sub>2</sub> (g) + 3H<sub>2</sub> (g) ⇌ 2NH<sub>3</sub> (g)    Δ*H* = −92 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>

What is the effect on both the rate of reaction and the equilibrium yield of NH<sub>3</sub> when the temperature is increased?

|   | **Rate of reaction** | **Equilibrium yield of NH**<sub>**3**</sub> |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | Decreases | Decreases |
| **B** | Decreases | Increases |
| **C** | Increases | Decreases |
| **D** | Increases | Increases |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Two separate effects must be considered: one kinetic (rate), one thermodynamic (equilibrium position)

Effect on rate:

- Higher temperature → molecules have greater average kinetic energy
- A greater proportion of molecules have kinetic energy ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub> → more successful collisions per unit time → rate increases

Effect on equilibrium yield:

- The forward reaction is exothermic (Δ*H* = −92 kJ mol<sup>–¹</sup>)
- By Le Chatelier's principle, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that opposes the change (the endothermic direction, absorbing the added heat)
- For an exothermic forward reaction, raising T shifts the equilibrium backwards (to reactants) → less NH<sub>3</sub> → yield decreases

**A** is incorrect as rate always increases with temperature; this answer gets both effects wrong

**B** is incorrect as the rate does not decrease with increasing temperature; this answer confuses rate with yield

**D** is incorrect as it falls into the "faster means more" trap. Higher temperature does speed the reaction up, but for an exothermic equilibrium it also shifts the position backwards, reducing yield

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always analyse the two effects on the position of equilibrium separately:
> 
> - **Rate** depends on kinetic factors (temperature, catalyst, concentration). Higher T always = faster rate, no matter whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
> - **Equilibrium position** depends on Le Chatelier (temperature + Δ*H* sign; pressure + change in moles of gas; concentration).
> 
> Three common misconceptions flagged in examiner reports:
> 
> - **"Faster means more product"**
> 
>   - This is wrong:
>   
>     - Rate is how fast the equilibrium is reached
>     - Yield is where the equilibrium settles.
>   - A reaction can be fast but low-yielding, or slow but high-yielding.
> - **Catalyst confusion**
> 
>   - A catalyst lowers *E*<sub>a</sub> for both the forward and reverse reactions equally.
>   - It speeds up the approach to equilibrium but does **not **shift the position. Yield is unchanged.
> - **Left/right contradictions**
> 
>   - When stating the direction of the shift, always match it to what you've claimed.
>   - "Shifts right" means forward, toward products
>   - "Shifts left" means backward, toward reactants.
>   - Examiner reports flag candidates getting the direction right in their reasoning but wrong in their final statement.
> 
> The Haber process is Edexcel's classic example of industrial compromise where a lower T gives higher yield but slower rate. So, real industrial conditions (450 °C, ~200 atm, Fe catalyst) are a trade-off between yield and rate.

parts.problemMd:
A group of students carry out an experiment to find the concentration of chlorine, Cl<sub>2 </sub>(aq), in a solution.

Excess potassium iodide solution is added to a 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> sample of the chlorine solution.

Cl<sub>2 </sub>(aq) + 2I<sup>− </sup>(aq) $\rightarrow$ 2Cl<sup>− </sup>(aq) + I<sub>2 </sub>(aq)

The iodine produced is titrated with a solution of thiosulfate ions of known concentration, using starch indicator.

2S<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq) + I<sub>2 </sub>(aq) → S<sub>4</sub>O<sub>6</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq) + 2I<sup>− </sup>(aq)

The concentration of the Cl<sub>2 </sub>(aq) is between 0.038 and 0.042 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> .

What concentration of thiosulfate ions, in mol dm<sup>−3</sup> , is required to give a titre of approximately 20 cm<sup>3 </sup>?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- The number of moles of chlorine in 10 cm<sup>3</sup> can be calculated by $\frac{0.042}{1000}$x 10 = 4.2 x 10<sup>-4</sup>

  - You can use a value between 0.038 and 0.042 mol dm<sup>−3</sup>
- Therefore the number of moles of iodine = 4.2 x 10<sup>-4</sup>
- The number of moles of thiosulfate is double the number of moles of iodine 4.2 x 10<sup>-4</sup> x 2 = 8.4 x 10<sup>-4 </sup>moles
- Therefore the concentration of thiosulfate = $\frac{8.4\times10^{-4}}{20}$ x 1000 = 0.042 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

**A** is incorrect  the ratio of thiosulfate to chlorine used in the calculation is 1 : 2

**B** is incorrect  the ratio of thiosulfate to chlorine used in the calculation is 1 : 2

**D** is incorrect the ratio of thiosulfate to chlorine used in the calculation is 4 : 1

parts.problemMd: What is the most suitable volume of 0.1 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> potassium iodide solution, in cm<sup>3</sup>, to add to the 10.0 cm<sup>3 </sup>of chlorine solution?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- The number of moles of chlorine in 10 cm<sup>3</sup> can be calculated by: $\frac{0.042}{1000}$x 10 = 4.2 x 10<sup>-4</sup>
- Potassium iodide must be in excess, therefore if 10 cm<sup>3</sup> of chlorine is added the number of moles added would be greater than 4.2 x 10<sup>-4</sup>

  - $\frac{0.1}{1000}$ x 10 = 1.0 x 10<sup>-3</sup> moles
  - The ratio of potassium iodide to chlorine is 2:1
  - 5 x 10<sup>-4 </sup>moles of potassium iodide would give this reagent in excess
- If only 8.4 cm<sup>3</sup> is added, then the number of moles would be:

  - $\frac{0.1}{1000}$ x 8.4 = 8.4 x 10<sup>-4</sup> moles
  - $\frac{8.4\times10^{-4}}{2}$ = 4.2 x 10<sup>-4</sup>
  - As the potassium iodide is in excess, this would not be enough

**A** is incorrect as this is the exact amount if the concentration is 0.038

**B** is incorrect as this is the exact amount if the concentration is 0.040

**C** is incorrect as this is the exact amount if the concentration is 0.042

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- Starch will turn blue-black in the presence of iodine
- In the reaction, iodine is being reduced to iodide ions, therefore the colour change is from blue‐black to colourless

**A** is incorrect as the colour change is the wrong way around and without the starch indicator

**B** is incorrect as this is the colour change without the starch indicator

parts.solutionMd:

- When warmed with sodium hydroxide solution, ammonium ions produce ammonia gas, which is an alkaline gas:

  - NH<sub>4</sub>Cl (aq) + NaOH (aq) → NH<sub>3</sub> (g) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + NaCl (aq)

**A** is incorrect as  Ca<sup>2+</sup> does not produce an alkaline gas when warmed with sodium hydroxide solution

**B** is incorrect as Mg<sup>2+</sup> does not produce an alkaline gas when warmed with sodium hydroxide solution

parts.problemMd:
5.00 g of calcium carbonate is heated until it fully decomposes.

CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) → CaO (s) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g)

What is the volume of CO<sub>2</sub> produced, measured at RTP?

[*M*<sub>r</sub>(CaCO<sub>3</sub>) = 100.1; Molar volume of a gas at RTP = 24 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>]
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Calculate moles of CaCO<sub>3</sub>:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

moles of CaCO<sub>3</sub> = $\frac{5.00}{100.1}$

moles of CaCO<sub>3</sub> = 0.0500 mol

- From the balanced equation, 1 mol CaCO<sub>3</sub> produces 1 mol CO<sub>2</sub>,

moles of CO<sub>2</sub> = 0.0500 mol

- Calculate the volume of CO<sub>2</sub> produced:

volume = moles x molar volume (at RTP)

volume of CO<sub>2</sub> produced = 0.0500 x 24

volume of CO<sub>2</sub> produced = 1.2 dm<sup>3</sup>

**A** is incorrect as 1.1 dm<sup>3</sup> uses the STP molar volume (22.4 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> at 0 °C, 101 kPa) instead of the RTP value (24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> at 25 °C, 100 kPa), a common RTP/STP mix-up

**C** is incorrect as 2.4 dm<sup>3</sup> applies a wrong 1:2 stoichiometric ratio; the equation shows 1 mol CaCO<sub>3</sub> produces exactly 1 mol CO<sub>2</sub>, not 2 mol

**D** is incorrect as 120 dm<sup>3</sup> treats the mass (5.00 g) as moles directly, skipping the m to n conversion

> **[exam-tip]**
> At RTP (25 °C, 100 kPa), 1 mol of any gas occupies 24 dm<sup>3</sup>, don't use 22.4 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> (the STP value)
> 
> Always work through the steps in order:
> 
> - mass
> - → ÷ *M*<sub>r</sub>
> - → moles
> - → x ratio
> - → moles
> - → x 24
> - → volume
> 
> Two common slips to avoid:
> 
> - Treating a given mass as if it were moles (skipping the m → n conversion), the January 2022 examiner report specifically flagged this as a recurring error
> - Multiplying by 22.4 instead of 24 even when the question states RTP
> 
> For related Group 2 chemistry, remember that thermal stability of the carbonates increases down the group, BaCO<sub>3</sub> requires the highest temperature to decompose, MgCO<sub>3</sub> the lowest.

parts.problemMd: Which statement about the reactivity of Group 2 elements with water is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Reactivity with water:

  - Mg slow with cold water (readily with steam)
  - Ca steady
  - Sr vigorous
  - Ba very vigorous
  - Reactivity **increases** down Group 2
- Going down the group, atomic radius increases.

  - This means that there are more inner shells leading to **increased shielding** of the outer electrons
  - So, the **first ionisation energy decreases**
  - The two outer electrons are lost more readily resulting in greater / increased reactivity

**A** is incorrect as ionic radius **increases** (not decreases) down the group, and reactivity increases (not decreases), both factual errors

**B** is incorrect as while nuclear charge does increase, the effect is outweighed by the increased shielding; net effect is IE falls, not rises

**D** is incorrect as reactivity changes dramatically down the group (Mg vs Ba behaviour is qualitatively different), forming the same ion does not mean forming it at the same rate or energy

> **[exam-tip]**
> For full marks on structured questions, you need the full reactivity chain:
> 
> - Atomic radius increases
> - → shielding increases
> - → first IE decreases
> - → reactivity increases
> 
> Two common slips to avoid:
> 
> - Saying "more electrons = more reactive" as your whole explanation, this doesn't give the mechanism
> - Claiming that Mg reacts with cold water in the same way as Ca. It doesn't (Mg is slow with cold water and forms MgO + H<sub>2</sub> with steam, which is a different product from Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>)
> 
> Contrast this with Group 7, where reactivity decreases down the group because oxidising power falls.

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: Reactivity decreases down the group because ionic radius decreases

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: Reactivity decreases down the group because nuclear charge increases

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: Reactivity increases down the group because first ionisation energy decreases

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: Reactivity is constant down the group because all Group 2 elements form 2+ ions

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- Barium sulfate forms a white precipitate which is represented using the state symbol, (s)

- Sodium nitrate is soluble

**A** is incorrect as  NaNO<sub>3</sub> is soluble

**B** is incorrect as  the charge on the barium ion is incorrect

**C** is incorrect as  the charge on the sodium ion is incorrect

parts.problemMd:
Magnesium nitrate decomposes on heating.

2Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> → 2MgO + 4NO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub>

What is the total volume of gas formed at room temperature and pressure (r.t.p.) when 0.005 mol of magnesium nitrate decomposes completely?

[Molar volume of a gas at r.t.p. = 24 000 cm<sup>3 </sup>mol<sup>−1</sup>]
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- The gaseous products formed in the reaction are NO<sub>2</sub> and O<sub>2</sub>
- Using the stoichiometry of the reaction, 2 mol of Mg(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> produces a total of 5 mol of gas (4 mol NO<sub>2</sub> + 1 mol O<sub>2</sub>)
- The amount of gaseous products formed from 0.005 mol is:

  - 0.005 x $\frac{5}{2}$ = 0.0125 mol
- This will occupy a volume of 0.0125 x 24 000 = 300 cm<sup>3</sup>

**A** is incorrect as it assumes the ratio of magnesium nitrate to gaseous products is 1:5

  - This makes making it harder for them to gain an electron and form a 1- ion

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the reaction of potassium iodide with concentrated sulfuric acid.

Which of these would **not **be seen?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- The reaction of sodium iodide and concentrated sulfuric acid is:

  - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>(l) + KI (s) → HI (g) + KHSO<sub>4 </sub>(s)
  - HI is seen as misty fumes
- Sulfuric acid oxidises the hydrogen iodide to several extents:

  - The concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises HI and is itself reduced to sulfur dioxide gas:
  
    - 2HI (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>(l) → I<sub>2 </sub>(g) + SO<sub>2 </sub>(g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
    - Iodine is seen as a violet/purple vapour
  - The concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises HI and is itself reduced to sulfur:
  
    - 6HI (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>(l) → 3I<sub>2 </sub>(g) + S (s) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
    - Sulfur is seen as a yellow solid
  - The concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises HI and is itself reduced to hydrogen sulfide:
  
    - 8HI (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>(l) → 4I<sub>2 </sub>(g) + H<sub>2</sub>S (s) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
    - Hydrogen sulfide has a strong smell of bad eggs
  - On cooling, I<sub>2</sub> (s) is formed which is a black solid

**A** is incorrect as  the reaction produces misty fumes of HI

**B** is incorrect as the reaction produces the black solid I<sub>2</sub>

**C** is incorrect as the reaction produces the yellow solid S

parts.problemMd: One of the reaction products is the gas H<sub>2</sub>S. What is the **change** in oxidation number of sulfur as H<sub>2</sub>S forms?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because:**

- The oxidation number of sulfur in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is +6
- The oxidation number of sulfur in H<sub>2</sub>S is -2
- The change in oxidation number is (-2) - (+6) = -8

**B** is incorrect as -6 is the change in oxidation number when S (s) forms

**C** is incorrect as  -2 is the oxidation number of S in H<sub>2</sub>S

**D** is incorrect as +6 is the oxidation number of S in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>

parts.problemMd: Which of these** increases **as Group 7 is descended?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- Halide ions act as reducing agents as they can donate electrons to other species:

  - 2X<sup>-</sup> → X<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>-</sup>
- As you go down the group, the ionic radius increases and the attraction between the outer electrons and the nucleus decreases
- Therefore the larger the halide ions, the more readily they will lose their outer electron, so their reducing ability increases down the group
- This is demonstrated by the halogen displacement reactions where a more reactive halogen will displace a less reactive halogen from a halide solution of the less reactive halogen

  - Iodide ions lose their electrons more easily than bromide ions
  - Bromide ions lose their electrons more easily than chloride ions

**A** is incorrect as  the oxidising ability of the molecular halogens decreases down the group

**C** is incorrect as  the electrostatic attraction between nucleus and outer shell of electrons decreases down the group

**D** is incorrect as electronegativity decreases down the group

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: oxidising ability of the molecular halogens

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: reducing ability of the halide ions

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: electrostatic attraction between the nucleus and outer shell of electrons

- When sodium hydroxide solution is added to ammonium chloride, ammonia gas is produced which will change the colour of the indicator paper, thus identifying ammonium ions

**A** is incorrect as  a flame test will not positively identify ammonium ions and barium nitrate will not positively identify chloride ions
