parts.problemMd:
Solid potassium bromide reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid.

Which of these substances does **not** form?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- When potassium bromide and sulfuric acid react:

  - H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>(l) + NaBr (s) → **HBr** (g) + NaHSO<sub>4 </sub>(s)
- The sulfuric acid then oxidises HBr which decomposes to form bromine, hydrogen gas and sulfur dioxide

  - 2HBr (g) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>(l) →** Br**<sub>**2 **</sub>(g) + **SO**<sub>**2**</sub><sub> </sub>(g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
- Hydrogen sulfide is not produced in either reaction
- A reddish brown gas of Br<sub>2</sub> would be observed
- You must also be able to give the observations and equations for the reaction between sulfuric acid, and chloride / iodide ions

**A** is incorrect as  bromine is formed

**B** is incorrect as  hydrogen bromide is formed

**D** is incorrect as  sulfur dioxide is formed

parts.problemMd:
A student adds chlorine water to an aqueous solution of an unknown potassium halide. A small volume of cyclohexane (density = 0.79 g cm<sup>–3</sup>) is then added and the mixture is shaken thoroughly.

The upper layer turns purple/violet.

Which halide was present in the original solution?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Oxidising ability of halogens decreases down Group 7: Cl<sub>2</sub> > Br<sub>2</sub> > I<sub>2</sub>
- Cl<sub>2</sub> can therefore oxidise Br<sup>–</sup> and I<sup>–</sup>, but cannot oxidise F<sup>–</sup> (F is above Cl) or Cl<sup>–</sup> (same element, no redox)
- Cyclohexane (density 0.79 g cm<sup>–³</sup>) is less dense than water (1.00 g cm<sup>–³</sup>), so it forms the **upper** layer. Halogens are non-polar and far more soluble in cyclohexane than in water, so they concentrate in the upper layer
- Key cyclohexane-layer colours: Br<sub>2</sub> = orange; I<sub>2</sub> = purple/violet
- Upper layer purple/violet → I<sub>2</sub> → the original halide must have been KI:

Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2KI → 2KCl + I<sub>2</sub>

**A** is incorrect as Cl<sub>2</sub> **does** oxidise Br<sup>–</sup> to Br<sub>2</sub>, but Br<sub>2</sub> in cyclohexane is **orange** (not purple); this distractor catches students who stop at "displacement occurred" without checking the colour

**B** is incorrect as Cl<sub>2</sub> and Cl<sup>–</sup> are the same element, no redox is possible; the cyclohexane layer would stay colourless

**C** is incorrect as F<sup>–</sup> cannot be oxidised by Cl<sub>2</sub> (fluorine is above chlorine in Group 7); no reaction occurs and the cyclohexane layer would stay colourless

> **[exam-tip]**
> This question combines three pieces of Group 7 knowledge, all three must be correct to land the answer:
> 
> - which halogen can oxidise which halide
> - the colour of each halogen in a non-polar solvent
> - which layer cyclohexane forms when added to water
> 
> Colours to memorise exactly, the January 2022 examiner report specifically flagged candidates writing "iodine is brown in cyclohexane" as a recurring error:
> 
> - **I**<sub>2</sub>** in cyclohexane** → purple / violet (pink also accepted)
> - **I**<sub>2</sub>** in water** → brown / yellow / pale orange
> - **Br**<sub>2</sub>** in cyclohexane** → orange (yellow, brown or red-brown also accepted)
> - **Br**<sub>2</sub>** in water** → orange / yellow / brown
> - **Cl**<sub>2</sub>** in cyclohexane** → pale green / near-colourless
> 
> Cyclohexane (density ≈ 0.78–0.79 g cm<sup>–³</sup>) is less dense than water (1.00 g cm<sup>–³</sup>), so it floats on top as the **upper** layer, where the halogen concentrates and gives the cleaner, more distinctive colour.
> 
> In structured (Section B) questions asking you to describe what you'd see, mark schemes require a **two-part** answer: **layer + colour** (e.g. "the upper / cyclohexane layer turns purple"). Giving the colour alone loses the layer mark, and vice versa.

parts.problemMd:
What is the effect of increasing temperature on the average energy of the particles in a reaction and on the activation energy of the reaction?

|   | ** ** | **Effect on the** **average energy** | **Effect on the** **activation energy** |
|---|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **A** | unchanged | decreased |
| ☐ | **B** | unchanged | unchanged |
| ☐ | **C** | increased | decreased |
| ☐ | **D** | increased | unchanged |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- The average energy of the particles is shown by the peak of the curve on a Maxwell-Bolztmann distribution curve
- When the temperature increases, the curve flattens and the peak shifts to the right, showing that the average energy of the particles increases
- The activation energy remains unchanged but the proportion of particles with energy equal to or exceeding the activation energy increases

**A** is incorrect as the average energy of the particles in a system increases with temperature and activation energy is not affected by temperature

**B** is incorrect as  the average energy of the particles in a system increases with temperature

**C** is incorrect as activation energy is not affected by temperature

| ☐ | **B** | X | Z |
| ☐ | **C** | Y | W |
| ☐ | **D** | Y | Z |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- An increase in temperature increases the mean energy of the molecules so the curve shifts to the right
- A catalyst provides an alternative pathway for the reaction which has a lower activation energy, so the *E*<sub>a</sub> of the catalysed reaction will be to the left of the original, uncatalysed, *E*<sub>a</sub>

**A** is incorrect as   the curve is for a lower temperature

**B **is incorrect as  the curve is for a lower temperature and the *E*<sub>a</sub> has increased

**D** is incorrect as  the *E*<sub>a</sub> has increased

parts.problemMd:
Which conditions give the highest yield for the forward reaction?

NH<sub>4</sub>Cl (s) ⇌ NH<sub>3 </sub>(g) + HCl (g)  Δ*H *= +176 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B**** because:**

- The forward reaction is endothermic, so an increase in temperature will favour the forward reaction, increasing the yield
- There are more molecules on the RHS of the equation than the LHS, so lower pressure would shift equilibrium to the right, increasing the yield

**A** is incorrect as high pressure would favour the back reaction

**C** is incorrect as both these conditions would favour the back reaction

**D** is incorrect as  low temperature would favour the back reaction

parts.problemMd:
Nitrogen dioxide and dinitrogen tetroxide exist in equilibrium.

2NO<sub>2 </sub>(g) ⇌ N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4 </sub>(g)         brown gas      colourless gas

When an equilibrium is set up in a gas syringe, the mixture is pale brown.

When the mixture is compressed the colour becomes
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****C**** because:**

- As the gas is compressed, the pressure increases and the particles move closer together
- As the particles are not spread out as much, the colour of the gas is more concentrated, making it darker in appearance
- The equilibrium shifts to the right to counter the change in pressure by favouring the reaction that produces fewer molecules
- More colourless N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> is produced, which causes the gas to become lighter

**A** is incorrect as when the equilibrium is re-established the mixture becomes lighter

**B** is incorrect as when the mixture is compressed it initially becomes darker

**D** is incorrect as  the colour change is reversed

parts.problemMd:
The Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution curves **X** and **Y** show the distribution of molecular kinetic energies for a fixed sample of gas under two different conditions.

![Graph showing the distribution of molecules by energy. Two curves X and Y intersect at energy Ea, with the right area shaded.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/2-energetics-group-chemistry-halogenoalkanes-and-alcohols/2-6-introduction-to-kinetics-and-equilibria/assets/001-graph-showing-the-distribution-of-molecules-by-e.png)

Which change could be responsible for the difference between **X** and **Y**?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Going from X to Y, the peak:

  - Shifts to higher energy
  - Becomes lower and broader
- But, the  total area under the curve is unchanged
- This is the signature of a temperature increase

  - Molecules move faster on average, the distribution flattens, and a greater proportion of molecules have kinetic energy ≥ *E*<sub>a</sub>

**A** is incorrect as adding a catalyst does not change the shape of the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve, it only shifts the *E*<sub>a</sub> marker to the left (a lower energy barrier). The distribution of molecular energies is unchanged

**B** is incorrect as changing concentration changes the total area under the curve (total number of molecules) but not the shape of the distribution

**C** is incorrect as pressure does not change the shape of the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve at constant temperature, kinetic energy depends on T, not P

> **[exam-tip]**
> Memorise the key signatures of Maxwell–Boltzmann curve changes:
> 
> - Temperature increase
> 
>   - The peak shifts right and lowers
>   - The distribution broadens
>   - The area under the curve is unchanged
> - Catalyst
> 
>   - The curve itself doesn't change
>   - The dashed line for E<sub>a</sub> shifts left
> - More particles (concentration)
> 
>   - The whole curve scales up (larger total area)
>   - The shape remains unchanged
> 
> Common slips to avoid when drawing Maxwell–Boltzmann curves on paper 2:
> 
> - Drawing a reaction profile instead of a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution
> 
>   - The January 2024 examiner report flagged a significant number of candidates doing this and scoring zero.
>   - Check the axes:
>   
>     - Maxwell–Boltzmann distributions have number of molecules on the y-axis
>     - A reaction profile has enthalpy.
> - Starting the curve away from the origin, or letting it touch or cross the x-axis at high energies
> 
>   - The October 2020 examiner report flagged this.
>   - The curve must start at the origin and approach the x-axis asymptotically (never touch it).
> - Labelling the y-axis as "Energy" instead of "Number of molecules with activation energy"

parts.problemMd: Compared to condition **X**, what is the effect of condition **Y** on the rate of reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Under condition Y, a **larger proportion** of molecules have kinetic energy ≥ E<sub>a</sub> (larger shaded area to the right of *E*<sub>a</sub>)
- More molecules have enough energy for a successful collision → more frequent effective collisions per unit time → faster rate
- Rate increases with temperature, often doubling or tripling for each 10°C rise, because the exponential tail of the Maxwell-Boltzmann curve is very sensitive to T

**A** is incorrect as rate increases (not decreases) with temperature

**B** is incorrect as rate continues increasing with T,  it doesn't reverse (this would only apply if the enzyme or catalyst denatured, which is outside the scope of this question)

**D** is incorrect as rate definitely changes when temperature changes

> **[exam-tip]**
> For full marks on paper 2 structured questions, you need to say: **"a greater proportion of molecules have kinetic energy equal to or greater than the activation energy"**
> 
> The January 2024 examiner report flagged students who referred only to "increased collision frequency" or "more successful collisions" without the **energy ≥***** E***<sub>**a**</sub> framing, lost marks. Generic references to "successful collisions" are not enough on their own.

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: The rate first increases then decreases

parts.problemMd: Which statement about the activation energy, *E*<sub>a</sub>, is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Activation energy is the **minimum** kinetic energy that colliding particles must have for a collision to result in a reaction
- On the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution curve, it's marked on the x-axis as a vertical line

  - Only molecules to the right of *E*<sub>a</sub> have sufficient energy to react
- *E*<sub>a</sub> is neither the average energy nor the overall enthalpy change

**A** is incorrect as the average kinetic energy is where the peak of the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution lies (where most molecules are), this is typically well below *E*<sub>a</sub>

**B** is incorrect as the difference in enthalpy between reactants and products is Δ*H* (not *E*<sub>a</sub>)

**D** is incorrect as the total energy released by a reaction is also Δ*H* (for an exothermic reaction), not *E*<sub>a</sub>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Don't confuse E<sub>a</sub> with Δ*H*:
> 
> - E<sub>a</sub> is the kinetic barrier a collision must overcome (always positive)
> - Δ*H* is the enthalpy difference between products and reactants (positive for endothermic, negative for exothermic)
> 
> A catalyst lowers E<sub>a</sub> by providing an alternative reaction pathway, but it does **not** change Δ*H*.
> 
> The January 2024 examiner report explicitly rejected candidates who wrote that a catalyst "gives molecules more energy". This is wrong because the molecular-energy distribution is unchanged by a catalyst; only the barrier is lowered.
> 
> The October 2022 examiner report also flagged students drawing double-headed arrows for E<sub>a</sub> or Δ*H*. Always use single-headed arrows. Double-headed ones are ambiguous and lose the mark.

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: *E*<sub>a</sub> is the average energy of the reactant molecules

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: *E*<sub>a</sub> is the difference in enthalpy between reactants and products

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: *E*<sub>a</sub> is the minimum energy required for a successful collision

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: *E*<sub>a</sub> is the total energy released by the reaction

- A primary halogenoalkane arises when a halogen is attached to a carbon that is itself attached to **one** other alkyl group as shown above

parts.problemMd:
1-bromobutane reacts with aqueous potassium hydroxide to form butan-1-ol.

Which type of mechanism describes this reaction?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The C–Br bond is polar, Br is more electronegative than C, giving the carbon a δ+ charge
- OH<sup>–</sup> has lone pairs of electrons and acts as a nucleophile (electron-pair donor), attacking the δ+ carbon
- OH<sup>–</sup> replaces Br<sup>–</sup> on the carbon: this is nucleophilic substitution

**A** is incorrect as electrophilic addition requires an electron-rich C=C double bond (e.g. an alkene) reacting with an electrophile, 1-bromobutane has no C=C

**B** is incorrect as electrophilic substitution typically applies to aromatic compounds, no aromatic ring is present here

**C** is incorrect as nucleophilic addition applies to polar π-bonds such as C=O in carbonyls (e.g. HCN + propanone), 1-bromobutane has only σ bonds

> **[exam-tip]**
> Always classify organic reactions using two words: the type (addition / substitution / elimination) AND the attacking species (electrophilic / nucleophilic / free radical).
> 
> For halogenoalkanes with KOH, the **solvent** decides the outcome:
> 
> - aqueous KOH → nucleophilic **substitution** (gives an alcohol)
> - ethanolic KOH → **elimination** (gives an alkene)

parts.problemMd:
Separate samples of some halogenoalkanes were dissolved in ethanol and a few drops of silver nitrate solution added. The faster the reaction of the halogenoalkane, the quicker a precipitate forms.

Which of these halogenoalkanes reacts the **fastest?**
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****A**** because:**

- The strength of the C-X bond where X is the halide, from strongest to weakest is:

  - C-F > C-Cl > C-Br > C-I
  - The C-I bond is the weakest so less energy is required to break it and CH<sub>3</sub>CHICH<sub>3 </sub>will therefore react the fastest
  - A yellow precipitate would be seen first

**B**, **C** and **D** are incorrect as the carbon-halogen bond is stronger than C-I

parts.problemMd: Which of these halogenoalkanes reacts the **fastest?**
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****B ****because:**

- CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CBr(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>3 </sub>is a tertiary halogenoalkane

  - The carbon atom bonded to the Br is bonded to three other alkyl groups
  - Tertiary alkanes react faster than secondary halogenoalkanes which in turn react faster than primary halogenoalkanes

**A** is incorrect as   secondary halogenoalkanes take longer to hydrolyse than tertiary

**C** and **D** are incorrrect as primary halogenoalkanes take longer to hydrolyse than tertiary

parts.problemMd: Which reagent and conditions convert 1-bromopropane to propan-1-ol?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Hydrolysis of a halogenoalkane to form an alcohol requires aqueous hydroxide
- OH<sup>–</sup> acts as a nucleophile, replacing the halide:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + OH<sup>–</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + Br<sup>–</sup>

- The solvent (water) is the key.
- Aqueous conditions favour substitution

**A** is incorrect as using KCN is a different synthetic route used to lengthen chains, not to make alcohols. It creates a nitrile (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CN), extending the carbon chain by one

**B** is incorrect as using KOH in ethanol favours elimination. The OH<sup>–</sup> acts as a base, removing an H<sup>+</sup> from a carbon adjacent to the C–Br. This forms propene, which is not an alcohol

**D** is incorrect as using NH<sub>3</sub> gives a primary amine (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>), not an alcohol. Further substitution can also give secondary/tertiary amines

> **[exam-tip]**
> The aqueous-vs-ethanolic switch is the most common mistake on paper 2. The January 2022 examiner report flagged this, saying that on a reagent-identification MCQ, fewer than 55% of candidates got it right.
> 
> Memorise the two conditions carefully. The only thing that changes is the solvent, but the product type flips:
> 
> 1. Aqueous KOH / NaOH
> 
>   - OH<sup>–</sup> acts as a nucleophile
>   - This favours substitution, forming an alcohol
> 2. Ethanolic KOH / NaOH
> 
>   - OH<sup>–</sup> acts as a base
>   - This favours elimination, forming an alkene
> 
> Same reagent, same cation, same temperature, same reflux. Only the solvent differs.

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: KCN in ethanol, heat under reflux

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: KOH in ethanol, heat under reflux

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: NaOH in water, heat under reflux

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: NH<sub>3</sub> in ethanol, heat under reflux in a sealed tube

- The structure of 2-methylpropan-2-ol is:

parts.problemMd:
A primary alcohol is heated under reflux with acidified potassium dichromate(VI).

What is the organic product?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Primary alcohols are oxidised in two sequential stages:

- Stage 1: RCH<sub>2</sub>OH → RCHO (alcohol to aldehyde)
- Stage 2: RCHO → RCOOH (aldehyde to carboxylic acid)
- **Reflux** keeps both product and unreacted oxidiser in the flask long enough for BOTH oxidations to occur

- So, a **carboxylic acid** is the final product
- Observation: acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> is **orange** and turns **green** (Cr<sup>3+</sup>) as it is reduced

**A** is incorrect as an aldehyde is the product only under **distillation** (limited oxidising agent + immediate removal of product); reflux goes further

**C** is incorrect as esters form from the condensation reaction between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol (esterification), not from oxidation of an alcohol

**D** is incorrect as ketones form by oxidation of **secondary** alcohols, not primary

> **[exam-tip]**
> Distillation vs reflux is the key thing to get right for primary alcohol oxidation:
> 
> - **Limited oxidising agent + distillation** → aldehyde (the product is removed as it forms, preventing further oxidation)
> - **Excess oxidising agent + reflux** → carboxylic acid (the product stays in the flask and gets oxidised a second time)
> 
> State the colour change as **orange → green**. Writing "yellow → green" will lose the mark.
> 
> In mark-scheme equations, the oxidising agent is written as **[O]**; a common error is writing H<sub>2</sub> as the by-product instead of H<sub>2</sub>O.
> 
> Tertiary alcohols are inert to this oxidation. The reason to give is that the C–OH carbon has **no hydrogen** attached, so no C–H bond can be broken to form a C=O.

parts.problemMd: Which of these compounds does **not** react with acidified potassium dichromate(VI)?

  - Primary alcohols to aldehydes
  - Secondary alcohols to ketones
  - Aldehydes to carboxylic acids (under reflux)
- CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3 </sub>is the ketone, propanone, formed from the oxidation of propan-2-ol
- The ketone cannot undergo further oxidation so will not react with the potassium dichromate(VI)

**A **is incorrect as  it is a primary alcohol so will react to form an aldehyde

**B** is incorrect as  it is a secondary alcohol so will react to form a ketone

**C** is incorrect as  it is an aldehyde so will react to form a carboxylic acid

parts.problemMd:
What is the minimum volume of oxygen gas, measured at room temperature and pressure, required for the complete combustion of 9.2 g of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>3</sub> (M<sub>r</sub> = 92)?

[Molar volume of gas at room temperature and pressure = 24.0 dm<sup>3</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>]
parts.solutionMd:

- The complete combustion of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>3  </sub>will produce carbon dioxide and water:

  - C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>3</sub> + 3½O<sub>2</sub> → 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O
- The number of moles of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>3 </sub>= 9.2 ÷ 92 = 0.1 moles
- 0.1 moles of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>3 </sub>requires 3½ x 0.1 = 0.35 moles of oxygen

parts.problemMd:
The oxidation of propan-1-ol by acidified potassium dichromate(VI) forms propanoic acid with a yield of 36% by mass.

What mass of propan-1-ol is needed to form 37.0 g of propanoic acid in this reaction?

[*M*<sub>r</sub> of propanoic acid = 74     *M*<sub>r</sub> of propan-1-ol = 60]
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is ****D**** because:**

- The number of moles in 37.0 g propanoic acid = mass ÷ *M*<sub>r</sub>

  - = 37.0 ÷ 74 = 0.5 mol
- The theoretical yield can be found by rearranging the formula:

  - Percentage yield = $\frac{\mathrm{actual} \mathrm{yield}}{\mathrm{theoretical} \mathrm{yield}}\times100$
  - Theoretical yield = $\frac{\mathrm{actual} \mathrm{yield}}{\mathrm{percentage} \mathrm{yield}}\times100=\frac{0.5}{36}\times100=1.38\mathrm{mol}$
- 1 mol of propan-1-ol produces 1 mol of propanoic acid, so 1.38 mol of propan-1-ol were required
- mass = moles x *M*<sub>r</sub> = 1.38 x 60 = 83.3 g

**A** is incorrect as the scaling of the reacting amount to take into account the yield of 36% is incorrect (36/100)

parts.problemMd:
This question is about enthalpy changes.

An experiment was carried out to determine the enthalpy change of combustion for ethanol.

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (l) + 3O<sub>2 </sub>(g) → 2CO<sub>2 </sub>(g) + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

1.19 g of ethanol was burned in a spirit burner. The heat energy from this combustion raised the temperature of 100 g of water from 21.6°C to 63.9 °C.

i) Calculate the number of moles of ethanol in 1.19 g.

[Molar mass of ethanol = 46.0 g mol<sup>−1</sup> ]

[Specific heat capacity of water = 4.18 J g<sup>−1</sup> °C<sup>−1</sup>]

**(2)**

iii) Use your answers to (a)(i) and (ii) to calculate a value for the enthalpy change of combustion of ethanol. Give your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures and include a sign and units.

**(3)**

iv) The value of the enthalpy change of combustion from this experiment was very inaccurate.

Give two reasons why this value was so inaccurate, apart from heat loss.

**(2)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) The  number of moles of ethanol in 1.19 g is:

- $\frac{1.19}{46}$ =  0.025870 **OR** 2.5870 x 10 <sup>-2 </sup>(mol); **[1 mark]**

ii) The heat energy required to raise the temperature of 100 g of water from 21.6°C to 63.9°C is:

- Calculation of temperature change (63.9 - 21.6) = 42.3 (°C); **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:

CH<sub>3</sub>OH + 1½O2 → CO<sub>2 </sub>+ 2H<sub>2</sub>O

|   | **C–H** | **C–O** | **O–H** | **O=O** | **C=O** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mean bond enthalpy / kJ mol<sup>−1</sup> | 413 | 358 | 464 | 498 | 805 |
parts.solutionMd:
i) The term ‘mean bond enthalpy’ is:

- The energy required to break one mole of a (specific) bond; **[1 mark]**
- In the gaseous phase / state **AND** 
Averaged over a number of (different) compounds / molecules; **[1 mark]**

ii) A value for the enthalpy change of combustion of methanol is:

- Calculation of the energy change to break the bonds (+) 2808 (kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>); **[1 mark]**
- Calculation of the energy change to make the bonds (–) 3466 (kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>); **[1 mark]**
- Calculation of the enthalpy change of the reaction 2808( kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>) −3466( kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>) = -658 (kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *There are several definitions within the enthalpy unit that you can be asked to recall so it is worth spending time learning these*
- *To calculate the energy required to break the bonds:*

  - *(3 × C-H) + (1 × C-O)+ (1× O-H) +(1.5 O=O)*
  - *(3 × 413) + ( 1× 358) +(1 × 464) +(1.5 x 498)*
  - *(+) 2808 kJ mol*<sup>*–1*</sup>
- *To calculate the energy released when bonds are made:*

  - *(2 x C=O)+ (4 x O-H)*
  - *(2 x 805) + (4 x 464)*
  - *= (–) 3466 kJ mol*<sup>*–1*</sup>
- *To find the enthalpy change:*

  - *Energy required to break bonds - energy released when bonds are formed*
  - *2808 − 3466 = – 658 kJ mol*<sup>*–1*</sup>

  - *The answer should have a – sign in front of it*

parts.solutionMd:

- Oxygen is an element

ii) The complete Hess cycle is:

**OR**
Δ*H *= − (−359) + (−394 x 4) + (−286 x 5); **[1 mark]**
- = -2647 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *The standard enthalpy change of formation of an element in its standard state is always 0 as there is no change that occurs - you would be awarded the first mark to state this*
- *The combustion products of an alcohol will be carbon dioxide and water, ensure that you balance the equations carefully - the balancing number of oxygen will be a fraction, you can write this as 6½ or *$\frac{13}{2}$
- *When constructing an equation to calculate the enthalpy change of combustion, use the arrows in the cycle to help you:*

  - *Two arrows start from 4C + 6½O*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 5H*<sub>*2*</sub>* and two arrows point to 4CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 5H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *This means there are two routes to get from 4C + 6½O*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 5H*<sub>*2*</sub>* to 4CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 5H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O *
  - *One directly:*
  
    - *The enthalpy change of this route = 4 x Δ*<sub>*f*</sub>*H**(CO*<sub>*2*</sub>*)** **+ 5 x Δ*<sub>*f*</sub>*H**(H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O) = 4 x (-394) + 5 x (-286) = -3006*
  - *One indirectly via C*<sub>*4*</sub>*H*<sub>*10*</sub>*O + 6O*<sub>*2*</sub>
  
    - *The enthalpy change of this route = Δ*<sub>*f*</sub>*H**(C*<sub>*4*</sub>*H*<sub>*10*</sub>*O) + Δ*<sub>*c*</sub>*H**(C*<sub>*4*</sub>*H*<sub>*10*</sub>*O) = -359 + Δ*<sub>*c*</sub>*H**(C*<sub>*4*</sub>*H*<sub>*10*</sub>*O)*
  - *The enthalpy change of both routes will be the same:*
  
    - *-359 + Δ*<sub>*c*</sub>*H**(C*<sub>*4*</sub>*H*<sub>*10*</sub>*O) = -3006*
    - *Δ*<sub>*c*</sub>*H**(C*<sub>*4*</sub>*H*<sub>*10*</sub>*O) = -3006 + 359 = **-2647 kJ mol*<sup>*-1*</sup>
- *It is very easy to get the calculation the wrong way around and end up with a positive number, so don't rush and write down your workings meticulously so as not to make an error in rearranging*
- *You will lose a mark if you don't get the sign correct*

parts.problemMd:
Sodium ethanoate is a component of reusable hand warmers.

In use, a supersaturated solution of sodium ethanoate recrystallises to form solid hydrated sodium ethanoate, releasing energy.

CH<sub>3</sub>COONa (aq) + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → CH<sub>3</sub>COONa.3H<sub>2</sub>O (s)      Δ<sub>r</sub>*H* = −19.7 kJ mol<sup>−1</sup>

A hand warmer has a mass of 63.2 g and forms 20.1 g of hydrated sodium ethanoate on recrystallisation.

Calculate the maximum temperature reached by the hand warmer if its initial temperature is 5.0 °C.

[Specific heat capacity of the hand warmer = 3.0 J °C<sup>−1</sup> g<sup>−1</sup>]
parts.solutionMd:
The maximum temperature reached by the hand warmer if its initial temperature is 5.0 °C is:

- Molar mass of hydrated sodium ethanoate = (2 x 12) + (9 x 1) + ((5 x 16) + 23 = 136 (g mol<sup>-1</sup>); **[1 mark]**
- Moles of hydrated sodium ethanoate = 20.1 ÷ 136 = 0.14779 (mol); **[1 mark]**
- Energy released = 0.14779 × 19700 = 2911.5 / 2.911 x 10<sup>3</sup> (J)
**OR** 2.911 (kJ); **[1 mark]**
- Δ*T* = 2911.54 ÷ (63.2 × 3.0) = 15.3562 (°C); **[1 mark]**
- Final *T* = 15.3562 + 5.0 = 20 / 20.4 (°C); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *This question uses the equations **q** = **mc **Δ**T **and Δ**H **= *$\frac{q}{n}$* but instead of having to use the temperature change to find Δ**H, **you are given Δ**H **and have to work backwards to find Δ**T** and then the final temperature*
- *The energy released per mole of sodium ethanoate as Δ*<sub>*r*</sub>*H **= -19.7 kJ mol*<sup>*-1*</sup>
- *The molar ratio is 1:1, so this is the amount of energy released when 1 mole of hydrated sodium ethanoate recrystallises*
- *To find the energy released when 20.1 g of hydrated sodium ethanoate is recrystallised, this value needs to be multiplied by the number of moles present in 20.1 g:*

  - *q** = Δ**H  **x** n **= -19.7 x 0.14799 = 2.9115 kJ or 2911.5 J*
- *Now use **q** = **mc **Δ**T** to find the temperature change, where **m** is the mass of the surroundings (the mass of the hand warmer), **q** is in joules and **c** is given in the question as 3.0 J °C*<sup>*-1*</sup>* g*<sup>*-1*</sup>*:*

  - *Δ**T **= *$\frac{q}{mc}$* = *$\frac{2911.5}{63.2\times3.0}$* = 15.3562 °C*
- *Δ**T **is calculated by final temperature - initial temperature*

  - *15.3562 = final temperature - 5.0*
  - *Final temperature = 15.3562 + 5.0 = 20.4 °C*

parts.problemMd:
Ammonium carbonate, (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> , is an ingredient in cleaning solutions for camera lenses.

These are aqueous solutions which contain no more than 1.8 g of ammonium carbonate in 100 cm<sup>3 </sup>of solution.

Calculate the maximum concentration, in mol dm<sup>−3</sup>, of ammonium carbonate in such a solution.
parts.solutionMd:
The maximum concentration, in mol dm<sup>−3</sup>, of ammonium carbonate in such a solution is:

Method 1

- Mass of ammonium carbonate in 1 dm<sup>3</sup> of solution = 1.8 x 10 = 18 (g dm<sup>−3</sup>); **[1 mark]**
- Concentration of solution = $\frac{18}{96}$ = 0.1875 (mol dm<sup>-3</sup>); **[1 mark]**

Method 2

- Number of moles of ammonium carbonate = $\frac{1.8}{96}$ = 0.01875 (mol); **[1 mark]**
- Concentration of solution = $\frac{0.01875}{0.1}$ = 0.1875 (mol dm<sup>-3</sup>); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Method 1 involves working out the concentration in g dm*<sup>*-3*</sup>*, then converting to mol dm*<sup>*-3*</sup>* by dividing by the Mr*

  - *M*<sub>*r*</sub>* = 2 x [14 + (4 x 1)] + 12 + (3 x 16) = 96*
- *Method 2 involves working out the number of moles of ammonium carbonate in 1.8 g by mass ÷ **M*<sub>*r*</sub>
- *Then calculating concentration in mol dm*<sup>*-3*</sup>* by moles ÷ volume (in dm*<sup>*3*</sup>*)*
- *Either method is equally valid*
- *A correct answer with no working scores 2 marks*

parts.problemMd:
In an experiment, a student investigates the enthalpy change of combustion of propan-1-ol.

State what is meant by the term standard enthalpy of combustion.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A complete definition must include all of the following:
> 
> - The enthalpy/heat energy change when 1 / one mole of a substance is completely burned in oxygen / reacts completely with oxygen **[1 mark]**
> - Under standard conditions (100 kPa and a stated temperature, usually 298 K) 
> **OR **
> with the reactants in standard states **[1 mark]**
> 
> "Standard state" is accepted for one of the two marks if the other marking criteria are met.
> 
> Talking about just "energy" is not accepted

> **[exam-tip]**
> Your definition must cover four components to score full marks:
> 
> 1. One mole of the substance
> 2. Complete combustion in excess oxygen
> 3. Standard pressure (100 kPa, not 101.3 kPa; this is an Edexcel IAL convention)
> 4. Reactants and products in their standard states
> 
> Omitting any single component typically loses a mark. The temperature is usually quoted as 298 K but the definition technically holds for any *stated* temperature, so "at a stated temperature" is accepted.

parts.problemMd:
Propan-1-ol burns completely according to the equation:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH (l) + 4½O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 3CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

The standard enthalpies of formation, Δ<sub>f</sub>*H*<sup>θ</sup>, are given below.

| Substance | Δ<sub>f</sub>*H*<sup>θ </sup>/ kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> |
|---|---|
| CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH (l) | –303 |
| CO<sub>2</sub> (g) | –394 |
| H<sub>2</sub>O (l) | –286 |

i) Complete the Hess cycle below by filling in the blank box.

![Chemical equation for combustion of propanol with enthalpy changes depicted, connecting reactants and products using arrows and labelled energy terms.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/2-energetics-group-chemistry-halogenoalkanes-and-alcohols/2-1-energetics/assets/006-chemical-equation-for-combustion-of-propanol-wit.png)

[1]

ii) Calculate the standard enthalpy of combustion of propan-1-ol.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The completed Hess cycle is:

![Chemical equation showing propanol combustion: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + 4.5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. Includes enthalpy changes ΔH. Box shows elemental forms.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/2-energetics-group-chemistry-halogenoalkanes-and-alcohols/2-1-energetics/assets/007-chemical-equation-showing-propanol-combustion-ch.png)

**[1 mark]**

ii) To calculate the standard enthalpy of combustion of propan-1-ol:

- Write the formation cycle formula:

Δ<sub>c</sub>*H*<sup>θ</sup> = ΣΔ<sub>f</sub>*H*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − ΣΔ<sub>f</sub>*H*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants) **[1 mark]**

- Substitute the values (Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup>(O<sub>2</sub>) = 0 because O<sub>2</sub> is an element in its standard state):

Δ<sub>c</sub>*H*<sup>θ</sup> = [3(−394) + 4(−286)] − [1(−303) + 4.5(0)] **[1 mark]**

Δ<sub>c</sub>*H*<sup>θ</sup> = [−1182 − 1144] − [−303] = −2326 + 303

Δ<sub>c</sub>*H*<sup>θ</sup> = **−2023 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) 1 mark for correctly completing the Hess cycle: blank box filled with 3C (s) + 4H<sub>2</sub> (g) + 4½O<sub>2</sub> (g)
> 
> The arrows must point UP from the elements to BOTH the reactants AND the products.
> 
> ii) 1 mark for correct formula Δ<sub>c</sub>*H*<sup>θ</sup> = ΣΔ<sub>f</sub>*H*<sup>θ</sup>(products) − ΣΔ<sub>f</sub>*H*<sup>θ</sup>(reactants)
> 
> 1 mark for correct substitution with stoichiometric coefficients: 3 x (−394) **AND **4 x (−286) **AND **1 x (−303)
> 
> 1 mark for final answer −2023 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> (exact; all data values in the table are integers)
> 
> A positive value is not accepted.
> 
> Allow error carried forward from an arithmetic slip in an earlier step.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Formation cycles use "**products minus reactants**". This is the opposite of bond-enthalpy or combustion cycles, which use reactants minus products.
> 
> Two common mistakes are:
> 
> 1. Forgetting stoichiometric coefficients
> 
> - Remember that Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup> of any element in its standard state is 0, so 4½O<sub>2</sub> contributes nothing.
> - Always multiply each Δ*H*<sub>f</sub><sup>θ</sup> by its stoichiometric coefficient (here, 3 x for CO<sub>2</sub> and 4 x for H<sub>2</sub>O)
> - Examiner reports noted that many candidates drew the cycle correctly but then forgot to apply the coefficients in the calculation itself.
> 
> 1. Wrong sign in the answer
> 
> - Combustion is always exothermic.
> - So, a positive answer tells you something has gone wrong and that you need to check the signs in your equation and calculation.

parts.problemMd:
The student carries out a simple calorimetry experiment to determine an experimental value for the enthalpy change of combustion of propan-1-ol.

The apparatus used is shown.

![Diagram of a calorimetry setup with a thermometer, metal calorimeter, water, clamped draught shield, spirit burner, and liquid fuel underneath.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/2-energetics-group-chemistry-halogenoalkanes-and-alcohols/2-1-energetics/assets/008-diagram-of-a-calorimetry-setup-with-a-thermomete.png)

- Mass of water in calorimeter = 200 g
- Initial temperature of water = 22.0 °C
- Maximum temperature of water = 44.5 °C
- Mass of propan-1-ol burnt = 0.60 g

(Specific heat capacity of water, c = 4.18 J g<sup>–1</sup> K<sup>–1</sup>; *M*<sub>r</sub>(CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH) = 60.0)

Calculate the experimental enthalpy change of combustion of propan-1-ol.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the experimental enthalpy change of combustion:

- Calculate the heat energy transferred to the water:

*Q* = *mc*Δ*T* = 200 x 4.18 x (44.5 − 22.0)

*Q* = 200 x 4.18 x 22.5

*Q*= 18810 J

- Convert *Q* from J to kJ:

*Q* = $\frac{18810}{1000}$

*Q* = 18.81 kJ

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of propan-1-ol burnt:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

moles of propan-1-ol burnt = $\frac{0.60}{60.0}$

moles of propan-1-ol burnt = 0.010 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the enthalpy change of combustion (sign reversed because combustion is exothermic):

Δ*H*<sub>c</sub><sup>θ</sup> = -$\frac{Q}{n}$

Δ*H*<sub>c</sub><sup>θ</sup> = $\frac{-18.81}{0.010}$−18.81/0.010

Δ*H*<sub>c</sub><sup>θ</sup> = **−1881 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct calculating *Q* = *mc*Δ*T* (18810 J **OR **18.81 kJ)
> 
> 1 mark for correct calculating the moles of propan-1-ol (0.010 mol)
> 
> 1 mark for correct calculating Δ<sub>c</sub>*H*<sup>θ</sup> (−1881 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> **OR** -1.88 x 10<sup>-3</sup> kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>)
> 
> Accept −1880 to −1885 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> The final answer must have a negative sign
> 
> Allow error carried forward from earlier incorrect values if the method is correct

> **[exam-tip]**
> Three common calorimetry pitfalls to avoid:
> 
> 1. Mass in *Q* = *mc*Δ*T*
> 
>   - *m* is always the mass of the substance being heated (the surroundings)
>   - So, the mass used in the calculation is the mass of the water / solution, not the mass of the fuel
> 2. Unit conversion
> 
>   - Forgetting to convert J to kJ (÷ 1000) before dividing by moles
> 3. Wrong sign
> 
>   - Forgetting to reverse the sign when calculating Δ*H* from *Q*
>   - *Q* is always positive (heat gained by the water)
>   - Whereas Δ*H* must be negative for an exothermic reaction
> 
> Compare your experimental value with your Hess value from part (b). The experimental value should be less negative than the Hess value, due to heat loss to the surroundings. If yours is more negative than the Hess value, check your working.

parts.problemMd:
Using mean bond enthalpies, the enthalpy change of combustion of propan-1-ol is calculated as –1920 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>.

Explain **one** reason why this bond enthalpy value differs from the value you calculated in part (b).
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> One reason why the bond enthalpy value differs from the Hess's law value:
> 
> Any **one **from:
> 
> - Mean bond enthalpies are average values taken from a range of different compounds
> - Mean bond enthalpies apply only to substances in the gaseous state, but propan-1-ol / water are liquids in this standard reaction
> - Bond enthalpy calculations do not include changes of state / enthalpy of vaporisation
> 
> **OR**
> 
> Doesn't account for vaporisation/condensation of the liquid species
> 
> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Vague answers such as "bond enthalpies are approximate / inaccurate / wrong" without reference to averaging are not accepted.
> 
> Answers that only name a species as liquid without linking to the gaseous-state assumption are not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> For any "why do bond enthalpy values differ from experimental?" question, the two key limitations to know are:
> 
> - Mean bond enthalpies are averages across many molecules, so they are not specific to your compounds
> - Bond-enthalpy calculations assume all species are gaseous, so vaporisation and condensation of any liquid species are not accounted for
> 
> Either point will score the mark here; structured questions sometimes ask for **both**, in which case you must give both to score full marks.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the forces between molecules and ions.

Some data for three small molecules are shown.

| **Molecule** | ***M***<sub>**r**</sub> | **Boiling temperature / °C** |
|---|---|---|
| Fluorine | 38.0 | −188 |
| Hydrogen chloride | 36.5 | −85 |
| Methanol | 32.0 | 65 |

Explain the large variation in boiling temperatures, given the small range in *M*<sub>r</sub> values.

Detailed descriptions of the forces involved are not required.
parts.solutionMd:
Explain the large variation in boiling temperatures, given the small range in *M*<sub>r</sub> values:

Chemical ideas expressed:

- Fluorine molecules only have London forces (instantaneous dipole-induced dipole) between them (as it has a symmetrical electron cloud/is a symmetrical/non-polar molecule.)
- Hydrogen chloride is a polar molecule as chlorine is more electronegative than hydrogen.
- HCl forms permanent dipole-permanent dipole interactions in addition to London forces.
- Methanol contains a hydrogen attached to a small electronegative element so can form hydrogen bonds (in addition to permanent dipole-permanent dipole interactions and London Forces)
- Hydrogen bonds are the strongest intermolecular forces so take the most energy to break
- London forces are the weakest intermolecular forces, so fluorine has the lowest boiling temperature

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *An answer scoring** 5** marks would include*

parts.problemMd:
(*) The boiling points of the three compounds are shown below.

| Compound | Boiling point / °C |
|---|---|
| Butane | –1 |
| Methoxyethane | +8 |
| Propan-1-ol | +97 |

Compare and explain the boiling points of butane, methoxyethane and propan-1-ol.

In your answer, you should include:

- the types of intermolecular force present in each compound
- the relative strengths of these forces and how they account for the boiling-point trend
parts.solutionMd:
All three compounds have similar relative molecular masses (*M*<sub>r</sub> ≈ 58–60) and therefore similar numbers of electrons, so the London dispersion forces in all three are approximately equal. Any differences in boiling point must arise from additional intermolecular forces beyond London dispersion.

Butane is non-polar, with only C–C and C–H bonds, so the only intermolecular forces present are London dispersion forces. As these are the weakest type of IMF, butane has the lowest boiling point of the three. Methoxyethane has polar C–O bonds, giving the molecule a permanent dipole, so it experiences both London dispersion forces and permanent dipole–dipole forces. However, methoxyethane has no O–H bond and cannot act as a hydrogen-bond donor, so its boiling point is higher than butane but well below propan-1-ol. Propan-1-ol contains an O–H bond and an O lone pair, allowing it to act as both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor; hydrogen bonding is the strongest IMF in this comparison, so significantly more energy is required to overcome it during vaporisation, and propan-1-ol has by far the highest boiling point.

The boiling-point ranking therefore follows the strongest IMF in each compound: LDF only (butane) < LDF + dipole–dipole (methoxyethane) ≪ LDF + hydrogen bonding (propan-1-ol). The very large gap between methoxyethane and propan-1-ol (+8 °C vs +97 °C) reflects the substantial extra energy required to break hydrogen bonds.

**[6 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> This question is marked using indicative points (IPs) and lines of reasoning (LoR).
> 
> 1. Award IP marks using the table below based on the number of indicative points present in the response.
> 2. Award 0, 1, or 2 LoR marks based on the quality of logical development.
> 3. Add the two scores together for the total mark (maximum 6).
> 
> | Number of indicative points | Marks for indicative content |
> |---|---|
> | 6 | 4 |
> | 5–4 | 3 |
> | 3–2 | 2 |
> | 1 | 1 |
> | 0 | 0 |
> 
> **Lines of reasoning (0–2 marks)**
> 
> - 2 marks:
> 
> - Answer demonstrates a clear and sustained line of reasoning; the comparison between the three compounds is logically developed with clear linkages between IMF type, IMF strength, and boiling point throughout
> - 1 mark:
> 
> - Some reasoning is present but the answer lacks full development or the links between IMF type, strength, and boiling point are not clearly sustained
> - 0 marks:
> 
> - Points are listed without development; no logical progression between ideas
> 
> *If any incorrect chemistry is present, deduct mark(s) from the LoR score. If no LoR marks are awarded, do not deduct.*
> 
> **Indicative points (IPs)**
> 
> - Butane is non-polar (only C–C and C–H bonds), so the only intermolecular force present is London dispersion forces
> - Methoxyethane has polar C–O bonds creating a permanent dipole, so the intermolecular forces are London dispersion forces and permanent dipole–dipole forces
> - Propan-1-ol contains an O–H bond (hydrogen-bond donor) and an O lone pair (acceptor), so it forms hydrogen bonds in addition to London dispersion forces
> - All three compounds have similar *M*<sub>r</sub> / number of electrons, so the London dispersion contribution is approximately the same in each
> - Hydrogen bonds are stronger than permanent dipole–dipole forces, which are stronger than London dispersion forces alone
> - The boiling-point ranking follows the strongest IMF in each compound: butane (LDF only) < methoxyethane (LDF + dipole–dipole) < propan-1-ol (LDF + hydrogen bonding)

> **[exam-tip]**
> For 6-mark IP/LoR questions on intermolecular forces, structure your answer molecule by molecule. For each compound, state the strongest IMF present, explain why it arises from the structure, and link the IMF strength to the boiling point value.
> 
> Open with a comparator line ("all three have similar *M*<sub>r</sub>, so London dispersion contributions are similar") to set up a clear framing for the examiner — this secures one indicative point and helps the lines-of-reasoning mark.
> 
> The most common failure is treating the three compounds in isolation without explicitly comparing IMF strengths. The strength-ranking IP and the overall boiling-point ranking IP are the high-level discriminators and are required to reach the top IP band.
> 
> Remember that methoxyethane has permanent dipoles but no O–H, so it cannot form hydrogen bonds as a donor — this is the key discriminator between methoxyethane and propan-1-ol. Any incorrect chemistry (e.g. claiming butane has dipole–dipole forces, or methoxyethane forms hydrogen bonds with itself) deducts from your reasoning marks even if other valid points are made.

parts.problemMd:
Potassium chlorate(V), KClO<sub>3</sub> , is a crystalline solid used in fireworks. It is produced by the Liebig Process in two stages.

| Stage 1 | Chlorine gas is passed through hot calcium hydroxide solution forming calcium chlorate(V), Ca(ClO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> . |
|---|---|

6Ca(OH)<sub>2 </sub>(aq) + 6Cl<sub>2 </sub>(g) → Ca(ClO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2 </sub>(aq) + 5CaCl<sub>2 </sub>(aq) + 6H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

| Stage 2 | Potassium chloride solution is then added to form potassium chlorate(V). |
|---|---|

Ca(ClO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2 </sub>(aq) + 2KCl (aq) → 2KClO<sub>3 </sub>(aq) + CaCl<sub>2 </sub>(aq)

The solution is heated to reduce its volume and then allowed to crystallise. The crystals are filtered off. 
The remaining filtrate is evaporated further to obtain more crystals.

i) Write the **overall** equation for the Liebig Process. State symbols are not required.

**(1)**

ii) Calculate the **overall** atom economy by mass for the production of potassium chlorate(V), KClO<sub>3</sub> , using your equation in (a)(i).

**(3)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) The **overall** equation for the Liebig Process is:

- 3Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 3Cl<sub>2</sub> + KCl → KClO<sub>3</sub> + 3CaCl<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O 
**OR** 
6Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> + 6Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2KCl → 2KClO<sub>3</sub> + 6CaCl<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O; **[1 mark]**

ii) The **overall** atom economy by mass for the production of potassium chlorate(V), KClO<sub>3</sub> is:

- *M*<sub>r</sub> of KClO<sub>3</sub> = 39.1 + 35.5 + 48 (= 122.6); **[1 mark]**
- *M*<sub>r</sub> of all products / reactants = 122.6 + (3 ×18) + ((71 + 40.1) × 3) = 509.9; **[1 mark]**
- Overall atom economy = (122.6 ÷ 509.9) × 100 = 24.044 = 24.0%; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *To find the overall equation:*

  - *Identify which species is produced in stage 1 and then used as a reactant in stage 2:*
  
    - *Ca(ClO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>
  - *Multiply either equation as necessary so that there are an equal number of moles of this species in both equations:*
  
    - *The equation in stage 1 shows 1 mol of Ca(ClO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* being formed and in stage 2, 1 mol of Ca(ClO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2 *</sub>*reacting, so in this case, no multiplication is necessary*
  - *To find the overall equation, add all of the reactants on one side of the equation, and the products on the other side of the equation:*
  
    - *6Ca(OH)*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 6Cl*<sub>*2 *</sub>* + Ca(ClO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 2KCl → Ca(ClO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 5CaCl*<sub>*2 *</sub>*+ 6H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O + 2KClO*<sub>*3*</sub>* + CaCl*<sub>*2*</sub>
  - *Cancel out any species which appear on either side of the equation - this will cancel out the species that is both produced in stage 1 and reacted in stage 2, as there are an equal number of moles on either side of the equation:*
  
    - *6Ca(OH)*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 6Cl*<sub>*2 *</sub>* + **Ca(ClO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 2KCl → **Ca(ClO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 5CaCl*<sub>*2 *</sub>*+ 6H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O + 2KClO*<sub>*3*</sub>* + CaCl*<sub>*2*</sub>
    - *6Ca(OH)*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 6Cl*<sub>*2 *</sub>* + 2KCl → 5CaCl*<sub>*2 *</sub>*+ 6H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O + 2KClO*<sub>*3*</sub>* + CaCl*<sub>*2*</sub>
  - *If you left the equation like this, you would score the mark, but it can be simplified further by combining the CaCl*<sub>*2*</sub>* and dividing by 2 to give the simplest whole number ratio:*
  
    - *3Ca(OH)*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 3Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* + KCl →3CaCl*<sub>*2 *</sub>*+ 3H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O + KClO*<sub>*3*</sub>* *
- *The marks scheme above shows the calculation of atom economy using the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* values for the simplified version of the equation, you would score the marks if you had used doubled the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* values if using the non-simplified equation - the atom economy is still the same*

parts.problemMd:
Explain the type of reaction that takes place in Stage 1 of the Liebig Process, using oxidation numbers.

6Ca(OH)<sub>2 </sub>(aq) + 6Cl<sub>2 </sub>(g) → Ca(ClO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2 </sub>(aq) + 5CaCl<sub>2 </sub>(aq) + 6H<sub>2</sub>O (l)
parts.solutionMd:
The type of reaction that takes place in Stage 1 of the Liebig Process is:

- Disproportionation reaction; **[1 mark]**
- As chlorine (atoms) are oxidised from 0 (in chlorine) to (+) 5 (in calcium chlorate); **[1 mark]**
- And reduced (from 0) to −1 (in calcium chloride); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *The question gives you a hint as it asks you to use oxidation numbers*
- *This indicates that it is a redox reaction*
- *Disproportionation is a particular type of redox reaction in which atoms of the same element are both oxidised and reduced*
- *Look out for the same element appearing in more than one species either in the reactants or in the products, then work out the oxidation number of that element in all of the species containing it in the reaction to see if disproportionation has occurred*
- *The oxidation number of Cl in Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* is 0 as it is an element*
- *The oxidation number of Cl in CaCl*<sub>*2*</sub>* is -1:*

  - *Ca is +2, so 2 x Cl must be -2 so that the overall oxidation number is 0, therefore each Cl is -1*
  - *+2 + (2 x -1) = 0*
  - *Chlorine has been reduced*
- *The oxidation number of Cl in Ca(ClO*<sub>*3*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>* is -1*

  - *Ca is +2, each O is -2 and there are 6 O atoms so -12 due to O atoms, so 2 x Cl must be +10 so that the overall oxidation number is 0, therefore each Cl is +5*
  - *+2 + (2 x +5) + (6 x -2) = 0*
  - *Chlorine has been oxidised*

parts.problemMd:
The crystals of potassium chlorate(V) formed also contain some halide ion impurities.

i) Describe a chemical test on a solution of these crystals to **confirm** that the impurities present are chloride ions rather than bromide ions. Include the expected results.

**(3)**

ii) 1.52 g of impure potassium chlorate(V), formed in the Liebig Process, was heated until the mass of solid remaining was constant at 1.02 g.

The reaction that occurred was

2KClO<sub>3 </sub>(s) → 2KCl (s) + 3O<sub>2 </sub>(g)

The impurities present did not decompose on heating.

Calculate the percentage purity of the sample. Give your answer to an appropriate number of significant figures.

**(5)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) A chemical test on a solution of these crystals to **confirm** that the impurities present are chloride ions rather than bromide ions is:

- Add (dilute) nitric acid / HNO<sub>3</sub> **AND** silver nitrate / AgNO<sub>3</sub> (solution); **[1 mark]**
- White precipitate forms / precipitate forms whose colour is difficult to distinguish (between white and cream); **[1 mark]**
- Which dissolves in dilute ammonia / dilute NH<sub>3</sub> / NH<sub>3 </sub>(aq); **[1 mark]**

ii) The percentage purity of the sample is:

- Mass of oxygen = 1.52 − 1.02 = 0.50 (g); **[1 mark]**
- Moles of oxygen = 0.50 ÷ 32 = 0.015625 (mol); **[1 mark]**
- Moles of potassium chlorate = 0.015625 × (2 ÷ 3) = 0.010417 (mol)
**OR**
Calculation of mass of KCl = 0.015625 x (2 ÷ 3) x 74.6 = 0.777 (g); **[1 mark]**
- Mass of potassium chlorate in impure sample = 0.010417 × (39.1 + 35.5 + 48) = 1.2771 (g)
**OR**
0.777 + 0.5 = 1.277 (g); **[1 mark]**
- % purity of sample to 2 or 3 SF = (1.2771 ÷ 1.52) × 100 = 84.019 = 84 / 84.0 (%); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 8 marks]**

- *For part (i) you would not be given credit if you stated either hydrochloric acid or sulfuric acid, as both will form a white precipitate with silver nitrate, giving false positive results for the test*
- *However, you would gain a mark for stating acidified silver nitrate or AgNO*<sub>*3*</sub>* and H*<sup>*+*</sup>
- *You could only gain the second 2 marks if you had identified the use of silver nitrate*
- *In part (ii), as the impurities didn't decompose during heat, the only reason for the decrease in mass is due to the loss of oxygen, which allows you to work out the number of moles of oxygen produced*

parts.problemMd:
In fireworks, potassium chlorate(V) decomposes. This thermal decomposition takes place in two stages with a solid catalyst.

4KClO<sub>3</sub> → KCl + 3KClO<sub>4</sub> 
KClO<sub>4</sub> → KCl + 2O<sub>2</sub>

i)  Give the systematic name of KClO<sub>4</sub> .

**(1)**

ii) A student investigated the role of the catalyst in this reaction.

**Procedure**

| Step 1 | Heat a sample of KClO<sub>3</sub> , in a test tube, with a known mass of insoluble catalyst until the mass remains constant. |
|---|---|
| Step 2 | Mix the contents of the test tube with water. |
| Step 3 | Filter the mixture and rinse with deionised water. |
| Step 4 | Dry the remaining solid. |
| Step 5 | Measure the mass of the dry solid. |

Explain how each of the steps in this procedure is needed to show that the catalyst is **not** used up in this reaction.

**(4)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) The systematic name of KClO<sub>4</sub> is:

- Potassium chlorate(VII) 
**OR** 
Chlorate(VII) potassium; **[1 mark]**

ii) Each of the steps in this procedure is needed to show that the catalyst is **not** used up in this reaction because:

Any **four** from:

- Heat to constant mass so all of the potassium chlorate(V) decomposes / reacts; **[1 mark]**
- The solid product or potassium chloride dissolves (when the water is added)
**OR**
The catalyst does not dissolve (when the water is added); **[1 mark]**
- The rinsing removes potassium chloride (solution), which would otherwise add to the mass of the solid when it dries; **[1 mark]**
- Drying ensures the final mass recorded is only that of that catalyst
**OR**
To remove water from the catalyst / ensure the catalyst is dry; **[1 mark]**
- The mass (of solid) recorded (at the end of the procedure) should be the same of that of the catalyst at the start
**OR**
To compare to the mass of catalyst / to check the mass (of catalyst) hasn’t changed; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *The first part of the name gives the metal ion, potassium, and the second part is chlorate as the negative ion contains chlorine and oxygen atoms*
- *The oxidation number of chlorine is +7*

  - *This is because overall the compound has an oxidation number of 0, K has an oxidation number of +1 and the four oxygen atoms have a combined oxidation number of -8, this means that the oxidation number of chlorine must be +7:*
  - *(+1) + (+7) + (-8) = 0*
- *This is shown by the Roman numeral (VII) after chlorate*
- *In part (ii), there are 5 different steps, and 4 marks available, so it is a reasonable assumption that you should attempt to give a reason for at least four steps*

parts.problemMd:
This question is about Group 1 metals.

When potassium is placed into a beaker of cold water, potassium hydroxide and hydrogen are formed.

i) Write the equation for this reaction. Include state symbols.

**(2)**

ii) This is a redox reaction.

State which element is oxidised and which is reduced.

Justify your answer by giving the initial and final oxidation numbers of any element that changes oxidation state.

**(2)**

iii) The reaction of potassium with water is very vigorous and a flame is seen.

State the colour of the flame.

**(1)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) The equation for this reaction with state symbols is:

2K (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)→ 2KOH (aq) + H<sub>2 </sub>(g) **   **
**OR**    
K (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) →KOH (aq) +1⁄2H<sub>2 </sub>(g)

- Correct equation; **[1 mark]**
- Correct state symbols; **[1 mark]**

ii) The element oxidised and the element reduced, using evidence of oxidation numbers are:

- K / potassium from 0 to +1
**AND**
oxidation; **[1 mark]**
- H / hydrogen from +1 to 0
**AND**
reduction; **[1 mark]**

iii) The colour of the flame is:

- Lilac; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *When a metal is added to water:*

  - *metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen *
- *From lithium, sodium and potassium, potassium is the only metal to burn with a flame when added to water, you should know this is lilac coloured, but purple will also score you the mark *
- *The oxidation number for any uncombined element is 0:*

  - *K = 0 *

parts.problemMd:
The label has come off a bottle known to contain **M**, a Group 1 metal which is stored in oil. A student carried out an experiment to determine the identity of **M.**

**Procedure**

Step **1   **

A small piece of **M** was wiped with tissue paper to remove the oil.
The piece of **M** was weighed and placed in a beaker of distilled water.

Step **2**

After the reaction had finished, the contents of the beaker and washings were transferred to a 250.0 cm<sup>3</sup> volumetric flask. The solution was made up to the mark with distilled water and mixed thoroughly.

Step **3**

A pipette was used to transfer 25.0 cm<sup>3 </sup>portions of this solution to conical flasks. Each portion was then titrated with hydrochloric acid of concentration 0.400 mol dm<sup>–3</sup>.

**Results**

| **Mass of metal, M** | 0.37 g |
|---|---|
| **Mean titre of hydrochloric acid** | 12.80 cm<sup>3</sup> |

The reaction taking place is shown.

**M**OH (aq) + HCl (aq) → **M**Cl (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

i) The indicator used was phenolphthalein. State the colour **change** at the end-point.

**(2)**

from ........................................... to ......................................

ii) Calculate the relative atomic mass of **M** and use it to identify the Group 1 metal, **M.**

**(4)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) The colour **change** at the end-point is:

- From (pale) pink; **[1 mark]**
- To colourless; **[1 mark]**

ii) The relative atomic mass of **M** and use it to identify the Group 1 metal, **M **is:

- Moles of HCl in titre = 5.12 × 10 <sup>−3</sup> **OR** 0.00512 (mol); **[1 mark]**
- Moles of **M**OH in the flask = 5.12 × 10 <sup>−2</sup> **OR** 0.0512; **[1 mark]**
- The molar mass of **M **= 7.23 (g mol<sup>-1</sup>); **[1 mark]**
- So, **M** = lithium / Li; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *Phenolphthalein will have been added to the conical flask containing the MOH solution which is alkaline*

  - *Phenolphthalein is pink in alkalis *
  - *It will change to colourless at the end point *
- *To identify **M**, work backwards:*

  - *Find the moles of HCl required to neutralise **M**OH   12.8 × *$\frac{0.400}{1000}$* = 0.00512 moles *
  - *The molar ratio of **M**OH to HCl is 1:1 so the moles of **M**OH is also 0.00512 *
  
    - *This is the number of moles in the 25.0 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* portion*
  - *Find the number of moles in the original 250 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* solution 0.00512 × 10 = 0.0512 moles*
  - *You can then use *$\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{\mathrm{number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{moles}}$* to determine the molar mass of **M** *$\frac{0.37}{5.12\times10^{-2}}$* = 7.23 g mol*<sup>*-1*</sup>* *
  - *Find the closest value on the Periodic Table  Lithium = 6.9*

parts.problemMd:

State how this would change the calculated value of the relative atomic mass of **M**. Justify your answer.

parts.problemMd:
Magnesium oxalate, MgC<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>, decomposes on heating to form magnesium carbonate and carbon monoxide.

MgC<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4 </sub>(s) → MgCO<sub>3 </sub>(s) + CO (g)

A 6.0 g sample of magnesium oxalate was heated for three minutes but the decomposition was only 70% complete.

Calculate the total mass of solid that remains.
parts.solutionMd:
The total mass of solid that remains:

- Calculation of mass of oxalate remaining 6.0 × 0.3 = 1.8 (g) will remain as oxalate;** [1 mark]**
- 4.2 g will decompose to carbonate 6.0 ‒ 1.8 = 4.2 (g) will decompose; **[1 mark]**
- *M*<sub>r</sub> of oxalate and carbonate used to give mass of carbonate (4.2 ÷ 112.3) × 84.3 = 3.15 (g); **[1 mark]**
- Final answer 3.15 + 1.8 = 4.95 (g); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Careful: **The total mass of solid that remains takes into account both MgC*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*4 *</sub>*and*<sub>* *</sub>*MgCO*<sub>*3 *</sub>*as shown by the state symbols in the equation*
- *Alternative method 1:*

  - *Calculate moles of oxalate: 6.0 ÷ 112.3 = 0.0534 (mol)*
  - *Calculate 70%: 0.7 × 0.0534 = 0.0374 (mol)*
  - *Calculation of **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of CO and mass lost: 28 × 0.0373 = 1.047 (g)*
  - *Subtract from original mass: 6.0 ‒ 1.047 = 4.95(3) (g)*
- *Alternative method 2:*

  - *Calculate mass that has decomposed: 6.0 × 0.7 = 4.2 (g)*
  - *Calculate moles that have decomposed: (4.2 ÷ 112.3) = 0.0374 (mol)*
  - *Calculate mass of carbonate: 0.0374 × 84.3 = 3.15 (g)*
  - *Addition of remaining solid: 3.15 + (6 ‒ 4.2) = 4.95 (g)#*
- *Alternative method 3: *

  - *M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of CO and oxalate: 28 **AND **112.3*
  - *Calculation of mass of CO: 6.0 × (28 ÷ 112.3) = 1.496 (g)*
  - *70% of mass of CO: 1.496 × 0.7 = 1.047 (g)*
  - *Subtraction of mass of CO: 6.0 ‒ 1.047 = 4.95(3) (g)*
- *All of the alternative methods can score 4 marks *

parts.problemMd:

Describe and explain the trend in the thermal decomposition of Group 2 carbonates.
parts.solutionMd:
The trend in the thermal decomposition of Group 2 carbonates is:

parts.problemMd:
Magnesium ethanedioate (MgC<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) decomposes on gentle heating to form magnesium carbonate and carbon monoxide.

MgC<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> → MgCO<sub>3</sub> + CO

i) State why the thermal decomposition of magnesium ethanedioate should be carried out in a fume cupboard.

**(1)**

ii) After heating a 6.0 g sample of magnesium ethanedioate for three minutes, the decomposition was 70% complete.

Calculate the total mass of the solid mixture that remains.

**(4)**
parts.solutionMd:
i) The thermal decomposition of magnesium ethanedioate should be carried out in a fume cupboard because:

- **Carbon monoxide** / **CO** is (a) toxic (gas); **[1 mark]**

ii) The total mass of the solid mixture that remains is:

- *M*<sub>r</sub> of MgC<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> = 112.3
**AND**
*M*<sub>r</sub> of MgCO<sub>3</sub> = 84.3; **[1 mark]**
- Mass of MgC<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> that reacts: 6.0 × 0.7 = 4.2 (g)
**OR**
Mass of MgC<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> that remains: 6.0 × 0.3 = 1.8 (g); **[1 mark]**
- Mass of MgCO<sub>3</sub> that is formed = (4.2 ÷ 112.3) × 84.3 = 3.15 (g); **[1 mark]**
- Mass of MgC<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> remaining = 6.0 ‒ 4.2 = 1.8 (g)
**AND**
Total solid = 3.15 + 1.8 = 4.95 (g); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *In part (i), you must be clear that it is carbon monoxide that is toxic, so you would not get the mark for saying, for example, that the fumes are toxic or 'it' is toxic*
- *You could explain its toxicity in terms of the reaction with haemoglobin and you would be allowed to refer to carbon monoxide as poisonous*
- *You can break down how to calculate the mass of MgCO*<sub>*3*</sub>* that is formed into two steps:*

  - *Calculate the number of moles of MgC*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*4 *</sub>*that have reacted:*
  
    - *moles = *$\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}=\frac{4.12}{112.3}=0.037399..\mathrm{moles}$
  - *As it is a 1:1 reacting ratio, this is equal to the number of moles of MgCO*<sub>*3*</sub>* produced, so the mass of MgCO*<sub>*3*</sub>* produced is:*
  
    - *mass = moles x **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* = 0.037399.. x 84.3 = 3.15 g*
- *There is an alternative method for calculating the total mass of the solid mixture:*

  - *Moles oxalate calculated:  6 ÷ 112.3 = 0.05343*
  - *Moles carbon monoxide calculated: 0.7 × 0.05343 = 0.03740*
  - *Mass carbon monoxide calculated: 0.03740 × 28 = 1.0472 (g)*
  - *Mass of solid remaining: 6.0 ‒ 1.0472 = 4.95(28) (g)*

parts.problemMd:

parts.problemMd:
This question is about redox chemistry, Group 2 and Group 7.

When chlorine water is added to a solution of potassium bromide, the solution turns orange.

State the changes in oxidation number of bromine and chlorine, and identify which species is the oxidising agent.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The changes in oxidation number are:
> 
> - Chlorine: 0 (in Cl<sub>2</sub>) → −1 (in Cl<sup>-</sup>)
> **AND**
> Bromine: −1 (in Br<sup>-</sup>) → 0 (in Br<sub>2</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> 
> The oxidising agent is:
> 
> - Chlorine / Cl<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> Chloride ions / Cl<sup>-</sup> is not accepted for the oxidising agent

> **[exam-tip]**
> The orange colour in solution confirms Br<sub>2</sub> has formed. Purple colouration would indicate I<sub>2</sub> in cyclohexane, which belongs to a different halide displacement reaction.
> 
> Three errors to watch for in this question:
> 
> 1. Reverse-direction equations:
> 
>   - Br<sub>2</sub> + 2Cl<sup>-</sup> → 2Br<sup>-</sup> + Cl<sub>2</sub> is chemically impossible
> 2. Unsigned oxidation numbers:
> 
>   - Writing "1" instead of "−1" will not score
> 3. Confusing oxidising and reducing agents:
> 
>   - The **oxidising agent** is itself **reduced** (gains electrons).
>   - Memory aid: **OIL RIG** (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain).

parts.problemMd: Describe and explain the trend in thermal stability of the Group 2 carbonates (MgCO<sub>3</sub> to BaCO<sub>3</sub>).
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The trend for Group 2 carbonate thermal stability is:
> 
> - Thermal stability increases down the group
> **OR**
> Decomposition temperature increases down the group **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation:
> 
> - The size/radius of the cation increases but has the same charge (so charge density decreases)
> **OR**
> The calcium ion is larger than magnesium ion **[1 mark]**
> - So the cation is less polarising / distorts the electron cloud of the carbonate ion less (weakening the C–O bond less)
> **OR**
> The covalent character of M–O bond decreases, which distorts the electron cloud of the carbonate ion less (weakening the C–O bond less) **[1 mark]**.
> 
> Vague references to "the ion" without specifying which ion polarises which are not accepted for the second mark.
> 
> Answers that talk about polarising the molecule or atom are not accepted for the third mark

> **[exam-tip]**
> Group 2 carbonate thermal stability is a common paper discriminator. The January 2022 examiner report noted: "We regularly saw 'thermal decomposition decreases down the group'. This response fails to score as it does not refer to either the temperature of decomposition or the thermal stability. Many candidates referred to polarisation of the ion, without specifying which ion was polarising which."
> 
> To score all three marks, state explicitly:
> 
> 1. Cation size increases down the group
> 2. Cation polarising power decreases
> 3. The carbonate anion is distorted less
> 4. A higher temperature is therefore required to decompose the carbonate

parts.problemMd:
A 1.25 g sample of impure limestone is analysed to find its percentage of calcium carbonate by a back-titration method.

![Laboratory setup showing a burette clamped to a stand above a conical flask, both partly filled with liquid, used for titration experiments](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/2-energetics-group-chemistry-halogenoalkanes-and-alcohols/2-5-group-7/assets/001-laboratory-setup-showing-a-burette-clamped-to-a-.png)

The sample is dissolved in 50.00 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.500 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> hydrochloric acid (an excess).

The excess hydrochloric acid is then titrated against 0.200 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> sodium hydroxide solution. The volume required to neutralise the excess acid is 25.00 cm<sup>3</sup>.

[Assume the impurities in the limestone do not react with the hydrochloric acid. *M*<sub>r</sub>(CaCO<sub>3</sub>) = 100.0]

Calculate the percentage by mass of calcium carbonate in the limestone sample.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the percentage by mass of calcium carbonate in the limestone sample:

- Calculate the initial moles of HCl added and the moles of NaOH used (equal to the moles of excess HCl)

moles = concentration x volume (dm<sup>3</sup>)

*n*(HCl<sub>start</sub>) = 0.500 x $\frac{50.0}{1000}$
*n*(HCl<sub>start</sub>) = 0.0250 mol

*n*(NaOH) = 0.200 x $\frac{25.0}{1000}$

*n*(NaOH) = 0.00500 mol = *n*(HCl<sub>excess</sub>) **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of HCl that reacted with CaCO<sub>3</sub> by subtraction:

*n*(HCl<sub>reacted</sub>) = 0.0250 − 0.00500

*n*(HCl<sub>reacted</sub>) = 0.0200 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the moles of CaCO<sub>3:</sub>

  - Apply the 1:2 stoichiometric ratio from CaCO<sub>3</sub> + 2HCl → CaCl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O + CO<sub>2</sub>:

*n*(CaCO<sub>3</sub>) = $\frac{0.0200}{2}$ 
*n*(CaCO<sub>3</sub>) = = 0.0100 mol

- Calculate the mass of CaCO<sub>3</sub>:

mass = moles x *M*<sub>r</sub>

*m*(CaCO<sub>3</sub>) = 0.0100 x 100.0

*m*(CaCO<sub>3</sub>) = 1.00 g **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the percentage by mass:

percentage by mass = $\frac{m \left(CaCO_{3}\right)}{total sample mass}$ x 100

% CaCO<sub>3</sub> = $\frac{1.00}{1.25}$ x 100

% CaCO<sub>3</sub> = **80.0%** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for initial moles of HCl = 0.0250 mol, showing *c* x *V* with volume converted to dm<sup>3</sup>.
> 
> 1 mark for moles of NaOH = 0.00500 mol, correctly identified as the moles of excess HCl.
> 
> 1 mark for moles of HCl that reacted with CaCO<sub>3</sub> by subtraction: 0.0250 − 0.00500 = 0.0200 mol.
> 
> 1 mark for moles and mass of CaCO<sub>3</sub> using the 1:2 stoichiometric ratio: *n*(CaCO<sub>3</sub>) = 0.0100 mol, *m*(CaCO<sub>3</sub>) = 1.00 g.
> 
> 1 mark for final answer 80.0% or 80%, including the % symbol.
> 
> Allow error carried forward across steps: if a step is wrong but the subsequent method is correct, later marks can still be awarded.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The core principle of back-titration is:
> 
> **n(reacted) = n(added) − n(remaining)**
> 
> The most common error is using the titre (moles of NaOH used) as the moles that reacted with CaCO<sub>3</sub>, skipping the subtraction step entirely.
> 
> The CaCO<sub>3</sub> + 2HCl reaction has a 1:2 ratio. Always write out the balanced equation and check the stoichiometry before dividing. A 1:1 ratio is the second most common error in this question type.
> 
> In percentage-by-mass questions, remember to divide by the **sample mass** (1.25 g), not by the mass of CaCO<sub>3</sub> alone.

parts.problemMd:
When chlorine is bubbled through cold, dilute sodium hydroxide solution, a disproportionation reaction occurs.

Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2NaOH → NaCl + NaClO + H<sub>2</sub>O

Explain why it is classified as disproportionation.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> This is classified as disproportionation because:
> 
> - Chlorine in Cl<sub>2</sub> starts at oxidation number 0 and is simultaneously reduced to −1 (in NaCl) **AND **oxidised to +1 (in NaClO)
> **OR**
> The same element (Cl) in the same starting species (Cl<sub>2</sub>) is both oxidised and reduced in the reaction **[1 mark]**
> 
> "Oxidation and reduction in the same reaction" without specifying the same element is not accepted.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Your disproportionation explanation needs three components:
> 
> 1. The **same element** (Cl)
> 2. In the **same starting species** (Cl<sub>2</sub>)
> 3. Simultaneously **oxidised AND reduced**
> 
> A common slip is writing "oxidation and reduction in one reaction." That covers every redox reaction, so it will not earn the disproportionation mark.

parts.problemMd:
Students were set a challenge by their teacher to produce a chemical clock measuring a 20 s time interval. They used an opaque solution that became transparent, allowing a black cross to become visible after 20 s.

![q4-paper-3-oct-2021-edexcel-ial-chemistry](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/2-energetics-group-chemistry-halogenoalkanes-and-alcohols/2-6-introduction-to-kinetics-and-equilibria/assets/008-q4-paper-3-oct-2021-edexcel-ial-chemistry.png)

The students investigated the effect of temperature on their results and plotted a graph.

![q4-2-paper-3-oct-2021-edexcel-ial-chemistry](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/2-energetics-group-chemistry-halogenoalkanes-and-alcohols/2-6-introduction-to-kinetics-and-equilibria/assets/009-q4-2-paper-3-oct-2021-edexcel-ial-chemistry.png)

In this type of experiment 1/t (where t is time) may be used as a measure of the rate of reaction.

i) Calculate the rate at 15°C to a suitable number of significant figures. Include units in your answer.

**(3)**

ii) Sketch a line showing how the rate of reaction varies with temperature for this reaction.

**(1)**

![q4a-ii-paper-3-oct-2021-edexcel-ial-chemistry](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/2-energetics-group-chemistry-halogenoalkanes-and-alcohols/2-6-introduction-to-kinetics-and-equilibria/assets/010-q4a-ii-paper-3-oct-2021-edexcel-ial-chemistry.png)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The  rate at 15°C to a suitable number of significant figures is:

- Calculation of rate: time read from graph = 33 seconds 
**AND** 
1 ÷ 33 = 0.0303; **[1 mark]**
- Answer to 1 or 2 SF: 0.030 / 0.03; **[1 mark]**
- Units s<sup>-1</sup>; **[1 mark]**

ii) A line showing how the rate of reaction varies with temperature for this reaction is:

![rates-graph](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/ial-chemistry-17/2-energetics-group-chemistry-halogenoalkanes-and-alcohols/2-6-introduction-to-kinetics-and-equilibria/assets/011-rates-graph.png)

- Line that shows rate increasing with temperature
**AND**
Line is curved with the gradient increasing; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *The question tells you to use 1/ t to calculate the rate *

  - *Read the value of t at 15 *<sup>*o*</sup>*C and substitute into the equation *
- *Looking at the graph showing how the temperature causes the time taken for the cross to disappear to vary;*

  - *As the temperature increases, the time taken for the cross to disappear decreases*
  - *The higher the temperature, the smaller the decrease in time taken for the cross to disappear*
  
    - *E.g. between 10 and 20 °C, the time decreases from 45 to 23 s, whereas between 50 and 60 °C, the time decreases from 8 to 6 s*
  - *This means that the rate of reaction increases with temperature, and the change in rate is greater at higher temperatures, shown by a curve with an increasing gradient on the rate vs temperature graph*
  - *The change in rate increasing with temperature can be counter-intuitive but you can think about how the rate is calculated to help:*
  
    - *Rate = 1/t*

| > *Temperature / °C* | > *t / s* | > *Rate / s*<sup>*-1*</sup> |
|---|---|---|
| > *10* | > *45* | > *0.022* |
| > *20* | > *23* | > *0.043* |
| > *30* | > *15* | > *0.067* |
| > *40* | > *anomaly - ignored* |   |
| > *50* | > *8* | > *0.125* |
| > *60* | > *6* | > *0.167* |

- *This shows that as temperature increases, the rate of reaction increases but the change in the rate of increase also increases at higher temperatures, giving a steeper gradient*

parts.problemMd: Evaluate the students' results and decide whether it is necessary to repeat their experiments.
parts.solutionMd:
